Gas more vulnerable to disruption: Our commodity strategist notes that the global gas market is structurally more vulnerable to disruptions than the oil market, as there are no strategic reserves. Qatari LNG cargoes cannot be diverted when the Hormuz passage is constrained. The consequences are particularly acute in Asia. Mainland China and India are the biggest recipients of Qatari LNG , while South Asia relies heavily on long-term contracted Qatari supply and has limited flexibility to replace volumes in the short term . Europe would also feel the impact. The market will end this winter with lower-than-expected storage levels, increasing the impact of a disruption in a relatively tight market (see Global macro: Crude reality (4), dated 4 March). Coal may act as a short -term buffer: While some countries may temporarily increase coal use to safeguard power supply during gas supply disruptions, this is unlikely to provide a more durable solution. Coal prices tend to rise during periods of energy market tightness, particularly when gas markets are constrained, prompting power producers to switch fuels (Figure 1). Clients are starting to ask about the risk of hikes. • We see at least three conditions for the Fed to hike: a stable labor market (u-rate <4.5%), further increases in core inflation (core PCE > 3.2%) and Powell as Chair. • These conditions are most likely to be met if the Iran shock is sustained but moderate. This “sweet spot” for hikes is likely within the $80-100 range on WTI. What cuts? Let’s talk about hikes Continued increases in energy prices and hawkish communications from the Fed, ECB and BoE have led to a massive sell-off in global front-end rates. At the time of this writing, markets have nearly priced out Fed cuts through end-2026. Less than three weeks ago, 60bp of cuts were priced for this year (Exhibit 1). Another way to think about market pricing is that investors now see balanced risks of cuts and hikes. Indeed, as we argued around Liberation Day, supply shocks create bimodal risks for policy, depending on whether policymakers are more worried about inflation or the labor market. Recently, clients have started to focus on the possibility of rate hikes. So, what would it take for the Fed to hike? We think it would take a lot. Stronger case for green energy: Rising energy security concerns are likely to prompt a global reassessment of the role of clean power in the energy transition, echoing the shift observed after the Russia-Ukraine war began. To put the scale in perspective, the LNG passing through the Strait of Hormuz (about 82 million tonnes annually) could generate approximately 600TWh of electricity if used in gas-fired power plants. By comparison, additional clean electricity generation globally in 2024 reached 858TWh, according to energy think tank Ember. This highlights the growing ability of clean energy expansion to mitigate the impact of geopolitical supply shocks, in our view. Renewables have become cost-competitive with fossil fuels in many markets (Figure 2). The combination of p eriods of elevated fossil fuel prices and the global fuel supply chain ’s vulnerability further reinforces the economic and strategic appeal of green power, in our eyes. Among renewable power technologies, we think solar is likely to benefit the most. Solar projects typically have shorter construction timelines and more flexible siting requirements, and are increasingly cost-competitive relative to conventional power generation. German consumers, meanwhile, face much slower adjustments in retail prices, courtesy of fully hedged suppliers and typically longer-term fixed contracts. So short-lived spikes get diluted more. But Spain and France are also the economies with the largest shares of (combined) nuclear and renewable energy in their total energy supply (30% and 57%, respectively, vs 20% in Germany and Italy). Beyond the first-round price impacts, their energy mix creates more supply security and less price pressure, relatively speaking. And don’t forget: initial conditions matter for any shock resilience “Initial conditions”, ie the health of the economy, will also matter for the resilience to the shock. The one that stands out here – albeit negatively – is Germany. True, 2025 fiscal innovations are about to feed through to growth, fairly mechanically. But the underlying momentum is bad. Job shedding across the industry and services sectors are a symptom of this. The 2022 energy crisis has created deep and still unhealed scars. So energy prices and supply are arguably Germany’s Achilles’ heel, and we are particularly wary of the risk of non-linear dynamics unfolding here. records.text: Figure 1). On Wednesday, March 18th, Israel attacked Iran’s main energy source infrastructure, the enormous South Pars gas field (Reuters, 18 March). Iran’s retaliation came briefly after, targeting refining infrastructure on the Ras Laffan complex in Qatar, the world’s largest liquefied natural gas plant. QatarEnergy CEO has reported that the facilities hit produce 17% of the country’s LNG exports and it will take three to five years to repair them (BBG, 19 March). The market is now coming to terms with the eventuality that Iran may be playing the long game, similar to China’s strategy during the US-China tariff standoff, and that early resolution can only come if the US declares victory and pulls out of the conflict. Even then, questions remain as to how Israel and Iran would react to that. The targeting of energy infrastructure adds another layer of complexity to the energy picture. Our commodities strategy team now sees Brent move higher in the $110-120/bbl range as their base case, assuming oil flows disruptions last for another 4-6 weeks. They also assign an indicative 30% probability to a bullish scenario with Brent reaching $150/bbl caused by i) a prolonged Strait of Hormuz outage through June 2026 (Figure 2), or further attacks on energy infrastructure damaging supply over the longer-term. The latest leg higher has been led by domestic investors, who are no longer underweight the USD for the first time in a year. Foreign investors are joining in, but this is not a simple unwind of crowded shorts. If it were, foreign flows would be much stronger. Instead, this looks like a recalibration: higher starting rates providing inflation shock insurance, underweights in high‑yielders being reassessed, and carry behaving more defensively than many expected. That combination helps explain why DM carry is holding up, why oil exposure is back in focus, and why USD buying now coexists with risk reduction rather than replaces it. This prompts us to make a handful of changes this week, the most important of which is to add a USD long against the SEK, and to cut out of our long EURGBP position, partly to reduce our GBP underweight to one unit (it is still a high yielder after all) but also to move the portfolio to be net short EUR. records.text: ted 11 March. KEY MESSAGES We don’t expect the three CEE central banks that we met during our recent investor trip to consider policy rate moves (in either direction) until at least H2. We believe there’s no panic among CEE policymakers. ‘Data dependence’ will guide reaction functions. The ECB's own reaction function will also matter. The bar for rate hikes remains high in the region for now, but recent upgrades to our CEE inflation profiles and Middle East tensions currently lean towards our original worst-case scenario. Czech inflation seems to us the most insulated against reflationary risks stemming from higher energy costs, considering the better starting point for inflation and larger growth risks (high beta to Europe). Hungary’s inflation is more exposed to a lengthier conflict scenario, but energy price caps, a cooling labour market and the possibility of a market-positive election outcome next month can help mitigate risks. Polish CPI inflation risks nearing 4.0% by mid-year should energy prices not drop before May. An economy on a stronger footing means policy-rate cuts could already be behind us. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals20 March 2026 ab 29 Global Oil Market UBS Scenario We expect Brent to rise above $120/bbl in the very near term as flows via Hormuz remain very disrupted. If the conflict de- escalates over the course of April and flows via the Strait resume, we see Brent falling back into the $80s by 2H26. We believe that the market is likely to factor in a structurally higher risk premium though, as tensions are likely to linger. Our base case for US shale is activity levels come down, while efficiency gains slow down. We forecast 2026 US liquids growth of 0.1Mb/d. Looking further out, rising efficiency and EVs' increasing impact should see demand growth slow sharply and peak oil reached by 2030, although this is likely to be followed by a long plateau rather than a sharp drop. We expect global spare capacity to decline as non-OPEC supply growth slows down more rapidly than oil demand growth, limiting the negative impact on prices. As investors' focus shifts away from a rising surplus to dwindling spare capacity and the need to rebuild inventories, we expect oil prices to remain supported going into 2027-28. Moreover, it cannot be fully excluded that the disbursement deadline will be extended (as only a qualified majority in the EU Council is necessary). Beside challenges regarding RRF in general, Hungary has not met preconditions for the RRF grant and loan scheme, resulting in 90% of its envelope (EUR 9.5bn) likely to be unused. On 7 March, Moody's warned that Romania's fiscal consolidation efforts are under pressure due to corruption, weak fiscal policy, reform fatigue, and upcoming 2028 elections. Furthermore, we understand that Poland faces significant hurdles due to administrative bottlenecks, including permit disputes and a shortage of project managers, with only a part of funds legally committed. The approach’s strengths are ecosystem dynamism and standard‑setting power. But the trade‑offs are policy variability and reliance on a patchwork of instruments rather than a single statute. This means companies need to plan for continued updates to governance, procurement, and export rules as political leadership changes. The good news is that CPI is still expected to slide down in the coming months. The bad news? Higher energy prices appear poised to lift CPI meaningfully over summer, adding yet another hump in the inflation profile. After a stronger print than expected, we expect CPI to stay broadly steady in February. We see headline CPI coming in at 3.02% y-o-y. Core CPI, we think, will rise to 3.17% y-o-y. Services CPI, we expect, will stay still at 4.36% y-o-y. And RPI, we project, will edge down to 3.67% y-o-y. Where to next? In our view, the inflation outlook has rarely been more uncertain than it is now. The Iran conflict has resulted in a surge in energy prices. Oil prices are tracking nearly 50% higher than pre-conflict levels. Gas futures are trading nearly 90% higher. The impact on the inflation outlook we expect will be meaningful. While we do not account for fiscal support in our updated projections, we think there is a high likelihood that government support can help curb energy inflation. For now, we condition our projections on market expectations as of 18 March. This has pushed our 2026 CPI projections up from 2.4% (in our last update) to 3%, with a peak CPI of nearly 3.2% y

Since AI, or at least generative AI models, is seen as a winner-takes-all or regional winner-takes-all race, companies will need to continue to pursue aggressive capex plans, or else risk falling behind their competitors. This seems to be happening in real time as hyperscalers have continued to revise up their capex forecasts. 3. AI uses will broaden to include tasks that require more energy usage, like image and video generation. According to MIT, energy used by large text models is around 0.931 watts per hour, while AI-generated videos require over 944 watts per hour. records.text: Global Oil Fundamentals20 March 2026 ab 27 5) Would high prices hurt demand? Higher prices could weigh on demand if sustained, although the impact is likely to vary across regions and sectors, depending on a range of factors including storage buffers subsidy, and end-user affordability. In the short term, we believe that oil consumption tends to be relatively insensitive to price changes, so significant adjustments are only likely if prices rise sharply (e.g., above $100/bbl) and remain high, as was seen in 2022. For now, the most direct effect is likely to come through disruptions from limited air travel in the Middle East and LPG shortages. The main risk to demand, in our view, is that ongoing geopolitical tensions could drive inflation higher, lead to stricter policies and financial conditions, and ultimately put downward pressure on GDP . We see this may have wider effects, especially if disturbances from the Middle East extend across global markets. Any change in demand will depend on both the extent and duration of the elevated price environment. Our model suggests that a 1% change in GDP leads to a 0.5Mb/d shift in demand. Based on this, we cut our 2026 demand growth by 0.4Mb/d to 0.8Mb/d, but raise the 2027 estimate by 0.3Mb/d to 1.3Mb/d. In particular, borrowers will no longer be required to maintain Replacement Cost Value policies on their roofs, and instead can opt for the lower coverage option of Actual Cash Value policies. In places like Florida, recurring disasters have coupled with irregularities and litigation to significantly drive up the price of RCV policies. That state has separately tried to address some of the issues via legislation, but roofs have still contributed to the steady and significant increase in insurance costs. Allowing borrowers to maintain a lower standard of insurance helps defray some of those recurring insurance costs, though it also leaves them more exposed in a natural disaster situation. At the time of writing, markets are fully pricing in a hike for June but not April. If the BoE is to hike, we think it would be more natural to do so in April which is a forecast meeting. If the MPC’s inclination is to hike, and its revised inflation pro- file is starting to be validated by then, it's not clear why it should wait any further. We now forecast hikes in April and July, taking rates to 4.25%. We expect inflation will fall back next year, but not until the spring. These scenarios will be published with the staff projections on the ECB’s website. The scenario analysis suggests that a prolonged disruption in the supply of oil and gas would result in inflation being above, and growth being below, the baseline projections. The implications for medium-term inflation depend crucially on the magnitude of indirect and second-round effects of a stronger and more persistent energy shock. The Governing Council will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular, the Governing Council’sits interest rate decisions will be based on its assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. records.text: ld the ECB start to tighten on the back of higher oil prices, we see no room for the EUR to benefit as the market pivots to focus on growth instead. As such, we set the rates spread coefficient to 0 in our modelling for all scenarios except S1, as we doubt that FX will trade higher rates positively if oil rises. Figure 2 shows the output from this modelling exercise where in S1 EURUSD is likely to be stable, according to CLEER . In the worst-case scenario, S4, the model suggests EURUSD could fall by almost 9%, bringing the pair firmly below 1.10. While the effect comes from higher eurozone inflation as well as higher oil weighing on the EUR, in the first two scenarios the overall contribution from relative CPI is still positive as we also expect higher US CPI to weigh on the USD in 2026 (see the latest update of G10 CLEER here). Although the modelling suggests S1 could see EURUSD stabilise, this does not account for the risk premium that will need to be taken out of the pair if oil declines. As such, we think EURUSD is likely to rally even if oil stabilises at higher levels than before in the benign oil price scenario. However, the modelling does underscore the current asymmetry for EURUSD whereby even a stable oil price at current levels could lead to significant demand destruction and given the weakness in the pair. Morgan Operational risk In regulatory reporting, operational risk capital is an individual component of total RWAs, alongside credit risk, market risk, and (if applicable) CV A risk. When calculating overall bank capital ratios, the denominator is the sum of all RWAs. The operational risk capital charge is based on a “business indicator” (BI), which is a function of a bank’s income and expenses (interest, fees, trading, etc.). This capital requirement is calculated at the bank- wide level, and the resulting operational RWAs are part of the bank’s total RWAs for regula- tory capital ratio calculations (instead of being assigned to a specific asset class). To estimate RW for a product, a percentage of the operational risk RWAs can then be assigned to a bank’s business line proportional to the line’s contribution to the BI. The impact of the former tends to be felt quickly, as crude oil priced feed through swiftly to prices at the pump, while utility costs tend to react with delay and necessitate more lasting dislocations in wholesale prices. In the base case of a sharp energy price shock that however fades in coming months, the fiscal costs related to shielding households and businesses look limited to mostly transport fuels and some support for consumers and particularly exposed companies. Our estimate for about €20bn in costs is admittedly a form of educated guess based on these assumptions. The relation between energy prices and fiscal cost is, however, likely non-linear. Once utility bills start displaying more pronounced upside movement, the inflation momentum – and with it, the potential fiscal costs of mitigation – risks changing dynamics. For one, the same factors that mean utility bills can be slow to rise, also means they tend to be slow to fall. Moreover, the cumulative impact on top of that from dearer petroleum products means that spillovers to non-energy prices are more likely. The government might in that moment no longer be able to limit fiscal support to energy-linked taxes and instead need to consider a broader range of tools. How long will the disruption last? How much supply loss will occur during this period? To what extent can oil releases offset the losses? With this oil price note, we discuss some of the potential impacts of the ongoing disruptions in our demand/supply balances. 1) How much oil loss from the Gulf should we expect? Around ~20Mb/d of oil and refined products typically transit via the Strait of Hormuz. Of the total 15Mb/d. of crude oil exports, c5.5Mb/d continue to flow out the region. The UAE is still exporting 2Mb/d of crude to Fujairah, up 1 Mb/d from pre-disruption levels. Saudi Arabia is rerouting close to 5Mb/d of crude to Yanbu. Iran exports 1.5-1.7Mb/d via Kharg Island through the Strait of Hormuz, maintaining volumes. Since alternative bypass routes are limited, these paths continue to carry inherent risks. The few available options for rerouting oil are vulnerable, as seen by recent attacks on the UAE Fujairah oil terminal, meaning there remains a risk of disruptions. Iraq announced it will keep crude production at 1.4Mb/d, (link), 70% lower than usual, primarily to supply domestic refineries and power plants. Even in a stress scenario where Italy/France, for example, repo rates trade close to the MRO rate, we would expect some premium attached to German paper and this should be reflected in relatively less cheapening of German funding rates. Thus, we believe that German repo rates are likely to remain stable and keep swap spreads stable, all else equal. This piece, however, considers risks to long-term prices from the Iran war beyond uncertainty around the timing of Hormuz reopening in light of recent strikes on energy infrastructure. Oil supply could be low for longer if production potential is damaged but higher if OPEC deploys spare capacity after reopening. Apparent demand could be higher on strategic stockpiling but weaker on demand destruction. Risk 1 (Price upside): Low oil output for longer. Looking at the 5 prior largest n supply shocks of the past 50 years, we estimate an average hit to production of 42% after 4 years, often due to infrastructure damage and low investment. Iran and the 7 other Persian Gulf countries produced 3.5mb/d and 21.8mb/d of crude in 2025 (together 30% of global crude). Risk 2 (Limit upside): OPEC stabilization. OPEC could deploy substantial spare n capacity after the Strait reopens to help stabilize tight markets. Risk 3 (Upside): Higher strategic stockpiling. As we set out last week, we see three factors that could shift our view in this direction. First, no fiscal support. This, we think, would push the MPC to hike Bank Rate. Second, growth remaining broadly stable, with unemployment continuing to unwind. The January labour market came with many silver linings with employment back up and the jobless rate staying put at 5.2%. Survey data have also erred on the more positive side, highlighting some cause for optimism. And while GDP disappointed to start the year (i.e. January), we still expect some positive momentum in Q1-26. Should we see positive growth, including unfazed PMI data in the coming months, this could strengthen the case for rate hikes. China’s 15th Five-Year Plan: China’s new five-year plan (2026–2030) charted a medium-to-long-term pathway for developing emerging sectors to achieve technological innovation and cultivate new growth drivers. China will support six ‘emerging pillar industries’: integrated circuits, aviation and aerospace, biomedicine, low-altitude economy, new types of energy storage, and intelligent robots. The country will also develop six ‘future industries’: quantum technology, embodied AI, hydrogen and nuclear fusion power, 6G mobile communications, brain-computer interfaces, and biomanufacturing. The National Development and Reform Commission’s chair said the combined output value of the six emerging pillar industries was close to RMB6trn by 2025 and is likely to double – or even more than double – by 2030, taking the figure above RMB10trn. He also pointed out the future industries are on the brink of a breakthrough and may become the next emerging pillar industries. As expected, the BoC held rates at 2.25%. Governor Macklem highlighted two sided risks in the statement and in the presser but sounded remarkably dovish relative to the other central bankers that spoke over the past week due to the weaker local economic fundamentals. Canada data saw significant deterioration over the last month. Unemployment rose to 6.7%, higher than expected, Q4 employment gains were unwound through February, and more significantly, core inflation came down to 2.3%, now running below target on a 3m/3m basis. Employment data has been particularly cyclical in the past few years as we highlighted before but the overwhelming trend has been lower highs and lower lows, pointing to a weakening labor market that has been marred by tariff shock, immigration changes, and cyclical pressures. The negative output gap, projected at -1%, points to an economy in excess supply. Inflation, which had been a concern for the BoC up until late last year, has been cooling. The BoC is expected to release updates to the core measures soon as part of the annual update. This adjustment may reweight shelter inflation, which would also lead to lower readings. The 15 th Five-Year Plan earmarks US$280bn for national data infrastructure between 2025-30, and the National AI Fund – sized at approximately US$8.3bn – targets investments across computing power, algorithms, data resources, and applications. While this does not mean the government will foot the whole bill for AI development with budget funding, state support is usually a good endorsement of such projects. It means they are then more likely to receive funding from commercial banks and state-backed funds, implying a more stable, committed pipeline of AI capex. China’s state-led vs US’s market-led model Both approaches deliver advantages and carry risks across different time horizons. Given the profound implications of AI, spanning the economy and national security, it is not clear which will be the ultimate winner. In their influential work on war duration, Bennet and Stam (1996) showed that when sides pursue maneuver strategies, wars tend to end quickly, as their rapid success or failure becomes clear. Attrition strate- gies rely upon tearing down the opponent; they are less risky and often last longer (think Russia-Ukraine war). Finally, punishment strategies that attempt to inflict substantial costs on the opponent and erode its resolve (think of guerrilla war- fare) tend to result in the longest wars. In the current war in Iran, the distinction between these strategies, which are well suited to describe land wars of the past, is somewhat blurred. The US and Israel approach is arguably closer to maneuver warfare; Iran’s is perhaps closer to attritional. Model predictions differ substantially depending on the strat- egy. The markets appear to be favouring this scenario. For us, the issue is not yet clear-cut. We agree that the probability of Scenario 1 declines with every day that the conflict continues, pushing us closer to Scenario 2. (In fact, one could even say that the ECB's new baseline scenario looks a lot like Scenario 2.) We hold 10Y swap spread narrowers given RV and potential increased domestic political noise and fiscal uncertainty. • Sweden: 10Y b/m swap spreads have recently widened to their highest level since August 2025 due to fiscal and liquidity factors. While current levels appear fair, we maintain a neutral stance with a medium-term bias for narrowing. • Japan: We maintain a narrowing view with a flattening bias this year in our baseline view. We think the 2s/5s spread curve should remain relatively steep and stable, while 7s/10s should modestly flatten. At the long end, we believe the scope for a widening is limited by fragile demand and fiscal risks, and the risk profile seems asymmetrical, skewed to the narrower side. • Australia: After a substantial widening in AUD term swap spreads we have turned neutral as assumed catalysts have largely played out. Cyclical factors (a front-end sell-off and cash curve flattening) have steepened the swap spread curve, and the AOFM’s issuance downgrade has crystallized a benign supply backdrop. Policy expectations have now repriced sufficiently previous upside risk for the housing market and mortgage credit growth is removed, a key driver of HQLA demand and bank ASW activity. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 20 March 2026 5 Hikes still not granted As a remainder, in our baseline scenario, where we don't expect a protracted conflict, we would still expect ECB cuts in 2027. If Brent and Dutch natural gas prices (TTF) are clearly moving to more "normal" levels, not far from the new baseline, by the June meeting, the ECB will likely look through a temporary inflation shock. If energy prices stay significantly elevated for longer, we would expect 50-75bp of hikes (at most) before the end of the autumn. We still think April is too early, absent further developments, for the ECB to consider hikes. And, we still think that hikes would, under the baseline and adverse scenario, be eventually followed by cuts in 2027. Forecasts: perhaps the bar for hikes is lower than thought The ECB staff projections came with a lot of information – it might take us a little longer to digest them fully. But we would flag a few elements that made us think that while rate hikes are still not obvious, the bar for them may be a little lower than we initially thought. Here are a few main points: • In the base case, headline and core inflation remain above the 2% target for the whole forecast horizon, at least on annual average. End-point headline and core inflation at 2.1% is broadly in line with the ECB inflation target, but that is built with a market pricing of c 40bp of ECB hikes by the end of the year. The BoE had little choice but to sound hawkish into a fresh inflation shock given recent history, and jaw-boning the market is an effective strategy in times of great uncertainty. However, it might not have intended a re-pricing of quite this magnitude. That may be one price of the new individual paragraphs (which have never been tested in a shock having only been used since November). While offering greater transparency, it arguably means less control of the overall messaging as the market reacts to individual comments (in this case referencing hike possibilities). Our read of the overall tone was that it was consistent with a base case to hold for the next few meetings to await more information on the scale, duration, and second-round effects of the Middle East conflict. Governor Bailey later cautioned against “any strong conclusions” about rate hikes (see Bloomberg, 19Mar26). Against that backdrop, the near 50bp of hikes priced over the next three meetings looks an overshoot. Jamie Searle Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: ast since the conflict started on 28 February are large and persistent enough to warrant a change to the euro area macro outlook. As we discussed in Assessing the Middle East fallout, 11 March 2026, the conflict affects the euro area through multiple channels, on both the supply and demand sides. First and foremost, disruptions to oil and gas markets and to key trade routes are a negative supply shock because euro area countries are net energy importers. Hence, this is a negative terms of trade shock, resulting in a transfer of purchasing power to the rest of the world and a negative income effect for domestic households and firms. In addition, shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have declined sharply following the the US-Israel intervention in Iran, with the number of ships passing through the strait now practically zero. A partial or complete blockage that continues creates global supply-chain bottlenecks well beyond the energy complex, in turn, are reinforcing imported inflation pressures in European economies. Based on the increase in Brent oil spot prices and future prices over the coming 12 months (an average of $89/bbl from $68/bbl) and of gas prices for TTF one-month-forward contracts, we estimate a deterioration of slightly less than 2% for the euro area, a significant negative shock about half the size of the terms-of-trade deterioration during the most acute phase of the Russia-Ukraine war. A meaningfully lower inflation starting point than what the NBH had originally assumed in its last forecast update, coupled with the recent fuel price cap announced by the government (which the NBH may assume will remain for an indefinite period in its next forecast update in late March, in our view), means that the NBH is unlikely to present a much worse inflation trajectory than what it assumed in March when it decided to cut rates by 25bp. Equally, however, we think the central bank remains particularly sensitive to global financial conditions and HUF performance. We think that the central bank is now likely to remain on hold until at least H2 2026 – we put our year-end policy-rate forecast of 5.5% under review but maintain that a terminal rate below 5.0% in the medium term makes sense. In our view, the NBH knows that it requires a healthy real- interest-rate buffer but believes that its current ‘mildly restrictive’ stance and the already cooling labour market give it the flexibility to not be (immediately) reactive to persistently high energy prices. At a high level, it seems reasonable to think that the productivity benefits from AI could put upward pressure on forward real rates (higher returns to capital, higher productivity, higher growth, massive AI capex investment), yet simultaneously be disinflationary (a technology- induced positive supply shock). Mechanically, this results in 5y5y CPI underperforming on a beta-adjusted basis, at least using an assumed historical beta. records.text: game changer in terms of replacing the decline in the EU’s exports to the US and China, at a time when the bloc is looking to diversify its supply chains, it does provide an important boost. The EU–Mercosur framework consists of two complementary parts: ▪ a broader Partnership Agreement (EMPA) encompassing political, regulatory and economic cooperation; and ▪ an Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) focused on tariff reduction and market access for goods. Together, they commit both blocs to phasing out progressively import tariffs on about 90–95% of goods over a 10- to 15-year horizon. The agreement also includes provisions on services, public procurement, intellectual property, food safety and dispute settlement mechanisms, while reinforcing shared commitments under the Paris Agreement on climate change. Ratification of the agreement in the EU is still ongoing. The iTA can be applied provisionally as early as May 2026, but the EMPA requires ratification by each EU member state. KEY MESSAGES The EU–Mercosur trade deal could boost Brazil’s GDP growth by about 0.2pp over the medium term, our modelling suggests, mainly by lowering the risk premium of EU investment in Brazil. The short-term impact is moderate and uncertain, though, as EU ratification of the deal could delay its full implementation. The deal’s emphasis on environmental and sustainability standards should create more opportunities for investment and trade, thereby improving Brazil’s investment case. BNP PARIBAS GLOBAL MAR

The BDC index is approximately 80bp wider this year, hovering near 260bp, as concerns about private credit are weighing on sentiment. This represents material underperformance compared with the rest of the investment grade bond market, and even some portions of high yield. This leads us to revisit what we believe is the most appropriate relative value relationship for BDCs: collateralized loan obligations. • Attachment point analysis shows that single-A CLO tranches are the best point of comparison between CLOs and BDC unsecureds. While these two asset classes have many differences, both have investment portfolios of predominantly leveraged loans that are financed with a combination of debt and equity. records.text: 20 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 17 Spain, with its lower excise taxes and higher oil-related energy HICP weight, exhibits a greater pass-through of oil price shocks to pump prices compared to the Euro Area average. This higher beta for Spanish HICP is consistent with historical trends (Figure 26), where Spain consistently had a higher oil weighting in HICP and lower taxes/excise duties (Figure 27 and Figure 28). Conversely, Germany's current higher taxes2 and lower oil-related energy HICP weight (driven by diesel) result in a reduced pass-through. Historically, Germany displayed a higher sensitivity (Figure 26), which has significantly decreased relative to other countries due to increased excise taxes and a decline in HICP oil weight (Figure 27 and Figure 28). Finally, while Italy previously exhibited the lowest beta, this trend has reversed due to lower excise taxes and a broadly unchanged oil weight (Figure 27 and Figure 28). These shouldn’t stop capex, but they should raise the cost and could limit the boost to growth. AI not a big factor in near-term monetary policy We do not expect AI to be a material factor in near-term monetary policy. It is likely to be modestly inflationary due to higher utility prices and a positive wealth effect, but not enough to warrant a shift in policy outlook. Yes, AI could be disinflationary in the long run, but it will probably also raise neutral interest rates by boosting productivity. This could make for difficult policy trade-offs for global central banks. US-China AI race: one goal, two very different approaches The US and China are the two countries competing most aggressively in the AI development race. The US leads in investment, innovation, and frontier models (the most advanced). Meanwhile, China benefits from a coordinated state‑led model, cheaper energy, and dominance in manufacturing capabilities and critical minerals. Mort- gage rates have retraced 23bp of prior declines month-to-date, just as the spring homebuying season is set to get underway. Even before the conflict, improvements in affordability had yet to translate into a meaningful pickup in activity. While a plunge in new home sales in January could plausibly be chalked up to a temporary weather effect, it also coincided with weaker momentum in both the NAHB and MBA builder application surveys at the start of the year. The NAHB survey has improved only marginally through March, and a partial rebound in February pending home sales merely retraced a fraction of the prior two months’ declines. Mortgage purchase applications, meanwhile, fell sharply in February and have only partially recovered in recent weeks. Looking ahead, the reversal of recent declines in borrowing costs and greater economic uncertainty are likely to keep housing demand weak. Persistent inventory shortages in key markets should continue to put upward pressure on prices. ECB Staff projections Growth Given the prevailing economic uncertainty, other than the new projections (the new baseline), the ECB is presenting a two scenario analysis. Baseline Scenario: Lower Growth than December, but Economic Resilience Cushions the Shock. The ECB's baseline scenario is conditioned on the futures prices for energy commodities as of March 11, 2026. Under this baseline, the oil price is projected to peak at around USD 90/bbl and the gas price at EUR 50/MWh in Q2 2026, subsequently declining in the following quarters. For the full year, oil prices are forecast at USD 81.3/bbl and the gas price at EUR 46.6/MWh. These figures represent significant changes compared to the December 2025 projections, with oil prices nearly 30% higher and gas prices 57% higher. Consequently, the baseline scenario projects euro area growth at 0.9% for this year (0.3 pp lower than the December projections) and 1.3% in 2027 (0.1 pp lower than December projections). The projection for 2028 remains unchanged. This revision is largely attributed to a downward adjustment in consumption, primarily driven by a real disposable income shock and increased uncertainty. (The ECB based the uncertainty on the VIX index, assuming an impact of 4 points. To put this into context, in 2022, the VIX rose by more than 10 points when comparing the averages of February 2022 to March 2022). records.text: Michael Metcalfe 18 March 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General One central bank battle after another: ECB vs BOE The 2020s have been unforgiving for central banks. They rescued economies during the pandemic, only to misjudge the recovery, accommodating both the post‑reopening inflation surge and the energy shock triggered by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Having only recently restored rates to something approaching normal, or at least heading that way in the case of the Fed and the BoE, they now face yet another supply‑driven energy shock. Markets have reacted instinctively. The assumption is that policymakers, chastened by 2022, will err on the side of caution: fewer cuts, perhaps none at all. As Alberto Cavallo’s work shows, large shocks now travel fast and the first fifteen days of data since the Iran conflict began bear that out. In the euro area, retail fuel prices are up around 10%, eerily similar to the first two weeks after Russia/Ukraine (Figure 1). Elsewhere, differences in tax regimes and administered prices have muted the rise (Figure 2), but the direction of travel is unmistakably familiar. The key question this week is whether each central bank will respond in the same way as interest rate markets appear to assume. The ECB and BoE provide a useful test. records.text: 19 March 2026 Focus Europe Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG The uncertainties are high. There are scenarios in which the data show little immediate pass-through, the situation in the Middle East dissipates quickly and the ECB can avoid hiking at all. There are also scenarios in which 2.50% policy rates become a staging post for further hikes, perhaps after a pause, if evidence on indirect and second-round effects begins to emerge. The ECB staff ‘adverse’ scenario encompasses a transitory shock with a more rapid normalisation of Middle East energy supply. The ‘severe’ scenario entails a more persistent shock with a latter and slowed normalisation of supply. Given the new attacks on regional energy infrastructure this week, we are arguably closer to the severe scenario in terms of level of disruption (inflation persistence risk), but closer to the adverse scenario in terms of actual energy pricing (level of inflation). Under the severe scenario, the ECB signals a higher likelihood of tightening policy (although, this could be contingent on the fiscal response): “The significant increases in inflation, especially under the severe scenario, would likely be partly offset by tighter monetary policy or fiscal support measures which could lower consumer energy prices – as was seen in the 2022-23 episode of high inflation”. records.text: US Economic Perspectives20 March 2026 ab 4 3. One issue with using a rule of thumb is that it fails to take account of why crude oil prices are rising. An increase in crude oil prices resulting from very strong domestic demand is likely to have a greater inflationary impact than an oil price rise coming from reduced supply. To try to abstract from this issue our rule of thumb is based on holding resource utilization and exchange rates constant. If the higher oil prices lead to a notably slower economy (which is not our forecast currently) then that additional economic slack will have a downward impact on inflation. Additionally, over the past few weeks there has been a small appreciation of the broad trade-weighted dollar that would be a small downward factor on inflation. Overall since last month's US Inflation Monthly we have raised out headline CPI projection for this year (2026Q4/Q4) by 0.51pp largely in response to the higher energy prices. In contrast, our core CPI projection is 0.02pp lower than last month as the small impact of the energy prices that we have put in has been offset by a 0.02pp lower than project February increase and a weakening of our projection for housing rents (based on continued weakness in new tenant rents). If crude oil prices move up more sharply, or stay elevated longer than suggested by the current futures curve ,we will adjust our forecast roughly in line with the rules of thumb above. Almost three hikes are now n priced in the European front-end, reflecting concerns about high and sticky commodity prices — consistent with damage to energy infrastructure that may limit the degree of inflationary relief — and the hawkish tone from the ECB and other major central banks. With central banks signaling openness to near-term hikes — rather than signaling patience in the face of a potentially temporary energy shock — there is likely to be a relatively tight link for market pricing to energy prices over the short term. Pricing is now toward the upper end of our economists’ risk scenarios, and given that each increment of higher energy prices should also lead to a tightening of financial conditions and weaker growth expectations, the hurdle to out-hawk the market from here becomes increasingly challenging. And with de-escalation — even if the path remains unclear — an ongoing risk to lower yields, we favour expressions that lean long with protection against near-term hikes; for example ERZ6Z7 flatteners, overweighted to the Z7 long. records.text: ECB Recap— Calm, Determined and Laser-Focused on the Energy Shock The Governing Council left rates on hold today against the backdrop of a significant further rise in energy prices caused by the ongoing war in the Middle East. Takeaways From Today’s Meeting Our first takeaway is that the staff made larger changes to the projections than we had anticipated. The level of GDP was revised down by 0.3%, while headline inflation was upgraded by a cumulative 1.0pp and core inflation by 0.5pp. This partly reflected the staff using a later cut-off date for the technical assumptions (with higher spot energy prices and futures) than we assumed. But the staff also incorporated stronger pass-through from energy into core prices than we had expected. Second, the ECB’s economic assessment was relatively balanced. On the one hand, it was notable that the Council stated that risks to the inflation outlook were tilted to the upside. On the other hand, President Lagarde emphasised the growth risks from higher energy prices and stressed that there were important differences relative to the last inflation surge, such as the labour market (which is solid but not as hot) and the absence of pent-up demand. Third, Lagarde’s communication on monetary policy was largely non-committal, as we had expected. Parents with ineligible children2 still have the option to open a Frühstart-Rente-Depot but will not obtain any subsidies. As it lays the foundation for private old-age provision, the system relies on a strict lock-in period. The capital is generally inaccessible for consumption until the beneficiary reaches age 67. This 60-year horizon allows for a high equity exposure in the portfolio as multiple market cycles can be ridden out. Short-term volatility would thus have limited impact on the final outcome. At age 18, the government envisages a seamless transition to the new Altersvorsorgedepot. However, even with natural gas prices remaining capped, fuel inflation increases, assuming Brent averages US$80/bbl in 2026 from US$58/bbl previously, will be large enough to push headline CPI to about 11%oya in April from 10% previously expected. The April peak is driven by higher oil along with the removal of the cap on mark-up for staple food. If, however, the mark-up limitation is kept then both core and headline inflation would spike later, possibly around October 2026, without changing the end-26 inflation forecast at 4.7%oya from 4.1% previous- ly. Romania’s inflation stands out in CEE context (Figure 4). Despite the higher forecast for inflation, we still expect the NBR to cut its key rate this year, but possibly by only 50bp instead of 75bp. This deviates from our view for CE3, where we forecast no further rate cuts this year. The reason is that the demand situation in Romania is very weak, with private consumption dynamics far worse than in Hungary, which also has weak growth, and with a negative output gap probably as large as -3% of potential GDP (we agree with NBR on the size of the output gap). GDP growth has slowed sharply in recent years: only 0.9% in 2024, 0.7% in 2026 and 0.5% expected for 2026, with risks of a worse outcome - while we see potential GDP growth at around 3%.

ISM, UBS Box: Rules of thumb for impacts of key economic shocks We usually rely on estimated time-series models to bring in the impact of various factors on our forecast. However, rules of thumb are often useful to give a rough idea of how important a shock is likely to be. Below are a few key rules of thumb that we use:  1 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate pushes down core inflation by 15bp.  Permanent $10 per barrel level shift in the price of Brent crude pushes up the level of CPI by 40bp and core CPI by 4bp.  A one percent decline in the dollar increases consumer import prices by 0.15 percent.  A one percent increase in import prices results in a 0.12 percent increase in core consumer prices.  A one percent increase in CRB spot food index equals about 8bp in prices of food at home with about 2/3rds in the first six months and 1/3rd in the six months after that. Other factors also matter, but we think the type of shock that would correspond to hikes would have the 2026 WTI average somewhere in the $80-100 range. This would be about a 25-50% increase from last year’s average. What would a hiking cycle look like? If the Fed does end up raising rates, we think 75bp of hikes is a reasonable central scenario. The Fed could make a case for taking rates back to where they were before last year’s cuts, on the premise that the labor market has stabilized and upside risks to inflation are similar to last spring. The Fed could also hike a bit less (50bp) or a bit more (100-150bp). But we wouldn’t expect a single 25bp hike in isolation, as that would convey a false sense of precision on policy transmission. We also don’t think a full-blown hiking cycle is in play, since the Fed isn’t as clearly behind the curve as it was in 2022.

Source: Barclays Research This represents the size and composition of AVUC today, but in reality, if a BDC were to default on its unsecured debt, AVUC would look much different at the time of default. This is because of the actions we would expect a BDC to take on its path to default, which would necessarily involve one or more breaches of its asset coverage test. For instance, in the event a BDC is required to post margin on a SPV facility, pledging incremental assets to that SPV would ultimately change the composition of AVUC. Because of the variety of sources BDCs have for liquidity generation (see BDCs: Lots of liquidity levers), and due to the fact that the vast majority of BDCs maintain very modest leverage/asset coverage metrics, we believe the probability of a BDC defaulting on its unsecured debt is very low today. This is corroborated by ratings agencies, given the majority of issuers are rated investment grade. records.text: th had a significant impact on the economy. On a broader note, even if Israel’s conflicts sometimes had limit- ed impact on growth, they nevertheless had a profound impact on the economy through other channels. For instance, decades of stand-off with Arab countries led to the accumula- tion of large debt in 60s and 70s, culminating in a fiscal crisis. Wars also have large opportunity costs due to conscription, delayed entry into the labor market, and loss of human capi- tal. That said, the IDF has been an integral part of the success of Israel’s tech story. Yet, among all the wars Israel has gone through, we think the last year’s 12-day war with Iran presents the cleanest template to the current conflict. It also makes it clear why the duration of the current war plays a significant role in Israel’s near-term outlook. Missile barrages flying from Iran (and Lebanon) present a significant disruption to the operating environment for most businesses and households. Distance learning, work from home, disrupted logistics and air links, call-up of reserv- ists and outflows of foreign labor, delays in investment proj- ects, etc. — all pile up to generate a significant contraction in activity. Back in June 2025, a twelve-day war was associated with a 4.6%m/m decline in BoI’s index of economic activity (Figure 6) and we estimate that it cut around 0.5%pt off the country’s annual GDP. 90 100 110 120 130 140 17 19 21 23 25 27 Index, 4Q16=100 Figure 6: Israeli GDP vs BoI's activity indica

Employment trends also a consideration: One pass- through of higher commodity prices could be via hiring in related sectors. Labor growth alongside rising energy prices should suggest some positive pass-through to households and consumption for energy exporters. For Canada and Australia, we compare job changes in the oil and gas industry to total employment. For higher commodity prices to support energy exporters’ economies, those industries should post stronger job growth. We would caveat that some related industries tend to benefit from indirect effects and hiring might appear with a lag, but as a starting point, labor trends in Canada’s oil and gas industry are broadly comparable to the national total. In contrast, this sector has seen above- trend job creation in Australia. Thus, there again appears to be a disconnect insofar as the current terms of trade shock has been more positive for Canada than for other DM energy exporters. For weekly trades in Q5, the MOVE signal is measured from Friday close to Friday close; we open at the next trading session and close at the end of that week. This separation of signal day and entry day ensures the signal is fully observable before execution. How Are Returns and Risk Metrics Calculated? Returns are computed from the daily percentage change in implied vol for each selected name. We apply the long/short sign to each name’s return and then take an equal-weighted average across the active legs to obtain the portfolio’s daily return. A trade’s hit is recorded when the cumulative return over its full holding window is positive; the hit rate is the fraction of such winning windows. The active-days Sharpe— the headline figure we quote—is the annualized Sharpe computed only on days with active positions, normalized for annualization. All positions are equal notional in vol terms across the three names. Considering the recent dataflow and market movements, we think the new path won’t show any cuts this year. We would expect the path to imply just a slight probability of a hike later this year (towards the end of 2Q/3Q), followed by cuts in 2027. We expected a cut in June this year, we postpone it to 1Q27 Our base case of one cut this year (June) has clearly become too narrow – higher January and February inflation readings and upside energy risks could easily push 2026 CPI averages above 3%. We therefore postpone the cut to 1Q27 (March), when inflation should be back on a more encouraging trajectory. As a result, we now see Norges Bank on hold for the whole year, with two cuts next year and an unchanged terminal rate of 3.5%. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 20 March 2026 3 Australia in Focus Nick Stenner, CFA Merrill Lynch (Australia) nick.stenner@bofa.com Johnny Liu, CFA Merrill Lynch (Australia) johnny.liu2@bofa.com Same shock, different outcomes The macro consequences for Australia and NZ hinge on the duration of the conflict and persistence of the energy shock. While a quick resolution is possible, risks skew toward a longer, costlier conflict. The longer the conflict lasts, the greater the upside risk to oil, LNG and other energy-linked prices. How this energy price shock transmits to Australia and NZ depends on their relative exposure and starting conditions, and they point to divergent macro and policy outcomes, in our view. External exposure and initial conditions matter NZ is more exposed to an oil price shock through imported refined petroleum products as it relies entirely on imported fuel from two countries. Australia is also heavily reliant on imported fuel but has a more diversified import base and a partial buffer from domestic energy production and oil-linked exports that reduce its net exposure. For example, Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal and LNG, so higher prices for these commodities will support national income. records.text: hilst most central bankers are scarred by the inflation shocks and subsequent "late" hiking cycle in 2022, Governor Macklem highlighted that the Canadian economy is in a significantly different position between then and now. Back in 2022, core inflation measures were trending higher, the output gap was close to 0, and there were widespread labor shortages which accelerated wage growth in H2 2022. Guidance also explicitly stated that the bank would look through short term inflationary spikes due to oil, unlike the Fed. Should the conflict resolve soon, we would expect hikes to be priced out and cuts to be priced back in. Should the conflict continue, the paid AU leg should offer some protection to the Canada leg and will depend on the evolution of data. The disinflationary risks from shelter and lower services may offset some of the pressure from oil and Canada's position as an oil exporter with FX benefits may counteract some inflationary pressures. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy Global Swap Spread Outlook 20 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Developed-market swap spreads reflect a blend of macro, policy, and market-structure forc- es that shift across cycles. At their core, they are shaped by the relative dynamics between risk-free government curves and swap rates: front-end spreads are sensitive to central bank policy paths, balance-sheet costs (e.g., SLR/leverage and liquidity regulations), and collat- eral abundance/scarcity, while long-end spreads hinge on term premia, pension and insurer hedging flows, and the supply profile of duration from sovereign issuance. Cross-currency funding conditions and basis markets influence foreign demand for government bonds ver- sus swaps, amplifying moves when FX-hedged yields swing. Dealer intermediation capaci- ty and repo market tightness drive the “plumbing,” affecting the government bond leg via specials and fails, whereas bank funding conditions, and for some countries credit percep- tions, typically embed into the swap leg. Inflows into the factor sit in the 86th percentile over the past 20 days, the strongest reading in nine months. While this result does not hold across EM, carry inflows in DM may be less counterintuitive than they appear. First, FX volatility, the usual carry killer, has risen, but not to crisis levels; our turbulence metric sits only in the 60th percentile. Second, a higher starting point for interest rates still offers some protection against the initial inflation shock. That protection will ultimately depend on how individual central banks respond, but for now the level matters. Third, the USD trend has left investors underweight a number of higher‑yielding currencies, notably the USD itself, while remaining overweight low yielders. Taken together, this combination of carry, oil sensitivity and flows argues for selective positioning rather than wholesale de‑risking. This prompts us to add a long USDSEK trade this week. records.text: 20 March 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Inflation outlook – disinflation detour We recently updated our inflation outlook (see here). The Iran conflict has sent energy prices soaring. At the time of writing, oil prices (Brent) are tracking around 47% higher than they were pre-conflict. Gas prices have risen over 90% during that same period. We conditioned our projections as of 18 March. Where do we see prices going? In our new baseline projections, we base our energy forecasts on the forwards as of 18 March. We do not take into account any fiscal support measures that could reduce energy inflation. But, to be sure, we think more fiscal support is likely. While we do not expect any immediate announcements, we see a high likelihood of policy measures to curb CPI, either through further cuts to policy costs in the Ofgem Price Cap, an extension of the fuel duty freeze (including temporary cuts), and/or a reintroduction of the Energy Price Guarantee (set at a lower threshold than in 2022). Incorporating market energy curves, our projections point to another disinflation detour by early summer. Indeed, the combination of higher pump prices and gas prices will see CPI rising back to 3% in July. The bad news is that energy markets are pricing in a longer uplift to energy prices than before – suggesting more upside risks to our projections. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 18 March 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Risk off and carry? KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Factor surprises. The first half of March has looked textbook on the surface- geopolitical stress, higher oil, a bid for safety - but the cross‑section of DM FX returns tells a more awkward story. Currency performance has been driven far less by data surprises or valuation, and far more by oil sensitivity, investor positioning, and the need to get back to benchmark. Traditional FX anchors in times of stress, current accounts or volatility, have barely registered. Most striking of all, this is not a carry crisis. Quite the opposite. Despite rising volatility, carry adjusted for volatility has attracted the strongest inflows in nine months, sitting in the 86th percentile over the past 20 days. The message is uncomfortable but clear: as long as volatility remains elevated but contained, investors still want to lean into the current level of yields as protection against inflation. Different central bank responses may eventually change this, but for now the higher yielders are winning and that means the USD. The USD finds strength at home. The second surprise has been the nature of USD demand seen so far this month. After a year in which risk‑off coincided with persistent USD selling, the pattern has flipped. The SARB in South Africa, the NBH in Hungary and the CBE in Egypt adopted a more passive stance, allowing their currencies to absorb part of the shock. The CBT in Turkiye, however, maintained the pre‑war pace of nominal depreciation. As a result, while the Egyptian pound, the forint and the rand weakened by 9%, 7% and 6.8%, respectively, the lira moved only 0.6% between 2 and 18 March. These different responses reflect: (1) idiosyncratic fundamental policy orientations; (2) varying macro challenges; (3) differing constraints; and (4) divergent expectations about the duration and severity of the conflict. In Turkiye, the CBT has accumulated a sizable reserve buffer over the past two years. Even after spending around $30bn since the onset of the war, its available FX liquidity for intervention is still around $165bn, including gold. FX stability remains an indispensable pillar of the current policy framework - crucial for sustaining disinflation and keeping resident dollarisation near historic lows. Against this backdrop, the CBT chose to keep the TRY broadly stable even as roughly $30bn of carry trade and short-term inflows were unwound in the first weeks of the war. The methodology proceeds in four stages: (1) VAR estimation, (2) impulse-response generation, (3) variance decomposition, (4) connectedness estimation and (5) frequency-domain filtering. 1. And if the shock is large enough, the Fed will probably be too concerned about the labor market to hike rates. Moreover, a very large supply shock would likely cause enough demand destruction that upside risks to inflation would start to diminish. Conversely, if the BoJ remains on hold for an extended period while the global economy avoids serious damage and other central banks adopt a more hawkish posture to combat infla- tion, policy divergence could drive further yen depreciation. This divergence has already pushed USDJPY from 115 to 160 over the past four years. Additional yen weakness would hit households hard, given their reliance on imported goods and services. If another delay in policy adjustment were to trigger renewed currency weakness, it could also weigh on the administration’s approval ratings. Against this backdrop, we continue to expect the BoJ to proceed with additional rate hikes once conditions stabilize. Category III & IV banks will have AOCI hit CET1: Currently, Category III & IV banks have their capital shielded from gains and losses on securities held in AFS. This protected their regulatory capital ratios in the selloff of 2022, though obviously many banks suffered during the regional banking crisis as depositors and investors became aware of the signifi- cant mark-to-market losses. One other interesting impact that it has had is that it has largely prevented smaller banks from selling these low-yielding securities because doing so forces them to immediately realize the hit to capital that the AOCI filter had protected them from. Over the next five years, they will be forced to linearly realize that loss (assuming no change in rates), thereby removing that disincentive. As we discussed in late 2023, the Category III/IV banks had roughly $450bn UPB of MBS in AFS, held at a 15% discount (fair value/amortized cost). records.text: 14 Europe Economic Weekly | 20 March 2026 depends on whether the SNB follows through, but given the emphasis on FX adjustment versus rate adjustment, we think the prospects for CHF selling are currently higher than 50%. The reluctance to move into negative territory is welcomed. We have made the argument for some time that negative rates are a blunt tool to combat deflation, similar to the experience of Japan. We believe a more activist approach to FX policy is advised along the path used by Singapore. Today’s emphasis on FX adjustment is therefore a welcome step. Given the prevailing global set-up, the resolve of the SNB may be tested sooner rather than later. Whilst CHF has weakened in the aftermath, the global backdrop is likely to limit sustained weakness. We think the cleaner way to express intervention risks is via skew which remains tilted towards CHF calls. One important point which was addressed in the press conference was whether intervention comes into conflict with the US Treasury FX Manipulation criteria. We agree with the SNB when they argue that it does not. Interventions are not being geared to gaining a competitive advantage but to protecting the inflation target. With the headline rate at the bottom-end of the target range, intervention is justifiable on the grounds that it will prevent deflation.

16 Global Economic Weekly | 20 March 2026 Latin America Carlos Capistran BofAS Christian Gonzalez Rojas BofAS Mexico trip notes – Iran conflict won’t stop Banxico Complete report: Emerging Insight: Mexico trip notes – Iran conflict won’t stop Banxico 17 March 2026 We spent two days in Mexico City meeting Banxico, the Ministry of Finance (MoF), the Ministry of Economy, as well as local analysts and investors. The main takeaways are: (1) Banxico will likely continue cutting rates despite the higher uncertainty amid geopolitical tensions; (2) Mexico’s policy mix is shifting to prioritizing growth from prioritizing stability; and (3) Mexico’s preferential treatment under USMCA will likely persist, but underlying uncertainty surrounding the agreement is unlikely to be fully resolved. Iraq (1990). Crude production in 1991-1995 was on average 84% (2.4mb/d) lower than in 1989 as the complete UN ban on all Iraqi oil exports after the invasion of Kuwait in August 1990 led to a collapse in oil revenues, investment, access to technology and infrastructure. Kuwait (1990). records.text: rtant. President Trump has demanded the cooperation of a range of nations in escorting ships through the Strait of Hormuz, but even allies have responded cautiously (March 17, Reuters). The US administration is trying to delay President Trump’s visit to China by a month, and there are no signs of an early resolution to the crisis. Japanese gasoline prices have risen a long way. This is in line with the increase in wholesale prices and originates with the rise in crude oil prices. On March 18, the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy announced that the nationwide average retail price of regular gasoline was a new all-time high of ¥190.8/l (as of March 16). The Nikkei reported on March 18 that the government expects the retail price to rise to ¥200.2/l on March 22, and that it will provide a subsidy of ¥30.2/l (with similar subsidies for diesel, heavy oil, and kerosene). If subsidies remain at this level, the ¥280bn subsidy budget will be used up in one month. An extension for the subsidies could be funded out of fiscal reserves. This would mean crude oil prices remain elevated. The futures market factors in high prices for an extended period, with prices expected to stabilize in April-June. Even if prices are adjusted using subsidies it is unclear how long this situation could be maintained given logistics bottlenecks. While not our main scenario, there is a considerable risk of major disruption. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: Global Synthesis The fate of the Strait As the Iran war enters week four, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to the Gulf's energy infrastructure are keeping energy prices elevated. All core central banks have responded with hawkish communication to the inflation risks, but the ECB and BoJ are most likely to hike rates first. Sun Tzu, Thermopylae and the Strait of Hormuz 'Ground which is reached through narrow gorges, [...], so that a small number of the enemy would suffice to crush a large body of our men: this is hemmed in ground. ' This is how Chinese general Sun Tzu (500 BC) describes in his work The Art of War one of one of the Nine Situations (chapter XI) in which an army can find itself. Even if not a 'ground' but a waterway, the Strait of Hormuz seems a perfect example of such a 'narrow gorge' that Sun Tzu defines as a 'hemmed in' situation. Iranians did not have to have read Sun Tzu to understand the importance of 'narrow gorges' in battle. They needed only to know the military history of ancient Persia: in the famous Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC, the vast Persian army under Xerxes experienced the struggle of trying to overcome a much smaller force of Spartan soldiers who defended the narrow pass of Thermopylae in northern Greece. Today, the tables have turned. records.text: r force strength in related sectors The nature of the shock matters : This rally in oil prices is supply driven, and we find that in this environment typically the correlation between terms of trade and FX weakens . This is perhaps because a supply shock can be viewed as contractionary for global growth, thus weighing on energy exporters given their broader sensitivity to global risk . In contrast, an increase in commodity prices due to demand would most likely be much more positive . Historically we observe that the correlation between FX and terms of trade is flat to worse after supply shocks, but this time around the correlation for CAD has improved while that of AUD and NOK have worsened .

records.text: Outlining the US version of the Basel III Endgame (B3E) The Basel III Endgame represents a full rewrite of the bank regulatory capital RWA framework currently implemented at the international Basel level, now being implemented domestically through the US banking regulatory agencies, the Fed, FDIC and OCC. B3E will replace Basel III Advanced, meaning that the US will have two ratios: 1) US Standardized, which includes SCB; and 2) B3E, which will also include SCB. Given the need to go through the full rulemaking process, the 90-day comment period, and the time to ingest comments and finalize the rule, we expect finalization could occur later in 2026, with go-live not before 2027. Category 1 and 2 banks will be subject to the B3E (for a list of different bank categories, regulations that apply to each category, and which of our covered banks fit into each category, see Exhibit 26). The full rulemaking process consists of five periods, each of which can take up to a number of months: 1) proposal, 2) comment period, 3) regulator review of comments and adjusting the rule for them, 4) final rule, 5) period between rule release and phase-in beginning. By the April meeting, the ECB will have the March final HICP print, the flash April print, the March and April PMIs, the CES and SPF inflation expectations surveys and the next Corporate Telephone Survey at least. The ECB could have enough evidence to act in April. June is also a long time away. Risk management could lower the hurdle for action in April. But there are also scenarios in which the situation in the Middle East dissipates quickly and the ECB can avoid hiking at all. For more discussion, see our ECB reaction. Resetting the top-down euro area macro forecasts: GDP growth to drop to 0.5% in 2026 We recently published two scenarios to help us understand the macroeconomic impact of the conflict in the Middle East. Scenario 1 assumed oil at USD85/bbl and gas at EUR50/MWh (spot prices). Scenario 2 assumed oil at USD120/bbl and gas at EUR75bn. Scenario 1 was a transitory shock that the ECB could look through. Scenario 2 was a much more significant shock with a larger and more persistent overshoot of the inflation target that would likely trigger some ECB tightening. Scenario two entails recession. Our HICP forecasts are updated frequently to reflect the latest energy prices. As published in this week’s latest Inflation Chartbook, we now expect headline HICP at 2.8% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2028. Yet, the uncertainty about the length of this conflict is high, and the signaling on likely war duration is mixed. In this note we take a step back from watching headlines and try to put this conflict into a different perspective. Interstate wars have certain statistical regularities — a fairly small number of observable factors usually make some wars last longer or shorter than others. Below we lay out a few statistical and stylized facts about the duration of interstate wars. We then proceed with a discussion of the importance of war duration for the Israeli economy. Wars are usually brief According to the Correlates of War database, 50% of wars in the past two centuries ended within about five months. Wars lasting less than 30 days have statistically been the most fre- quent (Figure 1). Out of the six wars Israel fought in the 20th century, three lasted less than a month. When it comes to oil prices, one important thing to keep in mind is that prices generally revert. Given this pattern, we doubt that the FOMC would hold off cuts solely on the grounds that y/y headline inflation remains elevated, absent scenarios in which oil prices are still high or ascending. Will the judgmental interventions made by US statistical agencies be reversed in coming months or will they continue to hold down inflation? Recent judgmental interventions have held down the inflation. The first intervention was the use carry-forward imputation done by the BLS to address the lack of data during the government shutdown. This imputation set not-seasonally- adjusted price levels for CPI items that would have been sampled in October equal to their most recently observed value. This effectively set October price increases equal to zero and created a downward bias in the CPI. records.text: 6. Most historical oil spikes linked to geopolitical shocks had a temporary impact but some weighed on equities and bonds for longer. As we wrote before, timing the market impact of geopolitical events is particularly difficult given usually high uncertainty and multiple potential outcomes, including a reversal of the shock. On average, equities recovered after a period of consolidation and the impact on bond yields has been modest (Exhibit 12 and Exhibit 13). In a lot of cases equities recovered quickly alongside oil prices normalising and bond yields generally declined as central banks buffered negative growth impacts - a good example is the Iraq war in the early 1990s. But some lasting energy shocks caused global stagflationary macro conditions and larger drawdowns for 60/40 portfolios like in the 1970s and 2022. records.text: US Economic Perspectives20 March 2026 ab 23 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Price inflation projection through 2028 After stepping down only 0.1pp from 3.0% in 2024Q4/Q4 to 2.9% in 2025 Q4/Q4 we project core PCE price inflation will return back to 3.0% this year as stronger energy prices and continued tariff pass-through offset slightly greater resource slack and slightly weaker inflation momentum. We project that core PCE inflation will rise to around 3.4% in the second quarter of this year before gradually declining to 3.0% by the end of the year. The gradual downtrend should continue in 2027 with Q4/Q4 inflation that year about 2.4% before reaching the FOMC's 2.0% inflation target in 2028. If this forecast is correct, 2027 would be the seventh year in a row that inflation was more than ¼ pp above the FOMC's 2.0% target. The underlying contour of the core inflation projection is a little higher this month in response to the surge in crude oil prices. In particular, we have added some additional strength in the next few months as energy-sensitive industries (such as airfares and package delivery) see price increases, though the crude oil futures price path suggest that most of the upward push will have faded by the end of the year and core PCE price inflation for the year as a whole is only about 0.1pp higher than last month. The clearest message from the statement and Powell was that economic effects of the Middle East conflict are uncertain. As expected, participants revised up their inflation and growth projections, with the median anticipating one 25bp cut each in 2026 and 2027. • As expected, the FOMC maintained the fed funds rate target range unchanged at 3.50-3.75%, amid elevated uncertainty, little change to labor market conditions, firm inflation readings and upside risks to the inflation outlook. • The statement, updated projections and press conference emphasized uncertainty and provided little clarity about the course of policy in upcoming meetings. Powell showed little conviction around the updated projections, emphasizing that "we just don't know" how geopolitical events will evolve. • As expected, the statement repeated that uncertainty about the economic outlook "remains elevated, " adding new language that the effects of developments in the Middle East on the economy are uncertain. It largely retained the characterization of economic conditions. Forward guidance continued to tie additional rate adjustments to "incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks" . • The sole dovish dissent sent a somewhat hawkish signal. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 20 March 2026 Citi Research 4 ‘Estimating’ Credit Quality The vast majority of private credit issuers are private companies borrowing from a narrowly defined lender club. As a result, fundamental information is severely limited for anyone outside of the lender group. One window into credit quality is provided by Standard & Poor’s which supplies credit estimates for roughly 3500 middle market and private credit loans. Estimates should not be confused with ratings, even though they both use similar scales. The former is expressed in lower case letters (e.g. b+, b, b-, etc.) and the latter uses upper case letters (e.g. B+, B, B-, etc.). Unlike ratings, estimates are requested by private credit managers, often for CLOs. Therefore, the growth in private credit CLOs in recent years assisted the growth in the number of private credit estimates. Estimates typically incorporate factors such as leverage, coverage, scale, etc. In other words, estimates employ similar factors that determine ratings for the public markets. The estimate starts with three years of audited financials that S&P requires. However, the agency does not have access to corporate management like it does for issuers obtaining credit ratings. The typical issuer in the credit estimate universe is a sponsor-backed, highly levered entity with a median EBITDA of $30mn.
