We compare performance of high disruption-risk loans to listed equities on the same names and found that equity markets seem to be showing greater dispersion in tech and services, with YTD declines in healthcare signaling potential downside to come in loan markets . Finally, we revisit the key indicators that we are watching as the AI cycle deepens. The BofA Vol Connectedness model seeks to serve as a leading signal for vol levels, as our historical back test results indicate that the normalized sum of all pairwise connectedness estimates (henceforth referred to as vol connectedness) Granger causes the average level of 3m ATM vols in EMFX up to 21 days out, but not the other way around – i.e.: knowledge of vol connectedness levels today can help forecast levels of vol levels a month ahead, but today’s vol levels do not help us forecast future vol connectedness. This suggests that connectedness can serve as a leading directional signal for EMFX vol markets. Specifically, vol connectedness can potentially provide systematic directional signals that help identify when (i) EMFX vol is likely to mean revert, and (ii) global shocks are likely to propagate into EM vol. Vol connectedness plays two distinct and complementary roles: 1. Early-warning / Mean-Reversion Timing: When connectedness across EMFX vols is low, our backtests suggest that the asset class has behaved in a more idiosyncratic, segmented manner. Historically, these periods have marked cycle bottoms in EMFX vol, with elevated odds of a rebound. records.text: 20 March 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Modelling retirement wealth scenarios To illustrate the impact of the proposed Frühstart-Rente on old-age provision, we have modelled potential outcomes based on a European stock portfolio with a lifecycle approach. This means that an investor starts with 100% equity and gradually shifts the portfolio towards fixed income when approaching retirement. The assumed annual return for the stock market proportion is based on the average net return of the Stoxx 600 Europe between December 2005 and December 2025 (6.2%), while the return for the fixed income share is based on the average return of the German bond index REX within the same time frame (1.88%). It measures the total performance of German government bonds, which is a conservative benchmark considering the 2010s were a decade with often negative interest rates. For simplicity, we disregard potential administrative and management fees in this simulation. We assume an average annual return of 6.2% (100% equity) between the ages 6-55, a return of 5.1% (75% equity, 25% fixed income) between the ages of 56-61, a return of 4.0% (50% equity, 50% fixed income) between the ages 62-64 and a 3.0% return (25% equity, 75% fixed income) from 65-66. A net neutral fiscal intervention specifically aimed at reducing inflation - temporary direct tax hikes aimed at funding temporary indirect tax cuts and caps in utility bills - would, in turn, ensure lowered measured inflation, would not be adding demand into a global energy supply crunch, and would leave more room for the BoE to act in a growth-supportive manner. This would leave us more constructive on UK fiscal, growth and inflation. However, we don't see any signs of a policy intervention being designed in such a fashion as of now. At this point, we see the downside risks to UK growth and fiscal outlook as at their most severe since early 2023, amplified by a central bank that seems to have guided the market towards a hike as early as April. While our base case is for a hold this year, we can see a path whereby the BoE attempts some front-loaded tightening in financial conditions, only to have to carry out a series of hikes with headline inflation rising in the summer. This is to say, for any comfort around our base case of no near-term hikes, barring the resolution of supply issues related to the Strait of Hormuz, we would want to see a clearer pushback against market pricing by Bailey, Breeden and Ramsden. We are also focused on any commentary by Chancellor Reeves in the coming days and weeks.

records.text: 3 Insights SPOTLIGHT CHARTS Resilience, holding on? The 2025 playbook taught us that disruptions to flows into risky assets, as captured by our Behavioural Risk Scorecard, were buying opportunities. One might therefore assume hopes of a similarly quick and durable rebound in the face of 2026’s shock. But the hurdles today are bigger, and last year’s resilience is now a risk. Perhaps the biggest challenge is that, after a prolonged run of risk‑seeking in 2025, there are now far more significant overweights across risky assets—equities, equity beta, risky fixed income and EM. Risk off and USD buying Prior to 2025, periods of weaker risk appetite were typically defined by USD buying in our risk scorecard; indeed, we flip the sign on USD holdings as an input of risk appetite. 2025 was unusual. When investors reduced risk between February and April, they were also heavy USD sellers, seeking to establish an underweight in the currency. A year later, risk‑off is once again coinciding with USD buying. This may reflect a return of the USD’s safe‑haven status, but it could also reflect a desire on the part of investors to get back to benchmark. USD data decoupling The USD’s usually tight link to US data surprises peaked in mid‑December and has been weakening since. The bond market, in contrast, appears to be paying more attention. records.text: Chair Powell’s press conference emphasized limited conviction about the near‑term policy path, stressing that the Fed does not yet know how geopolitical developments will feed through to inflation and activity and that policy is well positioned to react. Much as in January, additional cuts are likely to be being conditioned on evidence that monthly inflation is receding to target-consistent levels, particularly for goods prices. The updated SEP showed modest but important shifts. Participants boosted headline and core inflation projections for 2026 and revised up medium‑term GDP growth, alongside a higher estimate of trend growth, while the unemployment path was little changed. If anything, upward revisions to inflation were underwhelming, implicitly assuming that the current oil price shock will prove short-lived and that there will be little inflationary momentum from the elevated core PCE price prints in January and February. records.text: GEMs Viewpoint | 19 March 2026 3 What exactly we measure (and why) Our preferred statistic for connectedness, is the share of the near-term variation in each EMFX vol series that can be explained by shocks in other currencies. Operationally, this is the sum of the off-diagonal elements in a standard connectedness matrix built using EMFX 3m ATM vols (see Exhibit 2 and the Methodology section for more detail). Intuitively: the larger the off-diagonal mass, the more “global” the vol regime; the smaller it is, the more idiosyncratic (local) the regime. We smooth the daily readings to get a stable signal and then use the indicator in two complementary ways: a) As a regime filter: During periods of high connectedness, global factors tend to drive EMFX vols more so than individual idiosyncratic stories. In such regimes, we place more weight on our top-down, global view than our bottom-up signals. b) As an early-warning signal for vol mean-reversion: Our backtests suggest that connectedness troughs lead subsequent rises in vol (much more so then vol level- derived mean-reversion signals), making them useful early signals for long-vol expressions. Thus, when our connectedness signal sits in the bottom quintile, we treat it as a tactical “go-long EMFX vol” condition and focus on the names that screen cheapest. records.text: The impact of new entrants on aggregate S&P 500 valuation would also be smaller than many investors may expect. The impact on valuations was also a common investor concern ahead of Tesla’s addition in 2020. While S&P 500 constituents are weighted according to their free float market caps, valuation metrics such as price to earnings are calculated as an aggregate of its individual constituents rather than a cap-weighted average. For example, the S&P 500 P/E multiple is generally calculated as total constituent market cap divided by total constituent earnings. Mathematically, this calculation is equivalent to an earnings-weighted average of constituent P/E multiples, rather than a market cap-weighted average. As a result, even if a new entrant composes a large share of S&P 500 market cap and trades at an elevated valuation multiple, if it accounts for a relatively small share of index sales or earnings it will not meaningfully alter aggregate index valuation metrics. We expect corporate demand for equities will easily outweigh the sizable supply from issuance in 2026, although net demand will likely decline relative to the last few years. S&P 500 buyback growth has stalled in recent quarters, and the dollars of buybacks have struggled to keep pace with market cap, leading to a decline in the net buyback yield for the S&P 500. Higher inflation On inflation, two channels would be at play. On the one hand, higher energy costs would push prices up directly by raising production costs and, if persistent, indirectly through second-round effects via wages. On the other hand, weaker demand from higher energy bills could, however, dampen broader price pressures through the economy. Thus, the extent of the inflationary shock will depend on how these forces offset each other. As a result, the ECB will carefully monitor any signs of an increase in the frequency of firms repricing products, which could signal second-round effects. These include the euro area PMIs (24 March and 23 April), the Consumer Expectations Survey (27 March), the Survey of Professional Forecasters (4 May) and the Corporate Telephone Survey (mid‑June), alongside other high-frequency indicators such as commodity prices. In response to higher oil prices, the Japanese government has decided to release strategic petroleum reserves (SPR) and restart gasoline subsidies. Japan initially released 15 days’ worth (around 27 million barrels) of private sector crude oil and petroleum product reserves on 16 March, out of a combined public‑private SPR equivalent to 254 days of consumption. In addition, the government restarted gasoline subsidies on 19 March (providing subsidies to refiners through an existing JPY280bn fund), fully covering any portion of gasoline prices above JPY170. However, depending on oil prices, there is a risk that fund balances and contingency reserves could be depleted, necessitating additional fiscal measures. For example, in reaction to the 2022 Ukraine war, gasoline subsidies totaling JPY5.5trn were funded through a supplementary budget (JPY1.2trn), contingency reserves (JPY1.3trn) and a second supplementary budget (JPY3.0trn). Refer to important disclosures on page 23 to 24. 12949395 Global Economic Weekly Food for Hawks Global Letter: Food for Hawks As largely expected, the Fed, ECB, BoE, and BoJ all remained on hold. But the focus was on communication, with an across-the-board hawkish shift driven by the Iran war. Markets took notice, with zero cuts priced in for the Fed for remainder of the year, and more than 50bp of hikes priced in for the ECB and the BoE. Likely because of initial conditions, BoJ pricing is the exception to this move. The question is whether all this repricing is warranted. In our view, markets seem to be focusing mostly on inflation, while more disruptive scenarios for growth appear to be underpriced. US: What cuts? Let’s talk about hikes Markets have nearly priced out Fed cuts for the year. Clients are starting to ask about the risk of hikes. We see at least three conditions for the Fed to hike: a stable labor market (u-rate <4.5%), further increases in core inflation (core PCE > 3.2%) and Powell as Chair. These conditions are most likely to be met if the Iran shock is sustained but moderate. This “sweet spot” for hikes is likely within the $80-100 range

records.text: bsent the energy shock, two-sided risks might have kept ECB rates at 2% for longer than we originally thought. The energy shock changes the outlook. In and of itself, the energy shock is highly uncertain in terms of the evolution and duration of the conflict, but also the status of energy output from the Middle East. There is a growing concern that attacks on regional energy infrastructure could lead to a more persistent disruption to global energy supply and, hence, higher energy costs for longer. The path of inflation is highly contingent, but on today’s oil and gas prices and forward curve, HICP is likely to jump to 2.7% already in March, 3.2% in April and 3.5% in May. That will be the peak, but inflation will remain above 3% for the remainder of the year, averaging 3.0% in 2026 and falling back to 2.2% in 2027. Core is expected to average 2.3% and 2.2%, respectively. It is the prospect of core inflation remaining sticky above the 2% target — a slower and possibly incomplete convergence to target on account of indirect and second-round effects – that we think will drive a risk management policy response. There are obviously increasing downside risks to growth. But assuming the current inflation outlook holds – it can change quickly – we see the ECB hiking rates this year. Given the risk of inflation persistence, we now expect the ECB to hike rates to 2.50%, the upper end of the range of neutral. This would send a message of commitment to price stability as inflation rises

At the Fed, Chair Powell emphasized unusually high uncertainty and little conviction on the outlook, stressing that policymakers “just don’t know” how geopolitical developments will feed through to inflation. That caution was reflected in the March SEP , which showed modest upward revisions to trend GDP growth alongside higher inflation projections for 2026–27, underscoring growing concern about achieving price stability despite a firmer growth backdrop (see here). ECB President Lagarde stressed upside risks for inflation, while the BoE's Bailey said that he "stands ready to act" if inflation surges. Sharp moves in front-end rates. Two-year government yields were higher across the globe as investors started to price in the effects of higher energy prices on inflation, limiting central banks' abilities to lower interest rates. Futures markets are pricing in no cuts from the Fed in 2026 and 2.5 rate hikes from the ECB and BoE by year-end. In fact, 2y GIL TS are up almost 90bp since the start of the war, and 2y Bunds up more than 50bp. Two-year US Treasuries were also up 50bp until a large reversal late Thursday (now only up 42bp since February 27). The move in rates has caused financial conditions to tighten considerably. records.text: prices on growth, we use a measure based on work from Hamilton (2000 and 2009)1. This work found that the relevant transformation of oil prices when mapping to growth outcomes is to consider the current price level relative to the maximum price over some lookback period (e.g., over the past one or three years). The logic of this meas ure is that, over time, economic activity and decisions adapt to a new level of oil prices. As such, it takes oil prices rising above some recent level to adversely impact economic activity and potentially trigger a recession. Two versions of this metric are shown in the following figure. For any oil price level that does not hit the threshold – i.e., at the maximum price level over the past year or 3 years – the value of the indicator is set to 0. The positive values represent the percentage above the prior maximum for the oil price at that point. This measure introduces a natural non-linearity into oil price shocks, where any price level less than the maximum over some lookback period has zero effect and then the effect kicks in once that maximum level is exceeded. As can be seen in the chart, there is a reasonably close correspondence between the value of this oil price shock measure and past US recessions. 1 James D. Hamilton, "What is an Oil Shock?," NBER Working Paper 7755 (2000) . James D. Hamilton, 2009. We would identify CAPEX as one such cause - exporter economies should be able to benefit from the surge in energy prices if CAPEX has improved for those related sectors. The mechanism through which we think this works is returns from higher commodity prices are then recycled into more future capex, thus creating a positive growth cycle. This was the case in the first half of the 2010s, where capex was increasing across the G10 commodity bloc, leading to terms of trade being a strong driver of FX. In contrast for the latter half of the decade, as capex declined, then the FX terms of trade relationship weakened. In other words, exporter currencies were not able to benefit to the same extent from higher commodity prices because the income was not being put to work domestically. However now, capex is starting to rise again. This could help rationalize why CAD has had an improved correlation with terms of trade now relative to prior supply shocks. That being said, the capex trend has been seen in both Australia and Norway as well. As a result, it appears inconsistent that the terms of trade correlation has been stronger for CAD this time around while weaker for AUD and NOK. Employment trends also a consideration : One pass through of higher commodity prices could be hiring in those related sectors. records.text: US Rates Weekly 20 March 2026 Citi Research 11 G-SIB surcharge reform proposal As we discussed last week (US Rates Weekly: Front-end positioning squeeze), yesterday the Fed released the proposals to complete the implementation of Basel III and to make changes to the G-SIB surcharge calculation. The G-SIB surcharge proposal came largely in line with what Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman discussed last week. If approved, the proposals would result in reduction of capital requirements, for the systemic banks this would mostly be due to the G-SIB surcharge reform. The market reacted favorably to the proposed regulatory changes, and we saw 5y swap spreads widening on the news (see Figure 21). On the G-SIB proposal, the biggest differences from the 2023 proposal are the changes to the method 2 coefficients and the calculation of the short-term wholesale funding (STWF) component. On the coefficients, regulators are proposing a one-time adjustment to account for economic growth, in Figure 22 we report the current coefficients as well as their proposed adjustments. Additionally, going forward the coefficients will be indexed to GDP and adjusted annually to prevent future distortions, specifically if the economy expands the coefficients would be adjusted, but if the economy contracts the coefficients would stay the same. We estimate that if MAE increases by 0.1pp, the probability of de-anchoring would rise by 8pp. A de-anchoring scenario driven by shock persistence also appears unlikely at this stage, as it would require the shock not only to persist but also to do so without materially weighing on growth. records.text: 20 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 15 Euroland Strategy HICP oil sensitivity on the rise Given the magnitude of market moves in the wake of the recent events in the Middle East, the focus has been on the inflation implications of rising energy prices. While higher energy production costs can be expected to have relatively broad-based indirect - and potentially second round - effects on consumer prices, most of the immediate inflationary impact comes through direct effects on consumer energy prices. The magnitude of the oil pass-through varies over time and depends on (i) the sensitivity of retail energy prices to changes in wholesale prices and (ii) the weight of oil-sensitive energy components - fuels for transport (petrol and diesel) and liquid fuels (heating oil) - in HICP; it has risen noticeably this month. Retail fuel prices are composed of crude oil, refining margins, various distribution costs and margins as well as of taxes and therefore do not move one-for-one with changes in wholesale prices. In the Euro Area, taxes in particular account for a large share of retail prices1 , around 50-60% over time for petrol and diesel, somewhat lower for heating oil (Figure 21 & Figure 22). We estimate that in the case of petrol and diesel 60-70% of taxes are excise duties, which are levied per litre of fuel, i.e. are independent of the level of market oil prices, with the remainder mostly being VAT. We see the Fed path as asymmetrically tilted toward cuts In sum, for financial markets to think the median path for monetary policy is for the Fed to stay on hold between now and the middle of 2027, it must be assigning roughly equal probabilities between rate hikes and rate cuts. In our view, the Fed rate path remains asymmetric, with our baseline and downside scenarios carrying more probability-weighted rate cuts than our upside scenarios have probability-weighted rate hikes. We suspect a nontrivial amount of movement in the US rates market is due to position squaring instead of outright views on monetary policy, which often happens when risk limits are tested by periods of heightened volatility. Of course, for market pricing to reflect our view, someone has to put on that trade, and in current conditions, some reluctance to do so is clearly understandable.

Steepeners as the dominant strategy The results show that swap steepeners are the dominant strategy, as steepeners show not only the highest Sharpe ratio across strategies but also were positive in the aftermath of the shock, albeit at lower levels (see Figures 2 to 6). KEY MESSAGES By examining the Sharpe ratio of various trading strategies across Latam FX, swaps, local bonds and cross currency basis in past oil shocks, we identify steepeners in swaps as the prevailing approach, as the yield curves steepen during the shock, keeping the same bias for two months after oil prices reach a peak. 1s5s steepeners in Mexico, Chile and Colombia emerge as consistently strong performers both during the shock and in its aftermath. There is a similar pattern in paying 5y outright, however, the strategy tends to show strong reversions once oil prices reach a peak. In FX, a short CLP position delivers the highest performance in our analysis and remains consistent across periods in the post-event window, although the overall performance of FX trades lags behind rates or bond alternatives. records.text: US Outlook Thick fog, twitchy markets The main message from this week's FOMC meeting was uncertainty, with Powell characteristically reluctant to send concrete policy signals amid intensifying fallout from the Iran conflict. But markets are in no mood to await clarity, with futures moving quickly to boost the likelihood of rate hikes. • This week brought notable changes to pricing of the Fed's expected policy path, with traders• unwinding positions amid intensifying uncertainty about the Iran fallout. Market pricing no longer anticipates Fed cuts this year, with risks now weighted toward hikes. We think this is overdone, as we have a hard time seeing supply issues undermining broader disinflationary pressures on core for long. • The market move seems disproportionate with the cautious messaging from this week's• FOMC meeting, which emphasized uncertainty and provided few concrete signals about the Fed's next steps. The dot plot continued to show a 25bp cut this year and next, amid elevated inflation and a productivity-strengthened GDP trajectory, with Powell showing limited conviction in the dots. • We lack hard data since the onset of the conflict, but indicators on hand continue to suggest• that the economy will post above-trend growth in the current quarter, in the vicinity of 3.0% q/q saar, as activity rebounds from last year's shutdown. German governments of either political leaning have in the past not hesitated to pull fiscal levies if shocks were seen as both meaningful and genuinely exogenous. Moreover, as discussed earlier, the starting position is weaker this time around, both in terms of retail energy prices, but perhaps more importantly also in terms of industrial resilience; high energy prices are frequently cited as one of the structural reasons behind the multi-year decline of German manufacturing. And finally, coalition politics will, ultimately, nudge the government into more support than current CDU rhetoric lets on. What form would fiscal support take? Economic theory voices a strong preference for supporting incomes, effectively a decrease on the average cost of living for households or production for businesses, rather than limiting price increases, in order to preserve the price signal mechanism to dampen demand (and attract supply where wholesale markets are concerned). Germany’s policy of paying households and businesses the difference between the costs of energy and a reference price, but only on 80% of their consumption (70% for businesses) above certain usage threshold is an example of such an income support policy. For a direct, fundamental view, we utilize quarterly data from BDCs, which report non-accrual and Payment-In-Kind (PIK) interest utilization. Instead of relying solely on the non-accrual rate, we created a "BDC Stress Indicator" by combining it with the PIK utilization rate. While companies may switch to PIK pay from cash pay for many reasons, it can be the first clear sign of distress, preceding a formal non-accrual classification. In addition, our analysis found an optimal lag of 5 months. records.text: But we are sceptical that the ECB would only hike once, as it has rarely done so historically and because its updated strategy calls for it not to respond to moderate supply-driven deviations of inflation from target. We instead expect the Council to lean against inflationary pressures by maintaining a hawkish communication. Our baseline forecast therefore remains for the Council to keep policy on hold this year and next. Our simulations suggest that the ECB would need to hike 50-75bp in the staff’s adverse scenario, where energy prices continue to rise and significant second-round effects into core inflation emerge. That is consistent with our very adverse scenario, where we would expect the ECB to hike by 75bp with sequential 25bp steps from June (with an April start possible). We believe that the probability of this hiking scenario has risen given the continued upward pressure on energy prices in recent days. A further escalation of the conflict (for instance, with more destruction of energy infrastructure) could bring the economy closer to the ECB staff’s severe scenario, in which our analysis would call for 100bp to 175bp of policy tightening. In such a situation, the Council would likely start to raise rates in April and make use of 50bp increments. As more countries join the con- flict, it prolongs wars — war aims change, bargaining space narrows, coordination gets complicated. So far, the GCC, Türkiye and Azerbaijan have shown restraint despite Iranian attacks. • Proxies. A weaker player often resorts to horizontal esca- lation of the conflict — new geographies, new actors — and asymmetric warfare. Signaling on relative capabilities gets noisier, bargaining gets more complicated, and the conflict gets extended. Hezbollah has opened a front in Lebanon. The Houthis and Iraqi militia have so far remained restrained; Kurdish militias have also not entered the scene. • Credible commitment. War is a costly bargaining mecha- nism, yet a mutually beneficial settlement is elusive when at least one side cannot credibly commit to adhere to a potential agreement. Decades of a standoff have left little trust between the sides — the US and Israel will doubt Iran’s commitment regarding nuclear and missiles pro- grams, Iran will doubt the other side’s commitment to avoid future attacks. This creates incentives to build deterrence (by inflicting higher costs), which takes time. Index-level loan spreads have widened by nearly +50bps YTD but have traded sideways since the Iran conflict at 504bps and below our year-end forecast of 610bps. We think that there is more repricing to come.

Asian assets broadly sold off since the onset of the US– Israel–Iran conflict, as oil prices rose and the DXY surged back above 100. The initial risk -off move was most pronounced in FX, while Asian equities and bonds managed a modest rebound over the past week amid hopes that tensions could ease by end -March, following comments from the Trump administ ration. Despite this stabilization, real -money sentiment remains highly defensive. Outflows persisted across all EM asset classes over the past 5 -day, 10 -day, a nd 20-day windows, with 17 out of the 20 EM FX we track experiencing net outflows. Against this backdrop, we assess which Asian economies are most exposed by taking a deeper dive into oil reserve adequacy, energy’s contribution to total inflation, balance -of-payments dynamics, and foreign appetite for domestic assets. We believe the magnitude of price action over the past two weeks has not fully reflected differences in underlying fundamentals. As a result, we have made marginal adjustments to our EM Asia relative-value trades, replacing long CNHINR with long TWDINR, while retaining our long SGDIDR position. Source: Citi Research Stagflation becoming less of a wildcard. Stagflation defined by our quant macro- team would involve oil prices around $150, a 30% probability according to our oil strategists. We have discussed previously the difference between a stagflationary environment and a stagflationary impulse. A point that Chair Powell made with reference to the 1970s (and we did in Quantitative Global Macro Strategy - Stagflationary Vibes). Using our regime classifications, we see two flavors of stagflation, neither of which is close – one where financial conditions meaningfully tighten and one where they do not (“transitory” inflation is looked through). So far central banks and market-pricing is leaning towards a tightening in response to this potential supply shock (stagflation with tightening). Despite the fact the economic data is far from these readings, the bull case from our commodities team ($150 Brent, 30% probability) and our economists’ estimates of the potential growth impact would likely bring such a regime in sight. records.text: Monetary Policy | Changing our call: The ECB kept rates on hold at today's meeting. A good starting point with inflation around target and neutral rates allows the ECB to wait and see how the Middle East situation evolves while inflation risks are seen to the upside. Recent further increases in energy prices, spot and future, have made rate hikes more likely in that context. We change our call and expect the ECB to raise rates in June by 25bp, followed by another 25bp hike in September. Faced with lower growth, we think the ECB will likely cut rates again in June and September 2027 to 2%, bringing rates back to neutral territory. Projections | Asymmetric impact on inflation vs growth: As new set of projections was presented today. By pushing the cut off date to 11 March, the ECB locked in an energy price path that already looks soft relative to current market levels, especially for oil. Even so, the baseline shows meaningfully higher inflation - with core above 2% across the whole forecast horizon. The impact of higher energy prices on growth is modest instead. The asymmetry in the inflation increase vs growth hit in the ECB's alternative scenarios only reinforces our impression of the ECB's view on the current balance of macro risks: adverse growth effects are meaningful but short lived, while inflation risks are larger and longer lasting. The Reconstruction Bill reveals the full scope of the Kast- Quiroz strategy: a supply-side tax restructuring (CIT, V AT, capital gains, contributions), offset by expenditure compres- sion (the 3% transversal cut plus gratuidad limits), and cush- ioned by a short-term demand stimulus (the 12-month hous- ing V AT waiver and employment subsidy). The logic is coherent and the political sequencing—wrapping the agenda in a reconstruction narrative—is shrewd. However, the fiscal arithmetic is tight. The bill simultaneous- ly introduces multiple revenue-reducing measures (CIT cut, property tax phase-out, capital gains exemption, temporary V AT waiver) while projecting savings primarily from expen- diture cuts whose specifics remain thin. Quiroz himself acknowledged that tax reductions must proceed gradually to maintain credibility, framing the strategy as one where pri- vate-sector investment should front-run the formal rate reduc- tions if the government’s commitment is to be believed. The MEPCO fiscal drain adds a material exogenous risk that could crowd out reconstruction spending. records.text: The equity market impact of proposed index inclusion rule changes Several major index providers have recently discussed the possibility of modifying requirements for index eligibility in anticipation of large IPOs expected in 2026. The proposed changes primarily relate to the minimum length of “seasoning” time between IPO and index eligibility as well as minimum float requirements. Both Nasdaq and FTSE Russell have launched public consultations seeking feedback regarding the potential methodological changes. S&P Dow Jones Indices has not launched an official consultation, but news reports suggest the provider is considering similar changes, and S&P recently wrote a blog post on the topic. The flagship benchmark indices for each of the three providers mandate seasoning periods between IPO and index eligibility but could potentially allow for fast-track additions in the future. Under the new proposals, Russell would move from assessing sufficiently large new IPOs on a quarterly basis to allowing for potential inclusion following 5 trading days. Similarly, for sufficiently large candidates, Nasdaq would remove its current 3-month seasoning requirement and provide a notice period of less than a month. S&P currently requires 12 months of trading post-IPO before a company is eligible for inclusion into the S&P 500. records.text: 19 March 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Asymmetric risk and transitioning from “good place” to “good base” For the past several months President Lagarde has described the policy stance as being “in a good place” at 2%. In other words, the policy stance was appropriate, there was no signalling of imminent change. At the March press conference, Lagarde said “We are starting from a good base. So I’m not saying that we are in a good place”. There is a change. A “good place” left open the possibility of policy moving in either direction. A “good base” is not a commitment to hiking. But the new wording is consistent with 2% policy rates being a floor. In other words, the risks are skewed towards hikes. Updating our ECB call – hiking from 2% to 2.50% Pre-conflict, we had been expecting the ECB to keep policy rates unchanged through 2026. We had expected the next move to be a hike in mid-2027 on the assumption that the risks to inflation rotate from near-term undershooting in 2026 (e.g., FX appreciation, China competitiveness) to medium-term overshooting from 2027 (e.g., German fiscal easing, tight labour market). Pre-conflict, there are a lot of moving parts and uncertainty was high, and it was becoming a bit less obvious that tailwinds would necessarily dominate headwinds. Absent the energy shock, two-sided risks might have kept ECB rates at 2% for longer than we originally thought. The energy shock changes the outlook. This is in contrast with Fed pricing of 24bp of cuts in 2026. We’re not quite sure that this is justified. Geopolitics creates fatter tails for the path of monetary policy, but starting points matter. In the US, inflation has been above target for over five years, which has begun to prompt some concern from policy makers. In contrast, Canada has seen inflation recently within the target range. When considering the labor markets, only the Fed has a dual mandate but the US unemployment rate is fairly stable . In contrast, Canadian job data remains soft, as observed for instance in the February labor force survey, which makes tightening monetary policy difficult. As a result, it is difficult to see the BoC “out hawk” the Fed. We consider two cases going forward. If central banks are required to turn more hawkish, there is more space for Fed cuts to be removed from here but likely little more that can be added to hikes for the BoC. Conversely, if there is a material hit to growth where the Fed is required to cut interest rates, there are likely negative spillovers into Canada that can see the current hikes removed from the curve. Amid a week of hawkish central n bank communication that emphasized the importance of inflation vigilance, the BoC ended up on the dovish end of the spectrum, noting the favorable starting point of inflation and downside risks to growth from trade, with a willingness to “look through” the energy shock. Our economists continue to expect BoC to remain on hold for the year and see a higher hurdle for hikes compared to a number of other G10 central banks. That relative stance, however, was not really reflected in the repricing of the policy paths throughout the week, with CAD 1y1y in line with peers for the week (Exhibit 2), potentially offering cross-market opportunities against markets where we see a more credible risk of hikes, such as the Euro Area. While the macro backdrop for Canada—a less severe growth hit given its position as an energy exporter, but similar inflation upside as peers—suggests less room for differentiation, we think the difference in reaction function should matter. While a front-footed approach potentially inflicting more growth damage should richen terminal relatively, a willingness to see through the shock calls for more risk premium further out and should skew a bit more towards belly cheapening than in other markets (for example Australia, see below). records.text: Goldilocks faces a balanced bear — assessing and managing 60/40 drawdown risk 1. Markets started the year ‘risk on’, boosted by the prospect of a ‘Goldilocks’ scenario of sturdy global growth, further declines in inflation and continued policy support. Our Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) shifted above 1 for the first time since 2021 to one of the highest levels since the 1990s. Since then a combination of concerns about AI disruption, private credit and more recently sharply higher oil prices and the Middle East war has weighed on risk appetite. Sharply rising oil prices have driven increased investor concerns about a worsening global growth/inflation mix and a sharp hawkish repricing of central bank policy paths. This has weighed on multi-asset portfolios with a limited opportunity set for diversification - the risk of a larger 60/40 portfolio drawdown (a ‘Balanced Bear’) has increased. We shifted tactically more defensive in our asset allocation shortly after the conflict escalated (OW cash, N equities/bonds/commodities, UW credit). We continue to see risks of further equity correction and think the buffer from bonds will remain limited near term. With current macro conditions and our baseline of a normalisation energy prices from Q2 we think the risk of a sustained, large 60/40 drawdown is still limited. To try to scale the potential risk in CPI terms, a simple chart of food CPI y/y alongside North American fertilizer prices y/y (with an 8m lag) shows a pretty strong positive correlation. Running a parsimonious OLS regression, we find an intuitive and statistically significant relationship (Figure 8). A few key nuances to highlight: • The R2 of the relationship with CPI food is quite low, at 0.16, implying that other factors influence food prices, not just fertilizer. As expected, fertilizer has better explanatory power for CPI food at home (R2 0.21) than CPI food away from home (R2 0.02). ° Yet past instances of fertilizer price shocks (2007-08; 2010-11; 2021-22) have all been followed by an acceleration in food-at-home CPI. This is because fertilizer prices tend to be pro-cyclical, ie, higher when demand is robust, and tend to respond to the same global shocks (energy/supply disruptions) that affect costs through the food value chain, including transportation and processing, which are more directly inflationary. For the third consecutive year, Chile missed its structural balance target— this time by as much as 2.5% of GDP, the worst deviation in the framework's two-decade history. The 2025 shortfall is particularly troubling because it occurred in the absence of the usual suspects for driving poor fiscal performance: no pandemic, no commodity collapse, no external financial cri- sis. Instead, the miss reveals something more insidious— chronic revenue overestimation, structural spending rigidity, and a fiscal rule losing credibility. President Kast’s sweeping Reconstruction Bill, of which some details were unveiled last week, promises supply-side tax cuts financed by expenditure compression. But in our view the fiscal arithmetic is tight, and three years of broken promises have left little room for error. Cyclical deterioration may trump discretionary effects on deficits Fiscal policy took time to respond in 2022, and it might take even longer this time. True, Italy has implemented a temporary reduction in pump prices of EUR 25 cents per litre for 20 days (perhaps the political calendar helped that), but elsewhere, fiscal moves remain niche. Absent a suspension of EU fiscal rules (or at least talk thereof), large-scale fiscal support is unlikely. Consequently, we would focus more on the impact of weaker growth on deficits than potentially small and targeted discretionary fiscal measures. Non-energy related agenda items: France and Italy go to the polls The Italian constitutional confirmatory referendum on reform of the justice system and the second round of French municipal elections take place over the weekend, with the risk of creating some headlines. In Italy, the referendum outcome is seen as a potential trigger for speedier (though unrelated) electoral reform implementation and, if so, risks of an earlier general election than the regular 2027 calendar. We are not convinced of that argument and would caution against drawing firm conclusions on the back of this weekend’s referendum result. In our view, this would be a very negative outcome for credit spreads; JULI reached 168bp in March 2022 under the dual impact of a hawkish Fed and the Russia-Ukraine induced oil spike. We believe the odds of this scenario reoccurring now are relatively low given Fed Funds is 350bp higher and additionally the chairmanship is on the verge of transitioning from Powell to Warsh but a known known in this scenario would likely be a sharp equity selloff, as has happened in many a past oil spike scenarios. Which leads to a key known unknown which is how would pensions react to a backdrop of lower equities but higher rates, which in theory is fertile ground for pension derisking trades. It is notable in this regard that the pension funded ratio ended February at 109.4%, the highest since July 2001. We estimate that this has moved up to approximately 111% MTD given the sharp move higher in yields. Thus, at least in theory pensions are currently in an ideal position to entertain derisking activity

The EUR impact around the statement was mildly negative across the board, reflecting the ECB’s broadly balanced tone relative to a rather hawkish market pricing. There was less to see around the press conference, with Iran headlines dominating the FX price action. We do not think a balanced ECB stance is necessarily bad for EUR. Into the ECB meeting client feedback was (partly) conflicting: some thought a hawkish ECB could support the EUR temporarily, whereas many feared a potential ECB over-reaction and the negative growth implications thereof. Our short-term views remain that 1) oil prices will likely continue to trend higher while Hormuz flows remain very low, 2) Brent is likely to exceed its 2008 all time high if depressed flows keep the market focused on the risk of lengthier disruptions, and 3) any rise in market perceived risks of US export restrictions is likely to widen the Brent-WTI price gap further. This Oil Analyst focuses on the long-term outlook. Our base case is that a gradual recovery in flows in April leads to a moderation in Brent to the $70s by 2026Q4, but we next consider risks to long-term prices from the Iran war beyond uncertainty around the timing of Hormuz reopening in light of recent strikes on energy infrastructure. On the supply side, oil production could be low for longer if production potential is damaged, but higher if OPEC deploys spare capacity after reopening. On the demand side, apparent oil demand could be higher on an acceleration in strategic stockpiling but weaker on demand destruction. Risk 1 (Price Upside): Lower Potential Oil Output for Longer While the Hormuz shock is the largest oil supply shock on record, we analyze the persistence of oil production losses for the 5 largest supply shocks of the past 50 years (Exhibit 1). Looking across episodes, we estimate an average hit to production of 42% after 4 years (Exhibit 2), although there are large differences across episodes. Early cancellations are emerg- ing as costs surge. Petrochemicals face input shortages: con- strained Gulf naphtha and LPG have forced run cuts, force majeure, and prioritization across Japan, Korea, China, Tai- wan, Indonesia, and India, linking upstream feedstock scarci- ty to downstream production curtailments (Oil Flash Note, Mar 19th). Global commodity positioning firmed last week as esti- mated open interest rose 3% WoW to ~$1.9tn and net investor length increased 13% WoW to $194bn. Energy led the move as OI climbed 6% to $885bn and higher crude pric- es outweighed modest contract outflows. Natural gas OI fell on softer benchmarks. Net length rose on crude and TTF, while agriculture strengthened on corn and soy. Precious met- als saw $10bn of inflows into gold, lifting sector OI 1% to $352bn, though base metals were mixed with gains in alumin- ium and lead offset elsewhere. Environmental positioning edged lower. In macro terms, higher energy prices are feeding a near term bump in global headline CPI even as growth momentum holds near 3%, and DM central banks are leaning more hawkish as they balance stickier inflation against activi- ty (Commodity Market Positioning & Flows, Mar 17th). Iran may allow select Chinese and Indian tankers to tran- sit the Strait of Hormuz, but the relief to LNG supply would be minimal.

We would identify energy industry capex as one such cause – exporter economies should be able to benefit from surging energy prices if capex has improved for related sectors. The mechanism through which we think this works is that returns from higher commodity prices are recycled into future capex, thus creating a positive growth cycle. This was the case in 2010-2015, when increasing capex across the G10 commodity bloc led to terms of trade being a strong driver of FX. In contrast, as capex declined over 2016-2020, the link between FX and terms of trade weakened. In other words, energy exporters’ currencies could not benefit to the same extent from higher commodity prices because the income was not being put to work domestically. However, capex is now starting to rise again. This could help explain the CAD’s current improved correlation with terms of trade relative to prior supply shocks. That said, the same capex trend has occurred in both Australia and Norway as well. Even though oil prices will surely boost headline inflation prints in the coming months, we still think that the most reasonable baseline is deceleration in monthly core inflation prints later this year, opening the door for additional cuts that push the policy rate toward the median FOMC participant's assessment of neutral. This reflects a mix of complementary influences, including deceleration of goods prices as remaining level effects from tariffs peter out, some further slowing in housing rents, and a gradual decline in ex-housing service inflation (supercore) amid tame wage pressures. In our baseline, this all occurs against a backdrop where consumer demand is gradually losing some momentum as it adjusts to the slowed pace of labor market income—hardly fertile ground for a sustained inflationary shock to take root. To be sure, scenarios involving no cuts cannot be ruled out. The most plausible path to this likely involves core inflation prints more sluggishly elevated than in our baseline, perhaps extending into this autumn or later. In our view, this might arise if the remaining tariff effects play out more gradually than in our baseline, if the pass-through of high oil prices to core inflation is stronger than we expect, if war-related shortages of fertilizers and other critical inputs temporarily boost costs, or if supercore remains elevated for reasons unrelated to slack (such as a rising stock market). Given that BDCs are effectively income pass-through vehicles, the inability to pay dividends would be a material event and immediately bolster capital through earnings retention (to the extent the BDC is still profitable). This mechanism is not dissimilar from CLOs, in which failure of the overcollateralization (OC) test (discussed in Estimating the Software Selloff Effect on BSL CLO Spreads) causes interest that would have otherwise been paid to more junior tranches to be diverted toward redemption of more senior tranches until the test is cured. What this means for a BDC, though, is that failure to comply with the asset coverage test could result in a surrendering of its RIC status, since it cannot pass through the requisite 90% of taxable income to shareholders.6 Loss of RIC status means that the BDC would also become a cash taxpayer, forgoing the beneficial tax treatment that allows it to avoid paying entity-level federal income tax. That said, an asset coverage test breach is not necessarily considered an event of default for unsecured creditors. However, it can be considered an event of default under certain of their secured facilities. So while there is a significant amount of equity cushion beneath unsecured creditors when assessing their balance sheets on a consolidated basis, the negative implications of a BDC's breaching its asset coverage test leads it to become a binding constraint for how it manages its balance sheet.

records.text: GEMs Viewpoint | 19 March 2026 15 together across currencies are discounted as common noise rather than bilateral spillovers. For example, if ZAR’s residual shocks have high variance but also exhibit strong covariance with the rest of EMFX, the FEVD will interpret a “ZAR shock” as largely reflecting a global volatility impulse rather than a ZAR-specific driver. Conversely, if THB’s residuals show low covariance with other currencies, an innovation in THB is treated as genuinely idiosyncratic, and its contribution to other currencies’ forecast uncertainty is attributed cleanly to THB rather than to a shared disturbance. 4. From GFEVD to Connectedness Once the GFEVD has produced the full matrix of variance shares, showing how much of each currency’s forecast error variance is attributable to shocks in every other currency, connectedness is the summary of this matrix. Mechanically, the off-diagonal entries represent cross-market spillovers, while the diagonal entries represent own-market share. Our connectedness measure takes the sum of all off-diagonal entries (the spillovers that come from other currencies), which captures how much of the system’s forecast uncertainty is driven by cross-market interactions rather than idiosyncratic shocks. records.text: r in the week, a temporary uptick in repo levels emerged, driven by a sizable $81bn coupon settlement on March 16, which briefly pushed SOFR up to 3.70%. However, the pressure proved short-lived, as SOFR quickly retraced to 3.65% (flat to IORB) by March 17—suggesting the market absorbed the supply with little friction. Into the most recent closes, SOFR is now at 3.62%, while tri-party repo has traded closer to 3.60%, supported in part by the typical GSE period where cash enters the repo markets. That said, given the lack of any change to the Fed’s balance sheet operations, repo markets should remain orderly in the coming weeks. With ongoing RMPs and the seasonal T-bill paydowns, repo rates should remain broadly contained. Slight pressure may surface around quarter-end, coupon settlement periods and the April tax date, though should likely be short- lived rather than sustained. We will have to wait until the next RMP schedule is announced or the FOMC minutes (4/8/26) to see if there are any changes to the Fed’s balance sheet.

External outlook to be shaped by oil prices In estimating the March trade deficit, we have not assumed a surge in oil imports, given the lag between global crude prices and realized import values. From April, however, higher oil prices should feed through to oil and gas imports. Given India’s large oil bill, a $10/barrel change in crude typically widens the CAD by roughly 0.5% of GDP. Natural gas imports are smaller (~$14 bn/year), with 80–85% tied to long-term contracts, limiting price volatility; the primary issue is supply, including LPG, with Middle East disruptions as alluded to above. Given India’s close ties to the Middle East, the external out- look will hinge on oil prices and developments in the US–Iran conflict. Beyond oil, remittances and goods/services exports are important transmission channels. The BoP implications extend beyond the CAD: elevated oil prices could weigh on the macro backdrop and keep portfolio flows—especially equities—under pressure until prices stabilize, complicating CAD financing and keeping BoP conditions tight. If energy prices stay elevated for longer (which current energy future prices suggest), risks of cuts not materializing this year will rise. The BoE also opened the door to hikes. We still the BoE would need to see a larger and more persistent shock to be convinced to hike, given the economy/ labour market is weak, risks of second round effects are less than before, and rates are restrictive. Having said that modest hikes cannot be ruled out after today’s guidance with the bar somewhat lower than what we thought before this meeting, though still high. The BoE has noted that a larger or more protracted shock, which risked greater second round effects can increase risks of a hike. A scenario where BoE sees inflation move much higher or stuck above 3.5%-4% for long (rest of this year/early next year) can increase risks of second round effects and open the door to a hike. It is unclear however if we would have enough evidence by the April meeting that we are in a scenario to warrant a hike. Key would be data on inflation/wage expectations and further information on the likely scale and duration of the conflict. An extended hold/hike may be followed by deeper cuts in 2027 once the energy price moves stabilize as the BoE would have to contend with medium term growth and labour market implications of this real income shock.

Under its central scenario – which takes into account energy moves through 16 March – headline inflation was revised sharply higher, with upgrades of up to 0.7pp in some months of 2026. This also reflects headline CPIF already running c.0.5pp above the Riksbank's forecast from December, even before recent events. As for CPIF excluding energy, the Riksbank revised its profile c.0.2pp lower in 2026 and kept the 2027 projection at 1.7%. For 2026, this is largely a mark-to-market exercise: CPIF ex-energy was already running about 0.4pp below the forecast, suggesting that the Riksbank sees only a partial offset from the indirect effects of higher energy prices. On activity, revisions were fairly modest: 2026 growth was marked slightly lower, from 2.9% to 2.5% (calendar unadjusted), while the 2027 projection was revised 0.1pp higher to 2.6%. Pairwise connectedness is directly given by the individual off-diagonal entries themselves. In effect, the GFEVD provides the granular variance-share accounting, and the connectedness indices are structured aggregations of those shares, summarising how tightly coupled volatility is across EMFX and identifying which markets are transmitters versus receivers of volatility risk. Suppose Exhibit 24 represents the 10-day GFEVD for a three-currency system (BRL, ZAR, THB). This shows that 20% of BRL’s forecast error variance comes from ZAR shocks, while 5% comes from THB shocks. BRL’s recipient share is the sum of these spillovers (25%) showing BRL is exposed to the rest of the panel. On the transmitting side, the ZAR column shows that ZAR shocks account for 20% of the VAR forecast-error variance in BRL and 15% in THB, giving ZAR a 35% transmission score vs a 13% recipient score (estimated by ZAR’s row sum), making ZAR a net transmitter of volatility. THB shocks, by contrast, explain only 3–5% of variance in the others’ forecast errors while 20% of the variance in THB’s forecast errors can be explained by ZAR and BRL shocks, making THB a net shock recipient. The higher risk premium and need to refill inventories mean that we see prices staying higher through 2027. We leave long-term unchanged at $75/bbl from 2028. records.text: US Economic Perspectives20 March 2026 ab 3 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research An interesting few months ahead Often when previewing inflation over the next three to six months there are one or two questions that stand out as the likely dominant drivers of that path (even though ex-post the driver is often something that was not expected). This month the number of potential drivers looks larger than usual. We see 5 questions that likely will be key to the path of US inflation in coming months: 1. How high will crude oil prices go and how long will they stay elevated? 2. Will tariff pass-through continue at the gradual pace of recent months and for how long? 3. Will vehicle prices accelerate? 4. Will the judgmental interventions made by US statistical agencies be reversed in coming months or will they continue to hold down inflation? 5. Will the core CPI and core PCE prices continue to have oddly different inflation trends? While we do not have definitive answers to these questions, we discuss each question in turn and provide some guidance. Regardless of whether we are right or wrong, the next handful of months will be interesting from an inflation standpoint as these questions become resolved. 1. As more countries join the con- flict, it prolongs wars — war aims change, bargaining space narrows, coordination gets complicated. So far, the GCC, Türkiye and Azerbaijan have shown restraint despite Iranian attacks. • Proxies. A weaker player often resorts to horizontal esca- lation of the conflict — new geographies, new actors — and asymmetric warfare. Signaling on relative capabilities gets noisier, bargaining gets more complicated, and the conflict gets extended. Hezbollah has opened a front in Lebanon. The Houthis and Iraqi militia have so far remained restrained; Kurdish militias have also not entered the scene. • Credible commitment. War is a costly bargaining mecha- nism, yet a mutually beneficial settlement is elusive when at least one side cannot credibly commit to adhere to a potential agreement. Decades of a standoff have left little trust between the sides — the US and Israel will doubt Iran’s commitment regarding nuclear and missiles pro- grams, Iran will doubt the other side’s commitment to avoid future attacks. This creates incentives to build deterrence (by inflicting higher costs), which takes time. Bottom line: although most wars do end quickly, when regime‑survival incentives, asymmetric adaptation, and the history of conflict (devaluing commitment) all show up together, the right tail of the duration distribution gets heavier. Aside from our view that the ECB will not hike to the same extent as the 450bp it did last time, there were four factors that exacerbated the beta of 10y BTP-Bunds in 2022: 1) Political pressure was significant in 2022, culminating in the eventual resignation of Prime Minister Mario Draghi in the summer. The moves in July 2022 alone widened 10y BTP-Bund spreads by 40bp. 2) Italian debt/GDP was much higher, close to 150%, which exacerbated debt sustainability concerns; today, we are around 135%. The primary balance in 2022 also stood at a 4% deficit, whilst the last numbers for 2025 show a 0.8% surplus. For debt sustainability, the primary balance is key. For a given level of interest rates and GDP growth, the level of primary balance surplus needed to stabilise debt/GDP for Italy, in a range of scenarios, is very achievable, we argue (see Figure 3 on prior page). 3) The ECB has the Transmission Protection Instrument this time around to contain spread widening. Indicating its willingness to activate it should limit the extent of the moves, we think. 4) Italy’s credit rating was lower in 2022. Back then, Moody’s rated Italy at Baa3 with a negative outlook, one step from being rated below Investment Grade. records.text: The hawkish impulse from central banks has driven front-end rates higher, reflecting inflationary risk from higher energy prices as well as the absence of sufficiently strong growth concerns. US rate pricing looks hawkish versus the distribution of risks around our economists’ Fed path, and the continued selloff in terminal rate pricing seems misaligned with the nature of the shock and a market that is pricing Fed credibility. But the market needs an external mechanism—either deescalation or stronger growth downside—for lasting relief to materialize. We remain cautious on carry—be it vol selling or spread longs—despite improved valuations given the risk that opening the left tail around growth would present. The ECB and BoE paths now price hawkish outcomes, following central bank openness to near-term rate hikes and further commodity price upside. Both markets look over-priced vs our scenario analysis, however with front-ends tethered to energy prices the route to relief is harder to see in the near-term. We think growth concerns will ultimately stabilise forward rates, and—at least while hawkish risks remain—flatten curves. We raise our 10y Gilt forecasts for end-2026 to 4.4%. Japan rates have remained generally resilient, but are vulnerable to scenarios where growth downside concerns remain contained alongside a weak JPY. Moreover, the Commission’s framework includes the indirect benefits arising from liberalized services trade and other non-tariff barriers, elements that are absent from the current NiGEM configuration. Finally, changes in the trade composition between the two blocs are not accounted for. The level of net trade will increase gradually albeit moderately for Brazil, our modelling suggests, as both exports and imports grow over time. For the eurozone, there is an initial boost to exports, but after a decade this is more than offset by imports increasing, according to the model. Trade elasticities suggest bigger impact on Brazil: Adopting a different approach using estimated export- and import-price elasticities for Brazil, the EU– Mercosur deal translates to a 1.8% boost for Brazil’s exports to the EU and a 1.2% boost for imports from the EU, our analysis suggests. Introducing this trade-shock as an exogenous impulse in a four-variable VAR (real GDP, real exchange rate, exports and imports) yields an impulse-response pattern in which the effect on output is absorbed fully within 10 years, with negligible feedback on inflation or the exchange rate. The cumulative impact on real GDP growth over the 2030–2040 horizon is therefore about 0.20pp, we estimate, which confirms that the agreement functions as an integration shock that expands bilateral flows on both sides rather than a pure export boom. The current conflict contains elements of both trajectories. Near‑term dynamics could still deliver a short campaign, but the tail risk of a multi‑month conflict is non‑trivial. Macroeconomic impact on Israel Israel’s economic history is inseparable from conflict. That can shift, but it first requires the growth tail to become sufficiently pronounced and durable—either via a more consistently negative risk asset response to higher oil (Exhibit 1), and/or a clearer sign of labor market deterioration—with that higher hurdle reflecting the weaker diversification benefit of nominal bonds amid a supply shock. From what we know today, we believe the most likely path is for two 25bp hikes, in April and June. With the energy shock already underway and sizable upward revisions to the inflation path, such a move seems optimal. Moving the depo rate to 2.5% would take policy rates to the upper limit of the neutral range, which would be justified to lean against an inflation shock that has eliminated the risk of inflation undershooting the target consistently over the medium term. If the energy shock unwinds quickly, a 2.5% deposit may be sufficient to stabilise inflation at target over the medium term, with limited output and employment costs. If the energy backdrop deteriorates or inflation inertia becomes clearer, the ECB would still be well positioned to move gradually further into restrictive territory, even though the inflation-growth trade-off would then become larger. 20 March 2026 5 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: The fate of the Strait

records.text: Our macro-focused report collates insights from various alt- data sources, this month suggesting that consumption growth continued in line with recent trends. Employment seems to have stabilised, with positive details at the industry level, while job openings remained steady. Consumer spending continues to follow recent trend. Total spend increased +0.7% year-on- year for the four weeks ending 6 March, similar to the 0-1% trend observed since September 2025. Our alternative labour market data sources suggest that the UK's labour market entered the Middle East conflict in better shape than it was over the winter. While job openings were flat, an improved trajectory in the February vintage of derived headcounts suggests a flattening out of LFS employment as well, from a downtrend predicted previously. Moreover, industry- level headcount developments also paint a fairly solid picture of the UK labour market in February. This comes on the heels of a slew of January labour market releases, which supported the UK economics team's view that the labour market was easing, but approaching its trough (here). On edge Investors had to navigate another week in which macro uncertainty pushed markets around. Risk assets actually started the week on a positive note, as the lack of negative developments over the weekend provided some support. After rallying through the first two days of the week (CDX.IG -4bp, SPX +1.3%), markets reversed on Wednesday following further escalation in the Iran conflict and a hotter-than-expected PPI report, with the sell-off accelerating after the FOMC decision. The selloff extended to Thursday (both CDX.IG and CDX.HY were wider for the week on Thursday morning), but risk assets regained some footing by the close (more on that below). Despite the swings, SPX is down only 0.4% as of Thursday's close, while CDX.IG is nearly 3bp tighter and CDX.HY is 50cts higher. Thinking through the beta-adjusted performance of 5y5y BEs and CPI swaps We have been monitoring the performance of the 5y5y sector with interest, given that the near- term risks from the war in Iran are clearly headline inflationary, whereas the medium-term balance with the potentially disinflationary impulse from AI is more nuanced. Moreover, the sector failed to rally meaningfully in January, or drop in February, before taking a leg lower in recent days. Indeed, outright, 5y5y inflation swaps have recently sold off to their lowest level since early May 2025, when the market was still recovering from a recession scare post- Liberation Day, but on a beta-adjusted basis, the performance is arguably more stark (Figure 1). From a tactical perspective, entering longs on a beta-adjusted basis seems compelling at first pass. The impact of higher energy prices on growth essentially depends on two factors: how the cost burden is shared between households, corporates and the public sector; and the share of net energy imports in GDP . records.text: 20 March 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB policy meeting and updated ECB call President Lagarde exuded calmness at the press conference. Calmness is not to be misinterpreted as not needing to act. But the calmness left the impression that no action is being signalled yet. She said the ECB is "well positioned and well equipped" to deal with the energy shock. But she no longer described the ECB as being in a good place, but now describes it as starting from a "good base". That change in wording suggest risks are skewed towards hikes. We also got a new set of staff projections this round. The baseline projections incorporated energy price developments up to 11 March. But we also received two alternative scenarios under higher energy price paths, greater uncertainty, and stronger second-round effects. For more on the staff projections, see our ECB Reaction. Following the meeting, we have updated our ECB call. We now expect the ECB to hike rates in June and September, taking policy to 2.50%, the upper end of neutral. The energy shock has changed the outlook. On top of this, there is growing concern that attacks on regional energy infrastructure means a more persistent disruption to global energy supply and hence higher energy costs for longer. We are not ruling out a hike as soon as April if there is no resolution in the Middle East and disruption to energy supply looks more persistent. records.text: The US banking regulatory agencies, the Fed, FDIC and OCC, released 3 Notices for Proposed Rulemaking (NPRs): 1) the revised Basel III Endgame (B3E); 2) G-SIB buffer recalibration; and 3) changes to the US Standardized Approach. In aggregate, the proposals appear constructive for large cap banks, especially the changes to the G-SIB calculation. On our math, we now expect largely unchanged RWAs for the 7 G-SIBs + NTRS (the only Category II bank) under our coverage, and a ~$50bn/50bps decrease to CET1 $/% requirements when factoring in the G-SIB buffer changes, which compares to ~$155bn of large bank excess capital at the end of 2025. Further, the proposal includes an adjustment for bank balance sheet growth going forward that should limit G-SIB scores increasing in future years. The B3E proposal has a 90-day comment period, but does not propose an implementation timeline. We assess quantitative impacts based on currently available data and existing disclosure (originally per our report here). In our view, if finalized in-line with the proposal, the core changes to the B3E framework would represent a modest reduction to capital requirements, which we believe is largely expected by investors, given recent messaging from the banks and the Fed. Even so, the fact that the implied correlation is trading well above realized suggests that there is currently minimal premium priced in the curve option. records.text: . Our measures of central bank tone suggest the ECB is already leaning to hikes. Aggregate ECB speaker tone has turned net hawkish for the first time since November 2023 (Figure 3). With policy rates near neutral, rapid pass‑through into fuel prices risks pushing real rates sharply lower as headline inflation responds. Growth remains fragile but, with labour markets holding up, the perceived cost of precautionary tightening, which rate markets now discount, looks limited. The Bank of England looks different. Its tone has shifted away from outright dovishness, but remains well short of hawkish (Figure 4). Three factors help explain why. First, the energy price cap means the next move in household bills is actually down, delaying the inflation impulse into the second half of the year. Second, UK unemployment is rising faster than anywhere else in the G10, reducing the risk of second‑round effects. Third, policy is already restrictive, with rates around 75bp above neutral. The BoE does not need the insurance of hawkish rhetoric in the way the ECB might, so the fact that markets having stripped out all UK rate‑cut pricing looks overly pessimistic relative to both the BoE’s current tone and the more challenging economic backdrop. Outcomes for consumer spending and drilling activity are inversely correlated Given the run-up in energy prices, the most acute downside risks to our forecast are in the realm of consumer spending, which we expect to slow from 2.0% q/q saar during H1 26 to a below- trend pace of 1.5% q/q saar during H2, reflecting the drag on purchasing power from slowing labor market. However, gasoline prices have risen more than 30% in recent weeks, to average levels approaching $4 per gallon, so risks to this forecast are to the downside, especially if such prices are sustained for more than a few weeks. However, a long-duration energy price shock is also likely to receive more of offset from spending and production in the domestic drilling sector, which, historically, ratchets up when oil prices are at sustained highs. March FOMC: Mired in the fog of war The March FOMC meeting communicated a “ when in doubt, wait” posture. As widely anticipated, the committee remained on hold, with messaging leaning on uncertainty— especially about the economic effects of the Middle East conflict and higher energy prices—as the dominant theme. The tone of the statement was mildly hawkish: economic conditions were described as still solid, inflation as “somewhat elevated, ” and risks to the dual mandate as balanced, expressing little urgency to adjust policy. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy U.S. Fixed Income Markets Weekly 20 March 2026 J P M O R G A N Market views As the conflict in the Middle East drags into its third week, TIPS continue to be whipsawed by volatile moves in oil prices. Brent crude rose steadily throughout the week, reaching nearly $120/bbl early Thursday morning after attacks on Iranian and Qatari gas facilities. While prices quickly retraced lower following mollifying remarks from Israeli President Netanyahu on Thursday, prices whipsawed further on Friday following conflicting reports on the potential for further escalation. Our oil strategists still believe there remains upside risk to crude oil prices, as the current price reflects temporary factors that are unlikely to persist. Brent will ultimately reprice higher as current inventories are drawn down and global markets are forced to clear at tighter supply levels (see Oil Flash Note: The wrong price, Natasha Kaneva, 3/17/26). Net of carry, 5- and 10-year breakevens widened 6bp and 2bp, respectively, while 30-year breakevens narrowed by 1bp, over the week. records.text: • Bonds and stocks did not move in lockstep: Last April's move featured a textbook flight to• quality, as equities sold off sharply, with the S&P 500 falling about 20% and 30y yields rallying 40bp. Historically, these moves tend to put significant tightening pressure on long-end spreads. This year, equities and bonds have not moved in tandem. The recent equity drawdowns have been modest ( Figure 1) and certain sectors (ie, those sensitive to potential AI disruption) more than others. As tensions escalated in the Middle East, the oil shock led to an increase in long-end rates, even as risk assets weakened. The tightening move in spreads this year have been more gradual and less destabilizing, in our view ( Figure 2 and Figure 3). Since 2021, bonds have not been a good hedge for stocks during risk-off moves ( Figure 4). • VA proxy modestly in receiving territory: Our variable annuity (VA) proxy ( Figure 5), which• captures the direction and intensity of receiving needs, is modestly in receiving territory. In contrast, the proxy was solidly in receiving territory last year, given the correlated drawdown in stocks and rally in rates. Since then, repricing has been ongoing and on days has had the feel of more significant panicked capitulation and the bullish trend seen coming into this period has clearly been halted. Overall yields on our EM local bonds are 45bp higher (13bp more than UST yields), with some meaningful dispersion as popular higher yielding local bonds in energy importers such as South Africa and Romania are over 100bp higher, as Asia has outperformed. EM rates markets have shifted from pricing cuts to pricing hikes. Materially higher energy prices have stoked inflationary concerns in EM rates markets. From a relatively good growth starting point for EM, this has seen tighter monetary policy priced. In Asia, the mar- ket already priced modest hiking cycles pre-Iran conflict, which have now been priced more aggressively (most notably in Korea and India). Stopping QT , building a structural bond portfolio by buying short and intermediate maturities, and/or launching longer-term operations could ease any liquidity squeeze that emerges. Easier fiscal policy stance In response to the 2021-23 energy crisis, countries deployed a broad range of fiscal measures, amounting cumulatively to around 2.8% of GDP at the euro area level, to cushion the effects of elevated energy prices on economic activity and households’ purchasing power. We expect governments to ease the fiscal stance in response to this new energy shock, but the fiscal support is likely to be more limited in size and more targeted in scope. First, the size of the energy shock has been more contained so far. As noted above, the region is confronting this supply shock from a much lower starting point in terms of inflation. At the same time, much of the recent economic growth was productivity-led, with relatively limited spillovers to labour markets – very much unlike 2022, when the supply-driven global commodity price surge coincided with resurgent demand, sparking concerns of second-round inflation effects and inflation expectations being unanchored. In setting out a framework for how the region's central banks are likely to respond to the supply-side inflation shock, a key variable is likely to be the degree of flexibility for monetary policy to deviate from inflation targets. • BNM and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) are the region's two major central• banks that are not inflation-targeters. As a result, both central banks have historically been less focused on the quantity of inflation, ie, how high the latest CPI reading is, and more on its quality – responding only when that pickup in price pressures is driven by demand, not supply. Ironically, however, these were also the two central banks that were closest, in our view, to tightening monetary policy before the Middle East conflict broke out.
