Key takeaways • Well positioned: Before the war in the Middle East, the euro area was "in a good place": resilient growth, strong household and corporate balance sheets, inflation near 2%, well- anchored long-term expectations, and a broadly neutral policy stance. With that starting point, the GC judges it is "well positioned" to adjust policy in response to the new inflationary shock. • Baseline and risk assessment: Staff produced the baseline forecasts with an 11 March cut- off (just two days before projections were finalized) and developed adverse and severe scenarios to explore the growth and inflation implications of higher and/or more persistent energy prices. • Tighter monetary policy needed: In line with the monetary policy strategy of incorporating not only the baseline, but also risks and uncertainty into decision-making, these scenarios point to the need for tighter policy if such outcomes materialise. • Sooner rather than later: President Lagarde highlighted the exceptional nature of this exercise and praised staff for delivering it. Citi’s base case is for one more hike in May. That said, our economists are skeptical that higher energy prices played no role in the decision to hike this week, and we still see risks of further hikes should the initial inflation shock from higher energy prices persist or broaden out (Australia Economics, 18-Mar-2026). Broadening is arguably more likely in Australia relative to peers given the positive output gap, tight labor markets (despite the recent uptick in unemployment, the unemployment rate remains below Citi’s NAIRU estimate - Australia Economics, 18-Mar-2026), and persistent supply-side uncertainty. records.text: Dutch pension funds sold EUR5bn of non-eurozone bonds during Q4, taking annual sales to EUR17.1 billion. In contrast, we estimate that Dutch pension funds bought EUR7.5bn of eurozone (ex-Netherlands) bonds in Q4 2025, possibly contributing to Bund and Buxl swap spreads richening in the same period . Equities de-risked slightly and credit allocation was increased: The Dutch pension sector’s value of equity holdings fell by EUR11bn in Q4 2025. Given that stock markets were higher during the quarter, in the absence of transactions the value of holdings should have increased, which leads us to believe that the decline was the result of net selling of around EUR20 billion. This may have been driven by some funds’ desire to de-risk their portfolios ahead of transition . Over Q4, the value of credits rose by almost EUR6bn. We believe this represents net buying and possibly accounts for some of the EUR7.5bn purchase of eurozone bonds cited above. The prior Basel framework did not explicitly define what constitutes a prudentially underwritten loan. The B3E proposal addresses this gap by defining a prudentially underwritten residential mortgage exposure as one that meets the criteria set forth in the Interagency Guidelines for Real Estate Lending Policies. These Guidelines establish expectations for sound underwrit- ing, including adequate assessment of the borrower’s ability to repay, appropriate documen- tation and adherence to supervisory LTV limits. Importantly, this definition is distinct from the CFPB’s Qualified Mortgage (QM) standard. As we understand the proposal, a non-QM loan may qualify as prudentially underwritten provided it was originated within the inter- agency guidelines’ framework, remains current, and has not been restructured or modified. We would welcome further clarification from the regulators on this point. Nonlinearities between oil prices and growth Introduction In recent analysis, we used the Fed staff’s model of the US economy (FRB/US) to show that a one -time oil price shock of as much as $60 per barrel would have limited effects on the economy (see Impact of oil price shocks a ‘frack’ -tion of what they once were ). In particular, a shock of that magnitude would reduce growth by about 0.2pp and lift the unemployment rate by about 0.1pp. We argued that this muted impact was rationalized by the shifting nature of the US economy, namely the advent of shale energy prod uction, which has made the US a major energy producer and exporter. This development has in turn insulated the economy from much of the adverse growth effects of oil price shocks. However, we cautioned that this model was linear and therefore may not capture any non-linear effects as the size of the oil price shock rises. records.text: 20 March 2026 Germany Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 The introduction of the Frühstart-Rente could act as a catalyst for a necessary cultural shift: systematically opening up capital markets to the broader population. By making a securities account the default for every 6-year-old, the government is effectively lowering the barrier to entry for millions of households. It will also bring Germany more in line with many of its international peers which already have policies encouraging their citizens to save via capital markets, as we noted here. However, the gradual rollout of the German programme highlights a notable disparity in fiscal priorities. While the federal budget allocates more than EUR 120 bn annually to sustain the current pension system, the modest EUR 1 bn required for this initiative is even being phased in slowly due to budget constraints. Initial annual costs will probably be below EUR 100 m. Because such a scheme only yields results in the very long term, any delay in its full implementation postpones the benefits. Beyond the financial considerations, such delays also defer the educational opportunity provided by the reform – a project designed to create a “learning by doing” environment and to teach the new generation to view volatility not as a risk that must be avoided, but as a fundamental feature of wealth creation over decades. Before we talk about our high-level expectations, it is important to discuss what default rates tell us. Simply put, a default is a breach of contract (i.e. the credit agreement that governs the loan). The lender has three sacred rights – maturity, principal amount, interest – and if the borrower violates any of these terms, then it is considered in default. Therefore, a default does not necessarily need to involve a complete restructuring where stakeholders take full write downs. In recent years, default events have migrated away from the traditional missed payments and bankruptcy filings to soft defaults such as a maturity extension in a capital structure the agencies deem unsustainable. records.text: 20 March 2026 UK economic notes Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG What do survey data tell us for food inflation? First, the latest BRC data showed a flat reading for food prices in February, with fresh food prices up 0.2% m-o-m and processed food prices down 0.5% m-o-m. Second, Kantar's Grocery Price Inflation data showed a slight uptick in momentum, rising 0.3pp to 4.3%. Third, the Food Foundation reported a strong 1.1% m-o-m rise in food prices, driven by price gains in things like eggs, salmon, sultanas, cabbage, cucumbers, and chopped tomatoes – to name a few. Fourth, Trolley data showed no change in the monthly average of its grocery basket (across nearly 50k items). Figure 8: Kantar data pointing to a modest rise in grocery prices Source : Deutsche Bank, Macrobond Figure 9: BRC data showing more tepid rise Source : Deutsche Bank, Macrobond Figure 10: Our dbDIG Tobacco Price Tracker pointing to more upside in Feb-26 Source : dbDIG, Macrobond What do our models tell us? For processed food, our models point to only a modest increase (0.2% m-o-m, CPI). Our models also point to a more meaningful rise for seasonal food and meat prices, with the former up 0.5% m-o-m and the latter up 0.7% m-o-m. Away from food prices, we expect some gains in alcohol and tobacco prices to feed through into the February print also. On alcohol prices, our trackers point to a 0.6% m-o-m gain (CPI), lifted primarily by higher wine prices. Indeed, new alcohol duty rates will have taken effect on 1 February.

Pulling it together, the product narrative for stablecoins is coming into focus while the use cases broaden. Indeed, the risk of large‑scale deposit migration from banks to stable- coins appears contained given the limits on passing yield to end holders. Moreover, as token- ized‑security adoption scales, the case for stablecoins as a settlement rail strengthens— expanding beyond today’s primary use of moving into and out of crypto and into broader capital‑markets workflows, even as the payments use case remains uncertain. Third, tighter oversight and evolving market structures are tightening controls and boosting operational resilience, but they also raise the bar—and the cost—for competing at scale. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 20 March 2026 Citi Research 8 The Challenge: Finding Reliable Signals in an Opaque Market Unlike the public loan market, where metrics like distressed ratios (the percentage of loans trading below a certain price threshold) provide clear warning signs, the private credit market offers no such price discovery. Furthermore, we lack routine credit ratings, company profiles, and consistent financial reporting for the small and mid-sized businesses that dominate this space. The nascent nature of the modern private credit market also complicates historical analysis. Its primary growth phase began during the pandemic and was supercharged by the 2022-23 rate hikes. This means the bulk of private credit loans are unseasoned and have not yet been tested through a complete credit cycle. While this has resulted in a default rate that is currently low and comparable to the syndicated loan market, it is not necessarily indicative of the asset class's true long-term risk profile. Often, BDC non-accrual rate is quoted as the closest metric to a "real" default rate. However, it is not 1:1 equivalent to the traditional default rates as it is a point-in- time measure and is not a cumulative 12-month rate as defaults are typically expressed. In addition, non-accrual rate is vulnerable to managerial discretion. records.text: First, high prices may reduce the oil intensity of GDP by accelerating fuel efficiency gains and shifts in other fuels. Specifically, there seems to have been a regime shift in late 2022/early 2023 (Figure 2). What exactly shifted is difficult to identify (CPI y/y had already peaked in June 2022, the SVB scare was in early 2023, the 2024 US election had not yet occurred, etc.), but we would offer another potential catalyst: AI. At a high level, it seems reasonable to think that the productivity benefits from AI could put upward pressure on forward real rates (higher returns to capital, higher productivity, higher growth, massive AI capex investment), yet simultaneously be disinflationary (a technology- induced positive supply shock). The main theme we discuss this month, however, is the potential cost of measures to shield the economy from the impact of the energy price increase. For more details, see main story and other developments sections. Deficit – The trend of Federal deficit widening continued in February, with the shortfall about €13bn wider than in January-February last year. This is not reflected in the same way in net borrowing, which does not have to follow revenue and expenditure patterns on the beat, as the government can use other resources. Revenues – Federal revenues were €59bn in the first two months of the year, compared to €64bn last year, which was however inflated by one-off effects. Expenditure – Federal expenditure has grown by €8bn or 9.6% compared to the same period in 2025 and stands at €93bn. Special funds – The Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality, the SVIK, saw new issuance of €3.2bn in February, bringing the total to €31.4bn. In light of today's MPM results and press conference, we maintain our forecast for a rate hike at the April MPM. New global economic baseline Last week, we had sketched out a tail risk scenario, where the oil price would average $100 for 2026. We had contrasted this to our pre-war baseline built on Brent future prices for 2026 averaging about $65. However, the 2026 average has now moved to $85. Oil markets are still in backwardation, with the Dec26 contract at $86, versus the spot Brent price of $112, implying some resolution to the supply situation. But a baseline scenario for the global economy now needs to be based on much higher oil prices than forecasts made pre-27 February. Somewhat lower growth, much higher inflation and some higher rates Under the new baseline assumption of $85 oil, we expect global growth in % Q4/Q4 2026 terms to be 2.9%, while global inflation will get pushed higher to 2.7% by end-2026, with the advanced economy aggregate at 3.1%. Advanced economies in aggregate are expected to grow only 1.7% 2026 under the current baseline (all Q4/Q4), driven by weaker growth in the euro area (0.7%), the UK (1.0%) and Japan (1.4 %). Emerging market economies’ growth is now 3.6%, with lower growth in many countries such as India, Indonesia, Korea, Poland and South Africa and few winners such as Russia and Brazil. records.text: 20 March 2026 UK economic notes Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG The look ahead: where to next? Since our last forecast update, the world has changed. The Iran conflict has sent energy prices soaring. At the time of writing, oil prices (Brent) are tracking around 47% higher than they were pre-conflict. Gas prices have risen over 90% during that same period. In a previous piece, we outlined three scenarios we see for inflation (among other variables) depending on the peak and duration of the shock. Excluding fiscal support, the spread in forecasts was wide, with our most aggressive scenario showing CPI peaking above 4% over summer. In our new baseline projections, we base our energy forecasts on the forwards as of 18 March. We do not take into account any fiscal support measures that could reduce energy inflation. But, to be sure, we think more fiscal support is likely. While we do not expect any immediate announcements, we see a high likelihood of policy measures to curb CPI, either through further cuts to policy costs in the Ofgem Price Cap, an extension of the fuel duty freeze (including temporary cuts), and/or a reintroduction of the Energy Price Guarantee (set at a lower threshold than in 2022). Incorporating market energy curves, our projections point to another disinflation detour by early summer. Indeed, the combination of higher pump prices and gas prices will see CPI rising back to 3% in July. The bad news is that energy markets are pricing in a longer uplift to energy prices

This distinction is important because it narrows the focus down to the type and location of secured debt can be issued at a BDC, which is critical to unsecured lenders. When we look at the various types of secured debt that BDCs use today, CLOs are not a true avenue through which unsecured lenders can be "primed, " although the potential for BDCs to sell minority stakes in their CLOs' equity is technically a call on the collateral pool to which unsecured lenders have claims. Banks' SPV facilities, however, are a source of secured debt that could, in theory, present priming risk. Banks could increase their lines of credit to BDCs, which itself dilutes unsecured creditors' claims on the portfolio's assets. But beyond this, a bank could theoretically issue a second lien or an unsecured note to the bankruptcy-remote SPV to which it lends that could further bolster its collateral claim in a more-stressed market environment. This would cannibalize some of the overcollateralization that unsecured lenders benefit from. Beyond being the priming risk that exists at the pre-existing secured debt layer, the notion of a newly formed secured debt layer is also feasible. We know that BDCs use secured revolvers that sit at the parent issuer — not at an SPV or in a CLO. We don’t think the CEE region is in the spotlight of vulnerability as it was last time. Today’s Iran shock is about price, not about supply shortages, so the hit to growth and FX is likely much more contained than last time. The region’s high real rates and lower inflation starting point allow central banks to wait and see, while post‑2022 energy supply diversification and better pricing management add further cushion. Our scenario analysis suggests rate hikes pressures only in extreme case of energy prices (e.g. oil to $150/bbl / TTF gas price to EUR150/MWh). Czechia looks most resilient on both energy exposure and policy room, so the CNB may be able to hold; Poland and Romania would be more pressured; Hungary is better cushioned but FX‑sensitive. If the energy shock unwinds quickly, a 2.5% deposit rate may be sufficient to stabilise inflation at target over the medium term with limited output and employment costs. If the energy backdrop deteriorates or inflation inertia becomes more evident, the ECB would still be well placed to move gradually into more restrictive territory. In 2027, something's gotta give: While we agree on the short-term impact on inflation from higher oil and gas prices, we are less sure about the ECB's view of a benign impact on growth of the renewed energy crisis. In 2022, the energy shock in Europe came in a context of a global rebound post-covid. This resulted in inflationary factors (supply-side bottlenecks, tight labour markets) that compounded with the surge of energy prices. On the real side, pent-up demand and generous fiscal responses were also important factors behind the resilience of growth in 2022-23 (which in turn also likely supported the ability of companies to pass the cost-shock to end-consumers). Without those factors, we suspect today's shock to growth could be more prolonged than the ECB assumes in its baseline and scenarios: on our estimates, after a large shock to their real income, European consumers need up to 6 quarters to adjust their spending. We would also assume world demand takes time to recover too. With that in mind, we suspect growth data will start to diverge from the ECB scenarios in late 2026. As a result, we think the ECB will first pause (in December 2026 and March 2027) and then lower rates back to neutral, with cuts in June and September 2027. Unsecured bondholders of BDCs benefit from the credit enhancement of the equity in the BDC, conceptually the same way senior tranches of CLOs benefit from the subordination of the lower-rated tranches and equity of the CLO. Our view, therefore, is that the pricing of those instruments should resemble each other (appreciating that they have different investor bases and pricing mechanisms, which we discuss later). A key component in underwriting any securitized product is to understand the structure's propensity to incur losses and assess how losses may alter the investment's loan-to-value (L TV). The inverse of L TV — known in securitized products as par subordination or credit enhancement — allows us to understand the attachment point (ie, the point at which principal would be impaired due to credit losses in portfolio assets) for any tranche of debt. To conceptualize this "attachment point" for BDC creditors, we can create a simplified L TV construct: the comparison of the total liabilities relative to the total assets of the BDC.4 Using this approach, we find that the median simplified L TV of BDC structures is about 47%, which translates to an attachment point of 53% (100% - L TV, in this case; Figure 3). records.text: European Economics 20 March 2026 Citi Research 4 Energy price shock – fiscal policy to the rescue? The energy price spike in the wake of the latest Middle East conflict has brought back the discussion of offsetting fiscal measures in Europe, including Germany. Retail prices for transport fuels have already reacted to the increases in the cost of crude oil: petrol (Euro-super 95) prices in Germany are up around 16% compared to the January-February 2026, while diesel prices have risen by 26% over the same period. Over a 12-month period, this would, on constant volumes, lead to an extra €13bn (0.3% of GDP) in expenditure for households and roughly another €9bn for businesses. Wholesale prices for utilities have broadly also increased and the first signs in retail prices are becoming visible too; according to Verivox (Mar 17th), the most competitive contracts for new household customers on a 12 month basis average now 9.9C/kWh, up 21% from February, though still somewhat lower than last year this time. Moreover, this refers only to new contracts; the low frequency of price resetting for utilities means that it might take both a longer period of elevated wholesale prices and another few months’ time to pass before household consumers start to feel the pinch more meaningfully. We think a first set of measures would therefore primarily focus on transport fuel taxation. Intuitively, those with lower starting asset coverage cushions require a lower percentage decline in asset value before reaching the 150% threshold. The corresponding attachment point in the CLO market sits between typical AA and single-A CLO par subordinations. More conservatively, this would imply that the attachment point for BDC unsecureds is most comparable to the single-A tranche of a standard BSL CLO structure, though there is differentiation at the borrower level. This tranche of the CLO stack, therefore, reflects the best point of reference for relative value to BDC unsecureds, in our view. What does credit support look like for unsecured lenders if a BDC's asset coverage failure is incurable? Morgan The monetary policy response will likely be driven by the interplay between supply and demand shocks, inflationary repercussions, the exchange rate, and the degree of fiscal loosening. But it is perhaps fair to say that the BoI sees the war shocks as largely negative supply shocks, which, if any- thing, demand a more cautious stance. Coupled with an already relatively conservative stance heading into the war (the economy in good shape, demanding little policy support, even as lower inflation opens space for a slight downward adjustment in rates) we think the chances for near-term rate cuts are slim. With uncertainty elevated and the inflation out- look worsening, we expect the BoI to remain in wait-and-see mode at the next few meetings. We have pushed out 50bp of previously expected 75bp of cuts into next year, but continue to see the terminal rate at 3.25% next year. A longer duration of the war would, other things equal, likely imply a longer pause in the BoI’s rate cutting cycle — supply-side would remain constrained, the fiscal stance would loosen, and risk premia would likely increase, which could affect the shekel. The original intent had been to underscore the strength of the bilateral alliance as part of a broader China strategy related to potential Taiwan contingencies, ahead of Trump’s planned visit to China (initially scheduled for late March). In 2025, Brazil exported USD50bn worth of goods to the EU, 14.3% of its total exports. Key items in Brazil’s export basket to the EU include crude oils, coffee, soybeans, copper and pulp. Prior to the agreement, several of these products already entered the EU market duty-free. Following the agreement, the EU will remove import tariffs on approximately 95% of tariff lines, covering about 92% in value terms of the EU’s imports of Brazilian goods. Tariff elimination will take place either immediately once the agreement comes into force, or through linear phaseouts over periods ranging from four to 12 years. Only a limited share of exports (around 5% of the value imported by the EU) is subject to tariff-rate quotas or non-tariff treatment, mainly agricultural and agro- industrial products (see Figure 9 in Appendix). Tariff liberalization does not fully translate into effective market access. Non-tariff barriers – particularly sanitary standards, traceability requirements and environmental regulations – remains especially relevant for agricultural exports. Lower tiers of bank debt and sovereigns have borne the brunt of the swap spread widening in March and the EU has underperformed most SSAs/EGBs owing to uncertainty around its funding needs. Whilst a new borrowing programme due to higher energy costs is unlikely in the near term, the risk/reward for the EU does not look overly attractive, in our view. Middle East conflict has taken its toll on SSA supply. The Iran-US/Israel conflict is entering its third week and primary SSA supply has been sporadic. During the first week of March only €6.2bn equivalent was issued in the main funding currencies (€, $ and £). The pace picked up during the second week with €21.3bn issued but almost half of this (€9bn) came from the EU. This week, as larger SSA names have remained sidelined only €7.5bn has been issued. At the time of writing, we have seen only 35bn of issuance this month so far, making this the third-weakest March for primary supply ahead of 2019 and 2013 (€33bn and €31bn issued; Figure 11). Given this, the overall funding completion rate for €, $ and £ benchmark SSA supply is at present 34%, notably lower than in the past two years (Figure 12). records.text: lines, we see two emerging themes from today's decision. The MPC is prioritising its inflation mandate. There were no 'ifs' or 'buts' – the MPC staked its view plainly: the committee was ready to act if needed. This was a line echoed by Governor Bailey, Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli, Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden, Deputy Governor Dave Ramsden, and Chief Economist Huw Pill. Ultimately, the key question for the MPC was whether the energy supply shock would impact medium-term inflation, with the committee noting that upside risks "appeared to have increased most notably since February". Downside risks to growth were moved to the back-burner, though the committee acknowledged the very different starting point to the energy shock, relative to 2022, including the prospect of a "more rapid or larger rise in unemployment". The focus on inflation in the minutes was notable, however. And, the MPC gave itself more optionality to pivot policy in either direction over the coming months. Urea, a nitrogen-based fertilizer, is the most vulnerable, with about 40% of all US imports coming from the Gulf. Potash, by contrast, is relatively insulated, given Canada supplies 75% of US imports, largely via non-Gulf logistics. Ammonia exposure is mostly indirect: while the US does not heavily import Gulf ammonia, the loss of Gulf volumes tightens the global nitrogen complex and lifts prices broadly. US farmers are preparing for the spring sowing season now, and fertilizer inventories matter more than ever. Articles and dealer commentary1 estimate that farmers have likely locked in about 75% of their fertilizer needs for the season at pre-war prices, leaving a 20-25% inventory gap. Monetary policy: The course of the conflict and magnitude of the shock are highly uncertain. We see the Fed as retaining a similarly optimistic baseline for growth as us – albeit with growing downside risk as evident at the March meeting – while taking on board the potential for inflation to move up toward 4% (see US February CPI preview: From tariffs to Tehran, dated 5 March). The textbook response to this type of shock is to dismiss energy-driven inflation as acyclical, ‘transitory’ noise and to focus instead on lasting cyclical impacts on activity. Critically, though, a central bank can set inflation aside only if it can be assured that inflation will naturally return to target on its own due to well-anchored long-term inflation expectations (LTIE). This is far from assured given inflation’s persistence since 2021. We expect the FOMC to adopt a symmetric policy bias at its April meeting – indicating that a rate hike or a cut is equally likely – provided energy prices remain elevated and the US unemployment rate is broadly stable (see March FOMC: Moving toward a two-sided policy outlook, dated 18 March). Gas prices remain high, even after de- escalation, still well above €50/MWh over the horizon. Inflation shock hinges on blockade’s duration: In each scenario, inflation remains well above target throughout this year. In the most benign case (S1), headline inflation stabilises around 3% y/y in 2026, in line with current market pricing. In S1 and S2, inflation climbs to 4% y/y by year end, before converging to target during 2027. These paths align more closely with the ECB’s adverse scenario, which now looks more likely, as its technical assumptions are based on the much lower 11 March price level. A key difference from the ECB’s outlook is their weaker second-round effects, which may reflect an effort to avoid signalling imminent rate hikes. Norway: Norges Bank heading towards a hawkish pivot Amid a broader shift toward tightening among European cen- tral banks, recent developments also tilt Norges Bank’s risk balance toward a rate hike later this year. For now, already restrictive policy and a stronger krone reduce the urgency to follow suit, and we expect rates unchanged next week. Gov- ernment subsidies will help to limit the impact of the latest rise in energy prices on consumers, but nevertheless some inflation pressure is likely to build. Moreover, the Bank has a pre-existing concern about sticky inflation and how that will interact with the current wage round underway. And Norway doesn’t have to worry about weak growth from the energy shock. A hike next week remains an outside risk, but the policy path is likely to be revised higher. We estimate that higher oil pric- es could add about 40bps and firmer core inflation about 10bps to the average 2026 rate profile. The ongoing NOK surge—now roughly 7% stronger YTD—should weigh on inflation and subtract around 30 bps. Asian assets were deeply impacted as part of the initial selloff, reflecting Asia’s status as a net oil-importing region and its heavy reliance on energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Our real-money flow indicators mirror these concerns, with Asia FX flows falling into the bottom quarti le, while the most open and liquid equity markets — particularly Taiwan, Korea, Thailand and India—have borne the brunt of the selloff since the conflict began (Figure 2).That said, as highlighted in our Theme of the Week on page 1, investors should increasingly recognize the significant divergence across the region. The key differentiators are oil reserve adequacy and the extent to which higher energy prices feed through to aggregate inflation. Korea, Taiwan, and China ho ld substantial strategic oil reserves —equivalent to 208, 150, and 120 days of consumption, respectively —providing a meaningful buffer against sustained oil price shocks. This stands in sharp contrast to South Asia, with Malaysia the sole net oil exporter in the region. Beyond buffers, policy flexibility will be critical. records.text: As one can see in Figure 4, FOMC participants remain quite split about the appropriate path for the policy rate. Even in 2026, seven participants would prefer making no adjustments to the policy rate, while five believe two or more 25bp cuts would be appropriate. In 2027, rate projections range from 2.4-3.9%, with at least one participant anticipating a hike. The range in 2028 is similarly wide, from 2.9-3.9%. The low end of these ranges is quite likely occupied by the dots of Governor Miran, who has made no secret of his preference for steep rate cuts. In part, these disagreements likely reflect differing views about the longer-run (neutral) dot, where projections range from 2.6-3.9% – again, with Miran likely occupying the lower end of the range. Although this range is unchanged from December, the median is 0.125pp higher, reflecting upgraded assessments by a number of participants who had been at or below December's 3.0% median. The standard natural rate framework would suggest that those upgrades likely reflect strengthened assessments of trend GDP growth by the same participants. Nonetheless, the wide range suggests that the degree of restrictiveness intended by a given participant likely varies much less than the dots do in any given year. At the press conference, Powell indicated that a policy of looking through the rise in energy prices is only appropriate provided inflation expectations remain anchored. While his tone was somewhat hawkish, he continued to downplay the possibility that the next move would be a hike. Given the highly fluid situation in the Middle East, Powell also downplayed the relevance of the forecasts contained in the Summary of Economic Projections (Table 1). Nonetheless, they are likely to be a good indication of how the Committee viewed economic develop- ments before the outbreak of hostilities. The residual covariance matrix is updated under a conservative Inverse-Wishart prior: it remains close to diagonal unless the data consistently exhibits correlated shocks. We estimate the VAR with one-sided, 50-day Gaussian kernel weights, so coefficients adapt gradually, and only past information is used (i.e.: no look-ahead). The result is a stable, smoothed, and economically plausible VAR that describes how each currency’s vol depends on its own and others’ past moves. 2. Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) via the Wold Representation Once the VAR is estimated, it is converted into its Wold moving-average form, which expresses today’s values of each currency’s volatility as a sequence of responses to past shocks. The impulse response is computed by feeding a one-unit shock into currency j and letting the moving-average system propagate it through all the lagged interactions encoded in the estimated coefficients. Each step reflects not only the direct effect of a shock in currency j on currency i, but also the indirect paths—such as j affecting a third currency, which then feeds back into i. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: WHAT MATTERS IN MARCH;WHO IS BUYING THE USD AND WHY THAT MATTERS What matters in March The market reaction in the first seventeen days of March to the conflict in the Middle East has been largely textbook, but with some important exceptions. Ranking DM currency returns against a range of market and macro factors reveals that performance has been driven by a narrow set of influences: recent sensitivity to oil prices, asset‑manager FX flows and holdings, and changes in 10‑year yields. Economic data surprises matter much less, as we argued in Risky Revelations last week, neither do FX valuations. None of this is surprising in isolation. In an oil shock, oil exposure should matter most; in any shock, flows and holdings tend to dominate as investors move quickly to get back to benchmark. What is more surprising is what has not mattered. Traditional FX anchors, current account positions and the level of volatility, have, for now at least, played almost no role in determining currency rankings. Nor has volatility delivered its usual verdict on carry. This is not a carry crisis. Quite the reverse. The simple rank of interest rates has mattered more than expected, and this is not just a price‑based result. Investor behaviour tells the same story. Across G10 currencies, the most robust FX factor flows over the past month have been into carry adjusted for volatility. records.text: e avenues available for priming at a BDC. Think back to the previous example of a BDC whose asset coverage test cushion was eroding. Also assume that this BDC has elevated leverage metrics (about 1.5x, for example) and a deteriorating portfolio of investment assets that it does not wish to (or cannot) sell, with no room to cut the dividend or reduce management fees — a firmly draconian setup. For this BDC, the cost of incurring a greater debt load is high — partially because the pricing of that incremental debt is likely to be onerous, and also because it is threatened with becoming a taxpayer if the asset coverage test is breached. In this scenario, the BDC may look to the equity market (including the preferred market) to find a capital injection before seeking more debt. However, if the equity capital markets are closed to it, or if it remained firm in its commitment to avoiding equity dilution, then the debt markets may be the optimal solution to meeting the dividend. If so, the BDC would likely, in our view, turn to a secured financing solution rather than the unsecured market. This is primarily because the cost of unsecured debt would likely be too burdensome, and the secured debt market will be able to assess portfolio quality with more granularity via its "ringfencing" of individual assets, or at least seek more comprehensive protections in the event of further portfolio degradation. Through the terms of trade channel, we identify three factors that are important for understanding how an energy exporter reacts to an energy-price shock: 1) The nature of the shock (supply versus demand) 2) Capex in the energy industry 3) Labor force strength in related sectors The shock’s nature matters: The current rally in energy prices is supply-driven and we find that in this environment, the correlation between terms of trade and FX does not improve. This is perhaps because a supply shock can be viewed as contractionary for global growth, thus weighing on energy exporters given their broader sensitivity to global risk. The BNPBCEPF outperformed STAR 50 by 12% over the past year but underperformed the broad market this year, given the energy, materials, and utilities strength due to regulatory cooling and geopolitical tensions. We expect the basket to generate a decent alpha in medium-to-long run, driven by robust policy support, and we prefer buying the basket on dips. According to Powell, if his successor is not confirmed by May 15, he plans to remain as FOMC chair until his replacement is confirmed, and he will remain on as a governor until any DOJ investigation is "well and truly over. " His plans after that are undecided. • We retain our baseline expectation that the FOMC will deliver a 25bp rate cut in September after seeing evidence that inflation has peaked on a m/m basis and is moderating, assuming that oil prices decline later this year. We expect another cut in March 2027, after seeing more moderation in inflation. We expect the FOMC's reaction function to be little changed, regardless of the new FOMC chair. Waiting in the fog As widely anticipated, the FOMC kept the federal funds rate target range unchanged at 3.50-3.75% in March amid elevated uncertainty, stable labor market conditions, firm inflation readings and upside risks to the inflation outlook. The statement included only modest changes, amplifying January's message of uncertainty and dependence of policy on data and developments. On balance, these are hawkish, but only mildly so, in our view. As before, the statement notes that "uncertainty about the economic outlook remains elevated," then underscores this sense of uncertainty by adding new language that "the implications of developments in the Middle East on the economy are uncertain." Core PCE falls to 2.5% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027 The disinflation process pauses, and in 2H26 there is a step-up in inflation despite lower oil prices. Core PCE ends 2026 at 3.1% and 2027 at 2.3%. Oil pushes inflation to a higher peak than baseline, but it also falls faster in 2027. Headline and Core PCE end 2026 at 3.5% and 3.0%. Federal reserve policy The Fed responds to employment softness and disinflation with cuts. We expect 25bp cuts in September and December, to a terminal range of 3.0–3.25%. Strong growth makes the Fed stop the cutting cycle in 1H26. As the impact from tariffs fades and disinflation resumes, the supply story becomes more evident. The Fed resumes gradual cuts by year-end and continues in 2027 to a terminal range of 2.75-3.0%. The Fed remains on hold through most of 2026, then raises rates in 4Q26 as inflation rises a

What started as a geopolitical risk premium is now increasingly evolving into pricing of physical market tightness. Our estimates indicate peak supply losses of close to 13Mb/d, as limited bypass options and storage constraints have led Gulf producers to significantly curtail output. This reduction far exceeds the previously anticipated 1Q surplus of 2.4Mb/d. We now see the 1Q market balanced, with March deficit at ~5Mb/d. As we are moving into 2Q, the supply loss should narrow to ~2Mb/d on average allowing the market to move back into a surplus of 0.8Mb/d. We expect balances to move back to oversupplied from 3Q onward 2.7Mb/d in 2H26, which will help refill storage. Prior to these disruptions, OPEC+ partners agreed to accelerate production returns for April to 203kb/d, compared with the previous rate of 137kb/d, after a pause in 1Q26. We model that OPEC+ will maintain this pace for the following 6 months prior to a full unwinding, although there is potential for a more rapid increase which would further support storage replenishment throughout the remainder of the year. Despite this, upward potential relative to prior updates remains constrained, as ongoing production capacity will limit additional supply. Russia-Ukraine deal in 2026 less likely The boon from sharply higher oil prices (further supported by Russian oil now trading at a premium vs. Brent) should strengthen Russia’s ability to cope with the war in Ukraine and reduces incentives for its leadership to agree to a cease- fire. records.text: US Rates Weekly 20 March 2026 Citi Research 7 The final key risk for the Fed / inflation, is the fact that core goods has been higher in PCE than CPI and that is likely to accelerate in the short-term (Figure 12). This is abnormal as typically the smaller shelter weighting, and higher healthcare weighting, in PCE tend to keep it below CPI (Figure 13). The recent divergence has been caused by the “computer software and accessories” category (Figure 14). This category includes computer software, phone apps and storage such as flash drives (which has increased by multiples over the past few months). Note that we think this category may be overstated in PCE because it includes services like cloud storage, which is a different category in CPI (internet services; for background see US Economics - Inflation Weekly – Computer software raises red flags for PCE). This implies some possible future edit of the category that perhaps leads to less pronounced inflation. Increased inflation in this category is a key risk in the Fed’s decision making process. For instance, Chair Powell alluded to the “two very strong goods inflation readings … which is very unexpected” and that tariffs “must have something to do with it – its either noise and it’ll come back, and that-that’s very possible, too” . However, the recent strength in goods has not likely been tariff driven. Our fear is the FOMC may be boxed in, in some sense, if this core goods print continues to move higher. Figure 12. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 20 March 2026 Weekly view From good place to good base As geopolitics in the Middle East escalate, the energy price shock to the European economy is growing in magnitude, and the risk of a more persistent shock has risen. For central banks in general, and in the European space in particular, we thought there was an option value in waiting in this environment. That’s what happened this week, with the ECB, BoE, SNB and Riksbank all on hold. But there were nuances that deserve attention, of course: The ECB was fairly neutral in its language, we thought: data dependence and the meeting-by-meeting approach still rule. The “good place” for monetary policy before the geopolitical escalation has become a “good base” to confront the shock. The slightly hawkish twist comes from the new set of forecasts. The new base case, or any alternative scenario, see core inflation above target over the forecast horizon. The crucial implicit assumption: second round effects will be faster and bigger this time, because the last inflation shock was too recent. This probably also reflects the ECB’s own experience and sensation. We previously argued that rate hikes are not obvious, but a mix of persistently high inflation and uncertainty into the June meeting could get the ECB to a small hiking cycle (50-75bp). But this was never really in doubt given the unfolding uncertainty in the Middle East. With energy prices expected to rise in the coming months, the inflation outlook has rarely been so uncertain. We take three messages from today's decision. The unfolding energy shock has unified the MPC. Indeed, today's decision came with a resounding 9-0 vote tally - the first unanimous vote since September 2021. Put differently, the size and scale of the shock was enough to coalesce the entire MPC to pause and reassess the policy outlook – underscoring the magnitude of the potential inflation shock. The Bank is officially in 'wait-and-see' mode. The MPC's message was simple: "All members stood ready to act as necessary to ensure that CPI inflation remained on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term." The Bank's easing bias was removed. Any talk of rate cuts was pushed to the back-burner. And despite increasing trade-offs between growth and inflation, the MPC has given itself enough optionality and flexibility to move policy in either direction – a big shift from February. In parallel, authorities are intervening directly into fuel markets to stabilize fuel prices. • Aviation shows the strain most visibly. As jet fuel approaches $200/bbl, carriers are shifting from cost management to outright service withdrawal, with many routes rendered uneconomic. As of March 18, several Asian airlines, including Qantas, Air India, Cathay Pacific, and IndiGo, have introduced phased fuel surcharges. Long-haul Air India tickets from Asia to Europe or North America now carry a $125-200 surcharge per passenger, with an additional $4.30 on domestic flights—effectively pricing out many leisure travelers for the upcoming summer season. Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) and Air New Zealand were among the first carriers to cancel or reduce flights due to soaring jet fuel prices. • In many regions, demand isn’t being reduced by choice but by the physical absence of inputs. Asian and European steam crackers rely on naphtha and LPG from the Persian Gulf, and with those feedstocks constrained, shutdowns and curtailments are occurring immediately. Asia is the most exposed, sourcing more than 50% of its naphtha from the Middle East. Japan offers a clear example. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 20 March 2026 Citi Research 11 Beyond the 12-Month Forecast: A Scenario-Based Outlook While our quantitative model provides a reliable medium-term forecast, its predictive power diminishes over the long term. Furthermore, the baseline default rates themselves appear deceptively low. Despite widespread concerns, the S&P private credit default rate stood at 4.5% as of December 2025—comfortably below the 5.6% for broadly syndicated loans. This apparent stability, however, masks significant forward-looking risks that could cause default rates to rise abruptly: 1. Sector Concentration: The private credit market's heavy concentration in the software sector creates a vulnerability to industry-specific shocks, such as the disruption threatened by artificial intelligence. 2. Looming Maturity Wall: A significant volume of private credit loans is set to mature in 2027-2028, creating a "refinancing cliff " where issuers will be forced to secure new financing in what may be a much higher-rate and less liquid environment. 3. Hikes are only feasible when the shock is sustained but moderate, such that concerns about inflation meaningfully outweigh worries about the labor market. Exhibit 5 illustrates this dynamic in a stylized manner, as a function of WTI crude oil prices. Other factors also matter, but we think the type of shock that would correspond to hikes would have the 2026 WTI average somewhere in the $80-100 range. This would be about a 25-50% increase from last year’s average. What would a hiking cycle look like? If the Fed does end up raising rates, we think 75bp of hikes is a reasonable central scenario. The Fed could make a case for taking rates back to where they were before last year’s cuts, on the premise that the labor market has stabilized and upside risks to inflation are similar to last spring. The Fed could also hike a bit less (50bp) or a bit more (100-150bp). But we wouldn’t expect a single 25bp hike in isolation, as that would convey a false sense of precision on policy transmission. We also don’t think a full-blown hiking cycle is in play, since the Fed isn’t as clearly behind the curve as it was in 2022.

records.text: 20 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 50 Deutsche Bank AG Neutral expectations The updated SEP will be a key point of focus at tomorrow’s FOMC meeting. Our economists expect the median headline and core PCE inflation projections for this year to move up to 2.7% and 2.6%, respectively, with all other median economic projections unchanged. They see no revisions to the median calendar-year fed funds rate projections but anticipate the median longer-run dot will inch up a tenth to 3.1%. For perspective on that, today’s chart shows the history of the median SEP longer- run dot relative to a range of measures of expected nominal neutral derived from Treasury term structure models (ACM, Kim-Wright, DKW, and CR). The term structure-based estimates are a subset of the measures tracked on our r-star dashboard but may be particularly illuminating in environments where the neutral rate might be expected to move materially in the future (as may be the case today given the potential effects of AI). Indeed, declines in these measures presaged the substantial markdown in SEP projections that came over the 2010s. The range of term structure-based estimates currently spans 3.0-3.8% with a median of 3.7%, firmly above the SEP median even if it moves up as we expect. That is, through the lens of these models, the curve embeds expectations that the Fed’s policy rate will ultimately settle around its current level. We also cautioned that the US economy has limited experience with significant oil price shocks in this new regime of significant energy production. Indeed, the only quarterly changes in oil p rices of more than 25% since the GFC came in 2016 and 2022, both periods after a sharp prior decline in oil prices. Below, we assess the potential non -linear relationship between oil prices and growth. Oil shocks and recessions It is a well -known historical regularity in the US economy that past recessions have often coincided with sharp increases in oil prices. With the US being a significant net energy importer before the advent of shale in the 2010s, a sharp oil price spike acted as a substantial cost shock for US consumers and businesses with no offset through energy production, energy -related capex, or the trade balance. As shown in the next two charts, of the eleven US recessions between WWII and Covid, six were preceded by, or closely coincided with, a year-over-year rise in oil prices of at least 50%. Three of the other recessions (1953, 1957, and 1970) were also preceded by a rise in oil prices, thoug h of a smaller magnitude on this measure. While surges in oil prices have often been a necessary condition for recession, they are not necessarily sufficient. For the ECB, our analysis suggests three plausible scenarios: ‘Look through’, moderate reaction (50–75bp) or a more significant reaction (100–125bp). Deriving a 2y-yield forecast from this and plugging in our term premium framework, we estimate the 10y Bund yield could, by Q1 2027, rise to 3.35% and 3.45% in the moderate and significant reaction, up from 3.10% in a ‘Look-through’ scenario. We assume bond supply is unchanged, bond volatility rises further and the inflation risk premium climbs as inflation surges. No panic receiving from Dutch pension funds likely in the current environment: The conflict in the Middle East has caused significant volatility in front-end rates and broad uncertainty in financial markets. However, the two most important inputs to Dutch pension funds’ funding ratios, equities and long-end yields, have been much less affected so far. Although funding ratios have likely moved lower year-to- date, we believe the decline so far has been limited. We estimate that the current asset-weighted funding ratio of the January 2027 transition cohort is around 123%, retaining a large buffer from levels at which pension funds might become more concerned. Only if equities were to decline by another 20%, accompanied by a 50bp fall in 20y swap rates, would this buffer be meaningfully eroded, our analysis suggests. The unfolding Middle East crisis continues to cast a long shadow over the global economic outlook. For Colombia, however, the initial transmission channels present a paradox: rising oil prices constitute a positive terms-of-trade shock, injecting additional stimulus into an economy already operat- ing above potential. Herein lies the policy dilemma. With domestic demand already propelled by unsustainable fiscal and income policies, and the output gap decidedly positive, this external windfall threatens to amplify inflationary pres- sures across both headline and—more problematically—core measures. The risk is that buoyant household consumption, supercharged by improved terms of trade, will intensify already-elevated core inflation dynamics. records.text: Adjustments to the G-SIB calculation The US banking regulators have also proposed changes to the G-SIB calculation, specifically: 1) a one-time adjustment of the coefficient against which each bank calculates its G-SIB buffer to adjust for GDP growth since 2019; 2) a recurring, annual GDP deflator of coefficients going forward; 3) adjustments to the short-term wholesale funding component of G-SIB to ensure it is not an outsize contributor to G-SIB scores; 4) changing the calculations of the components to use daily or monthly averages, vs. end of period calculations for 4/5 components of the G-SIB calculation; 5) reducing buffer size from 50bps to 10bps; and 6) aligning with risk, by adding in additional factors into certain G-SIB components. The STWF changes drive ~50% of the decrease in G-SIB scores, and benefits MS the most amongst large banks. As we have written about previously (see here), the G-SIB calculation determines a buffer that is a component of the CET1 capital requirement. Currently, it is based on 5 components that contribute to a score (in bps). The score is compared to a scale, with 100bps increments. Any score within a 100bps increment corresponds to a G-SIB buffer. Buffers are currently 50bps. The B3E NPR changes the G-SIB calculation to daily/monthly averaging for the 4/5 components, for the scale to be split up into 20bps increments, and for the G-SIB buffers to change from 50bps to 10bps. The amount of loss content needed before a BDC's asset coverage test is breached is comparable to the amount of credit enhancement supporting single-A CLO investors. • CLOs' MVOC metrics provide a precedent to frame the moves in BDC unsecureds. The market value overcollateralization (MVOC) of CLO tranches is similar to BDCs' asset-coverage test. MVOC shows a high correlation to changes in CLO secondary spreads. Similarly, as the asset value of a BDC's portfolio changes, so too should the valuations of its debt liabilities change. BDCs have 20% exposure to software on average, while CLOs have more moderate exposure, at around 12%. CLOs' MVOC has declined amid the software sell-off, and based on the historical relationship between CLO spreads and MVOC, the difference in software exposures should lead BDC unsecured spreads to widen 20% more than CLO single-A spreads, all else equal. Since then, negotiations with three of the US's largest trading partners – Mexico, Canada, and China – continue to proceed on a separate track. In addition, Section 232 reviews on trade in semiconductors, lumber, and pharmaceuticals, among others, remain ongoing. On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court struck down the President's authority to impose tariffs under IEEPA. Section 122 tariffs will replace IEEPA tariffs in the short term, though uncertainty rises after the 150-day period when Congress would need to extend those tariffs. Replacing IEEPA with Section 122 tariffs of 15% and considering composition effects of US imports, we estimate baseline tariffs near 11%. In our view, near-term tariffs are likely capped below 'Liberation Day' levels – at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 19 March 2026 Citi Research 3 There has been little progress in resolving the Middle East conflict this week. Data published by the UAE Defense Ministry shows that while attacks by Iran are at lower levels than they initially were, they nevertheless continue. Some ships are apparently moving through the Strait of Hormuz, but only on a limited scale, and data collated by Bloomberg indicates almost zero voyages. Three weeks will have passed by the end of this week, so the effect on countries dependent on Middle Eastern energy will become more evident, and the problems are not confined to energy. The price of crude oil, which is the primary focus, remains largely range-bound but is moving higher. The concerted release of reserves appears to be limiting upside for prices. The flip side, however, is that the crude price may no longer be an appropriate metric of the severity of the situation. For example, naphtha derives from crude oil but reserves are limited, and the price of shipments Japan has risen sharply. This is starting to affect the selling prices of products that use naphtha as a feedstock. Not only will prices rise for a broad range of products, but there is also the risk of the supply chain being severed. How long these tensions continue will remain important. Stable funding rates As we mentioned above, funding rates have been relatively stable over the past few months and this has been a dominant force in keeping swap spreads stable, at least at the front-end of the curve. Looking ahead, the evolution of funding rates should remain the paramount driver for front-end spreads and to this effect the evolution of ECB balance sheet is expected to be significant as well. The ECB is continuing its balance sheet unwind at a pace of around €500bn/year and is expected to continue for the next several quarters. The ECB’s monetary policy review acknowledged the prospect of keeping excess reserves sufficiently high to enable the smooth functioning of funding markets. In a recent speech, Governing Council member Schnabel mentioned that central bank reserves now play a significant role in banks’ liquidity management, especially post-QE; banks usually prefer holding substantial reserves, which are risk-free and immediately usable, unlike government bonds that carry market risk. ECB staff analysis suggests that demand for excess reserves could range between €600bn and €2.2tn, depending on banks’ preferences and regulatory requirements. We assume that excess liquidity will eventually settle around €1.5 - €1.75tn which will ensure the smooth functioning of funding markets. records.text: Derivatives Long-end swap spreads: Deja vu? Price action in 30y spreads brings back memories of "Liberation Day, " but the drivers are different this time. The equity drawdown is not as severe and rates have increased, SLR relief gives banks/dealers capacity to step in, and spread wideners are less crowded. However, fiscal risks remain. This is a reprint of Long-end swap spreads: Deja vu?, published on March 17, 2026. • 30y spreads have tightened about 20bp from recent highs, drawing comparisons to the• "Liberation Day" move in 2025. While the price action is similar, current catalysts look less likely to drive a return to last year's extreme lows. • Key differences versus last year include weaker correlation between stocks and bonds,• improved balance sheet capacity from SLR relief, lower hedging demand, less crowded positioning, and no signs of foreign demand for USTs waning over the past year. • The main downside risk remains fiscal slippage from lower tariff revenues and a protracted• conflict in the Middle East that could result in increased defense spending. Long-end (30y) swap spreads have tightened materially over the past two months, retracing about 20bp from the mid-January highs back to the -80bp area, levels last seen in October. The move reflects a combination of risk-off dynamics, including weakness in stocks, particularly those sensitive to AI disruptions, the Supreme Court's IEEPA ruling reversing tariff collections, the nomination of Kevin Warsh as Fed Chair

The severe scenario posits a more pronounced price spike, with oil prices peaking at USD 145/bbl and gas prices at EUR 106/MWh in Q2 2026. These prices are then expected to decline at a much slower pace, remaining significantly above both the baseline and adverse scenario assumptions throughout the rest of the projection horizon. Uncertainty will be even higher, with the VIX indicator up by 14 pp, an increase likely to be higher than during the Ukraine/ Russia war. This scenario would imply a recession in the middle of the year, with GDP growth falling by 0.3% qoq in Q2 and 0.1% in Q3. Growth would remain below potential for the subsequent two quarters before accelerating well above potential thereafter (averaging around 0.5% GDP growth). On an annual basis, GDP growth would be 0.5 pp lower than the baseline in 2026 and 0.4 pp lower in 2027. The primary transmission channels in both the adverse and severe scenarios are lower real disposable income and heightened uncertainty. It is crucial to remember that these scenarios do not incorporate any counteracting fiscal or monetary policy measures. The ECB has not attributed any particular probability to any scenario, further highlighting the high level of uncertainty surrounding the current projections. Yet, the uncertainty about the length of this conflict is high, and the signaling on likely war duration is mixed. In this note we take a step back from watching headlines and try to put this conflict into a different perspective. Interstate wars have certain statistical regularities — a fairly small number of observable factors usually make some wars last longer or shorter than others. Below we lay out a few statistical and stylized facts about the duration of interstate wars. We then proceed with a discussion of the importance of war duration for the Israeli economy. Wars are usually brief According to the Correlates of War database, 50% of wars in the past two centuries ended within about five months. Wars lasting less than 30 days have statistically been the most fre- quent (Figure 1). Out of the six wars Israel fought in the 20th century, three lasted less than a month. On hold, unchanged path The Riksbank kept its policy rate unchanged at 1.75% at the March meeting. Had it not been for the recent spike in energy prices, we think the Riksbank would have signalled the possibility of additional easing this year. But, as expected, the Board adopted a baseline scenario in which the conflict in the Middle East has some moderate upside effects on inflation and, under this assumption, it left the forward guidance unchanged. Inflation projections were revised up, though they remain well below target for both 2026 and 2027, while growth was trimmed for this year (Exhibit 2). The overall economic assessment stayed relatively constructive but careful, highlighting some timid signs of recovery in consumption and the labour market. records.text: UK Watch | 19 March 2026 5 Admittedly, the main adjustment post-BoE has been in rates market, but given the increasing correlation between GBP and 10yr Gilts, the read-across has been straightforward. Curve flattening has been a positive for the currency but in the absence of a sizeable adjustment in asset price volatility. This remains a risk for GBP, but with long-gilts a long-held and well positioned trade, we think the ongoing adjustment in this position could prove further support for GBP. We remain constructive on the outlook for GBP through the rest of they year but are not looking for an accelerated pace of appreciation despite relatively light positioning. With little over a month to go until local elections, the domestic leadership question is the obvious near-term hurdle to contend with, though we doubt that there is much appetite amongst the ruling government to force change at this juncture. Nonetheless a hedge against a rise in domestic risk premium via higher vega positions seems appropriate

Barring that, we think the economy may withstand oil at around USD150/barrel for some time. That said, we see the below key impacts: ▪ Cost shock: Oil is a key input for a wide range of goods and services. Facing higher costs, firms shift away from that input – likely reducing real output – or pass along costs, raising prices. That higher inflation lowers real incomes, depressing consumer demand and business investment. This is the 1970s channel. ▪ Drain on consumer purchasing power: Direct spending on energy goods (mainly gasoline) and services is about 3.5% of consumer purchases. While some may change their behavior, history shows that gasoline demand is relatively inelastic (see Figure 18, and Killian and Zhou (2023) who estimate a price- elasticity of −0.2). Higher prices are akin to a tax mostly borne by consumers and paid to producers. The burden is greater on lower-income consumers, who also have a higher relative marginal propensity to alter consumption due to changes in disposable income. A USD1 per-gallon rise in gasoline prices is roughly equivalent to a USD100bn annualized decrease in spending power. Front-loaded imports from the EU: On the import side, Brazil bought USD50.3bn worth of goods from the EU in 2025, accounting for 17.9% of total imports. Brazil’s import basket mainly comprises manufactured goods (more than 95% of total imports). Before the agreement, only a limited portion of Brazil’s imports (USD2.5bn) from the EU entered the country duty-free, with non-electrical engines and machinery the most relevant items in this category. Under the negotiated liberalization schedule, only a very small share of imports will benefit from immediate tariff elimination (USD0.5bn), while the bulk will see tariffs phased out gradually. The agreement establishes specific provisions for sectors considered more sensitive, such as the automotive sector. A limited group of products is excluded from the tariff liberalization schedule (about 8% of total imports), mainly comprising selected agricultural goods, energy products, perfumes, chemical inputs, machinery and industrial components (Figure 10). Less significant for the EU: While the agreement could make the Mercosur market more accessible to European firms, the impact may be more muted for the EU given its weaker ties with the region at the moment. Revised capital rules and G-SIB surcharge This morning, the Fed, OCC, and FDIC released the much-anticipated revised proposal on capital rules. The proposal includes adjustments to Basel III capital requirements as well as updates to the G-SIB surcharge methodology. Overall, the rules appear to reduce overall capital requirements modestly, a stark contrast to the original 2023 proposal that would have raised capital by 19%. The proposal would index the G-SIB surcharge to nominal GDP , curb bank window-dressing around year-end by moving toward daily/monthly average calculations rather than year-end snapshots, and reduce cliff effects by assigning surcharges in increments. Importantly, the weighting for short-term wholesale funding would be revised lower to bring it in line with the originally intended 20% relative weighting. The updates to the G-SIB surcharge are especially pertinent to repo market dynamics, where banks have historically thinned balance sheet capacity in Q4 to manage their scores lower. records.text: Summary of Economic Projections: Risks skewed around rosy baseline In the latest round of economic projections, the median FOMC participant lifted expectations about both headline and core inflation in 2026, and GDP growth was lifted throughout the medium term. Revisions to GDP came alongside a notable upgrade to trend GDP growth, partly reflecting an extrapolation of recent positive developments with measured productivity. Median rate projections continue to show one 25bp cut each in 2026 and 2027, and a slight upgrade to the longer-run neutral rate (Figure 1). Revisions to the inflation trajectory looked somewhat underwhelming, in our view, likely reflecting an assumption that nearly all of the recent runup in oil prices will unwind by year-end. The median participant's projection of headline PCE price inflation in 2026 was boosted by just 0.3pp, to 2.7% Q4/Q4, just a fraction of the 0.5pp revision we had expected in our FOMC preview. Almost all of this can be traced to the median participant's projection for core PCE price inflation, which was marked up by 0.2pp, to 2.7% Q4/Q4. While this latter revisions seems large, it is likely that this almost entirely reflects higher-than-expected readings for core PCE price inflation in January (0.36% m/m) and February (likely about 0.4% m/m) rather than inferences about higher core inflation over the remainder of this year. Using those periods, we compared the performance of different trading alternatives from directional and relative value (FX, swaps, bonds and x-ccy) to spreads (1s5s slope for swaps and bonds). Specifically, we compare the Sharpe ratio performance of the different strategies. The Sharpe ratio is calculated on daily returns. Steepeners as the dominant strategy The results show that swap steepeners are the dominant strategy, as steepeners show not only the highest sharpe ratio across strategies but positive in the aftermath of the shock (albeit at lower levels) (see Fig 2 to 5). KEY MESSAGES By examining the various trading strategies across Latam FX/Rates under historical oil shocks, we identify steepeners in swaps and bonds as the prevailing approach, as the yield curves steepen during the shock and remain so in the two-month post-peak period. 1s5s steepeners in Mexico emerge as consistently strong performers both during the shock and in its aftermath. Paying Chile trades also typically prove effective across different shocks (e.g., pay 5y Camara, short 5y bond, 1s5s steepener). records.text: 6 Global Economic Viewpoint | 19 March 2026 What does this mean for 2026 growth? We expect the contribution of AI investment to US growth to increase from 0.3pp in 2025 to 0.4pp in 2026 (Exhibit 9). This is less than hyperscaler capex plans indicate, for several reasons. First, some of the planned investment could get delayed due to lead times for key inputs and construction times. Second, a lot of the inputs for the anticipated AI capex will be imported, limiting the upside to US growth. Third, inflation for AI supplies should continue to outpace the broader GDP price index, resulting in a smaller impact on GDP than the headline numbers from AI hyperscalers suggest. Fourth, some of the planned spending is likely for projects outside the US. Accordingly, we expect the acceleration of AI investment to have substantial spillover effects on capex suppliers like Taiwan, Mexico and Korea. This is a key reason why we recently raised our forecast for 2026 Taiwan growth from 4.5% to 8.0%. At this stage, we do not expect the energy shock related to Iran war poses major downside risks to Taiwan GDP, unless protracted geopolitical tensions, and thus extended gas shortages, become the base case. Meanwhile, our expectations for AI investment in China should provide a smaller but still positive boost to growth, given the more closed AI ecosystem compared to the US. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 19 March 2026 3 Our AI series kicks off with investment AI investment should keep driving global growth in 2026. Its contribution to US growth – where private investment dwarfs that of Europe and China – is set to rise from 0.3pp in 2025 to 0.4pp in 2026, with upside risk given this sits below hyperscaler capex plans. Meanwhile, China is snapping at the US’s heels. Its AI investment should provide a smaller (<0.1pp) but still positive boost to its economic growth this year. The AI race between the two countries is compelling. China may have earlier potential for an economy-wide productivity impact thanks to co-ordinated state-led deployment, while the US’s deep innovation could mean it ultimately stays out in front. In the near term, though, the greatest beneficiaries of AI spending will be the capex suppliers, like Taiwan, Mexico and Korea. records.text: Emerging Asia Outlook The lonely doves In contrast to the consensus view that central banks are clearly set to turn more hawkish, we believe the case for such a pivot in EM Asia is not as clear as many may think. Most are likely to take a wait-and-see approach in the near term, lest pre-emptive tightening turns out to be premature. If 2025 was a year of tariffs, then 2026 looks set to be a year of supply disruptions for Emerging Asia. The economic outlook is clearly dependent on how the conflict in the Middle East evolves – implying an unusually high degree of risk to our base case, which broadly assumes the price of Brent crude oil averages USD85/bbl this year. Our estimates suggest economic activity in Emerging Asia has historically been able to weather higher energy prices – this would not be the first time that Emerging Asia contends with USD100/bbl oil, after all. Our base case assumes that shortages, if any, are not severe – but this is a risk that financial market participants should not dismiss out of hand, in our view. Overall, we have reduced our GDP growth forecasts modestly across many economies in the region versus our most recent projections – but, as mentioned above, these crucially assume that shortages, if any, are not severe. records.text: Risk 2 (Limit Price Upside): OPEC Deploys Spare Capacity After Reopening Nearly all the world’s global crude spare capacity (that we estimate at 3.7mb/d before the war (Exhibit 5)) is currently constrained by Hormuz disruptions in the Persian Gulf. However, assuming no large persistent losses in potential oil output, history suggests OPEC is likely to deploy its spare capacity after SoH reopening to help stabilize tight markets and make up for some production losses during the disruption, when production dropped below the quota. For one thing, Saudi Arabia reportedly increased supply as part of a contingency plan in February 2026. Saudi Arabia reportedly told OPEC its oil supply to the market was 10.11mb/d while production was 10.88mb/d (vs. 10.10mb/d in January). Second, our prior study of four major disruption events suggests that combined production from Saudi Arabia and the UAE tends to rise quickly and significantly following supply disruptions, typically offsetting 70-90% of lost production within 2 quarters (Exhibit 6). Saudi and UAE production tends to remain higher than before the disruption even after the disruption eases (e.g. around the Libyan civil war). records.text: United Kingdom Outlook On hold, holding on We revise down our forecasts for real GDP in 2026 and 2027, but revise up inflation and unemployment in light of an intensifying energy shock. Following a 9-0 vote to hold and a more hawkish tone from the MPC this week, we expect Bank Rate to stay at 3.75% for the rest of 2026. • We expect real GDP to grow 0.7% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027 (previously 1.1% and 1.7%• respectively). This reflects a drag from the energy-price shock as real incomes and consumer and business confidence are eroded amid tighter financial conditions. • We revise up our inflation forecast for 2026 to 2.9% (+0.7pp) and for 2027 to 2.4%• (+0.4pp). This reflects current energy market pricing. At its peak (in Dec-26), the energy-price shock is assumed to raise headline CPI by 1.1pp, but by Dec-27 this impact is only 0.1pp. We forecast core inflation at 2.6% (+0.2pp) in 2026 and 2.2% (+0.2pp) in 2027. • The BoE held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its March meeting and adopted a more cautious,• hawkish tone than it had in February. We expect Bank Rate to stay at 3.75% for the rest of this year. We assess that keeping policy this restrictive for an extended period is sufficient to bring headline CPI back to 2% in two years time (beyond our published forecast horizon), consistent with the BoE's mandated target. • February public sector finance data this week supported our projections for borrowing• this fiscal year. records.text: MPC’s more decisive-than-expected hawkish shift triggered a sharp repricing in UK rates, with 2y Gilt yields rising around 25bp after the decision release, before Governor Bailey’s comments partly reversed the move. The change since end-February in market pricing for year-ahead policy rates has been much more aggressive in the UK than in the Eurozone. This is surprising both because the UK's policy starting point is more restrictive, and because the shift higher in 1y Euro and 1y UK inflation swap rates has been the same, at 190bp. As a result, the 1y "real €str" rate has fallen by 37bp more than 1y "real Sonia" since end-February, which looks wrong to us. While the sector has largely performed in line with credit yer to date in terms of excess returns, and traded in a tight range versus credit (at 1-5bp through), we think it is at a crossroads that should increase downside pressure on performance. We think there is risk for the sector to trade at a 10bp discount to credit, which would place it similarly to where it stood in late 2018-mid-2019. Sector headwinds including accelerating GLP-1 use, MAHA concerns, competitive activity, and inflation continue to affect top line performance. There are similarities in terms of the ratings pressure on a number of packaged food credits, where leverage is rising amid a need to reinvest in pricing given ongoing inflationary pressure on consumers and competitive dynamics. While M&A activity should remain subdued, the number of credits with low-BBB ratings and Negative outlooks (ie, potential to be fallen angel candidates) has risen quickly and should lead to further dispersion within the sector. This will lend itself to a greater importance for single-name selection in the sector. Finally, our analysis of sector performance during prior oil spikes, as indicated in As Goes Oil…, suggests that food & beverage has historically been among the worst performing sectors. The direct energy effect will add c.0.2pp to headline CPI in March and 0.5pp to Q2. The bigger jump then comes in Q3 when we expect the energy price cap to rise around 20% q/q creating a peak inflationary impact of the shock of 1.1pp. The current backwardation of the energy markets from Q2 27 and the implied base effects mean that this overall effect should fall back to be just a 0.1pp upward revision to headline CPI by Dec-27. We assess that the impact of the energy price shock on core CPI inflation will build more slowly, but be more persistent, peaking at 0.33pp in Q1-27 but still being 2.2% y/y by Dec-27. We now forecast headline CPI of 2.9% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027 (previously 2.2% and 2.0%, respectively) ( Figure 2). Importantly for the Bank of England outlook, this forecast horizon stops short of the BoE's own 2-3 year target for bringing headline CPI back to target (currently focused on Q2 28).
