This would also bring Germany more in line with many of its international peers which already have policies encouraging their citizens to save via capital markets. Germany faces a turning point in its pension policy For decades, the country has relied almost exclusively on the "intergenerational contract" – the idea that today’s labour force pays for today’s retirees. But as demographic reality changes, this contract will not be able to completely fulfil its promise. Coupled with the new "Altersvorsorgedepot" (old-age provision account), the introduction of the "Frühstart-Rente" (early start pension) marks a profound shift in this landscape. At first glance, a government grant of EUR 10 per month for every child of school age seems economically negligible. However, to view this merely as a social benefit is to miss the bigger picture. Instead of relying on traditional insurance products with strict guarantees (like the "Riester" scheme), the government is now decisively focusing on the higher growth potential of capital markets. Cornerstones of the Frühstart-Rente While the final draft of the law for the Frühstart-Rente is still pending, the German government agreed on key elements on December 17. These include energy generation, labor, financing needs, and more recently potential shortages causes by the Iran war. We argue that these will not stop companies from investing aggressively in AI but they could drive up the costs and limit the impact to the real economy. Iran war could cause LNG shortages and affect production of key AI inputs A recent risk to the AI investment outlook is the Iran war. It has driven up shipping costs, LNG prices, and costs of other commodities. Around 20% of global LNG supply passes through the Strait of Hormuz (Exhibit 13). Economies key to the AI supply chain like Taiwan is heavily reliant on external LNG supply, and Korea also being a net importer of LNG that is impacted by the Middle-East supply bottleneck. (Exhibit 14). So, the shortage from the Iran war could drive up the costs of AI inputs like servers, GPU and memory. We wouldn’t expect this risk to lead to less nominal spending on AI. However, it could lead to less real activity due to rising costs. However, the tone of the minutes was decidedly more hawkish and cautious than in February and, importantly, also more than markets had expected. The unanimity of the vote (9-0), added to that hawkish surprise, while individual MPC members' policy paragraphs opened the door to the possibility of rate hikes. However, using a series of frameworks for considering how the MPC might react to the evolving energy price shock, we come to a different conclusion. We find that, on balance, all four frameworks and the explicit communications from Governor Bailey, whom we view as currently the median voter, point to a hold rather than a hike in Bank Rate. We therefore believe Bank Rate will remain at 3.75% for the rest of 2026, with the path thereafter highly uncertain and dependent on how the energy price shock and data evolve. Officials in Thailand and Vietnam have been urged to use stairs, work from home, and limit travel, while Myanmar introduced alternating driving days to reduce road fuel demand. In parallel, authorities are intervening directly into fuel markets to stabilize fuel prices. • Aviation shows the strain most visibly. As jet fuel approaches $200/bbl, carriers are shifting from cost management to outright service withdrawal, with many routes rendered uneconomic. As of March 18, several Asian airlines, including Qantas, Air India, Cathay Pacific, and IndiGo, have introduced phased fuel surcharges. Long-haul Air India tickets from Asia to Europe or North America now carry a $125-200 surcharge per passenger, with an additional $4.30 on domestic flights—effectively pricing out many leisure travelers for the upcoming summer season. Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) and Air New Zealand were among the first carriers to cancel or reduce flights due to soaring jet fuel prices. • In many regions, demand isn’t being reduced by choice but by the physical absence of inputs. Asian and European steam crackers rely on naphtha and LPG from the Persian Gulf, and with those feedstocks constrained, shutdowns and curtailments are occurring immediately. Asia is the most exposed, sourcing more than 50% of its naphtha from the Middle East. Japan offers a clear example. records.text: US Economic Perspectives20 March 2026 ab 29 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Comparison to the forecast models As with most Phillips curve style models, our models were unable to forecast the inflation as it surged upward in 2021-2022 and, as expected, the majority of models were not a good guide as inflation has fallen. (Note that in the early part of 2022, the core PCE price inflation time-varying trend models and the component model remained above 4% throughout the forecast horizon, which at that point went through the end of 2024, compared to the 2.8% that has been published for 2024 inflation.) In particular, the models do not include an effect for changes in the mix of demand and the supply constraints that hampered efforts to satisfy this changing mix. We believe the combined effects of the changing demand mix and supply issues were far more important in driving the initial inflation surge in 2021 than were the standard Phillips curve driver of aggregate resource slack, though fiscal spending and monetary policy have likely accounted for a fair amount of the reason that inflation did not fall faster from that peak. Our forecast is above the models this year. The difference comes quite quickly as we expect four-quarter core PCE price inflation to rise in Q1 and Q2 of this year whereas the models expect it to fall. In particular the projection for most of the models is for core PCE price inflation to edge down from 2.9% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 2.7% or 2.8%

Morgan Earlier this week, we cautiously recommended entering into swap spread steepeners because term funding premium was more than two standard deviations above our estimate of fair value, which remains the case (Figure 7). We noted that one of the risks to this view is the geopolitical backdrop, and further escalation could result in the curve flattening fur- ther. Indeed, the spread curve has recently once again become highly negatively corre- lated with implied volatility (Figure 8). Previously, this correlation was most pronounced earlier this year when swap spread wideners were an attractive carry-seeking strategy as implieds continued to decline. The re-emergence of this correlation is not surprising, as (i) higher volatility has made carry-seeking strategies less attractive and has resulted in unwinds and (ii) risk-off sentiment has resulted in swap spreads narrowing. Therefore, while we still view the swap spread curve as too flat, we recognize that the volatility in the spread curve (and in markets in general) is too large, and the risk-reward tradeoff does not appear attractive. Therefore, we recommend unwinding steepening exposure and encourage patience before positioning for the swap spread curve to normalize (see Trade recommendations).

records.text: 20 March 2026 Germany Blog Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG At its core, the mechanism aims to ensure an early start to capital market-based private pension provision, turning every child into a shareholder in the global economy from primary school age. Unlike "Kindergeld", which is a cash transfer for immediate consumption, the Frühstart-Rente is an asset accumulation tool strictly earmarked for retirement savings. The federal government provides a monthly grant of EUR 10 per eligible child, running from age 6 to 18. Crucially, these funds flow directly into a Frühstart-Rente-Depot (early start pension account) that is exempt from the strict guarantee requirements that have been a key weakness of the current private pension system (Riester). This allows providers to invest in solutions with a high equity share – such as global ETFs – to capture the full equity risk premium over the long term.1 Additionally, capital income from the Frühstart- Rente will be tax-free until the start of the payout phase. The reform is expected to take effect on January 1, 2027, with contributions beginning retroactively on January 1, 2026. The first cohort that should benefit from the public subsidy was born in 2020. Parents can open a Frühstart-Rente-Depot for their child with a private provider. Crucially, if they do not, the reform utilises an "Auffanglösung" (automatic enrolment) to overcome inertia. Unlike voluntary schemes, in this case, the government invests automatically in a collective account.

records.text: We can use our existing ECB model to explore the potential monetary policy implications of the staff’s projections and scenarios. The logic behind our framework is to “invert” the staff’s projections and scenarios into “shocks” for growth and inflation, and then to calculate the monetary policy response of a range of Taylor rules and optimal control specifications. Our model points to 25bp of monetary policy tightening under the staff’s baseline projections, between 50-75bp under the adverse scenario, and 100-175bp under the severe scenario. The Path Ahead Our analysis suggests that the Governing Council will be under some pressure to hike even in the staff baseline projections scenario, where the conflict de-escalates and allows for a normalisation in energy markets, as also assumed in our baseline forecast and broadly reflected in commodity futures. Specifically, our Taylor rule and optimal control simulations point to one hike in this scenario. Base case remains a long hold Our base case remains that the Riksbank will be on hold for long. Before this shock, the Riksbank’s Board would have had a slight easing bias (vs the ECB’s “good place” characterization). Shifting towards hikes would require several months of high energy prices and probably some clear upward moves in medium-term inflation expectations, which for now remain well-behaved (Exhibit 7). Compared with the 2022 episode, the Riksbank may be inclined to respond more quickly if the spike proves persistent. However, the economic backdrop is now weaker and higher energy costs could further delay the recovery (the Riksbank is quite growth- sensitive). The slack in the economy should limit the risk of second-round effects, if the shock fades away quite quickly. In scenarios where energy prices normalise within around two months, we think the Riksbank would stay on hold in a wait‑and‑see stance. This week saw attacks on energy infrastructure that raised the specter of broader and more lasting supply disruptions. Although crude oil and natural gas prices have moved higher, they remain well below levels consistent with a sustained disruption of the current magnitude. While balancing the growth drag from higher prices with economic data showing stronger-than-expected global growth, the rising concern is that the energy supply shock will be magnified through some combination of building price increases, quantity constraints, and tightening financial conditions. Our model estimates suggest that a supply shock that keeps energy prices close to $100bbl through midyear (moderating towards $80bbl thereafter) would raise consumer prices roughly 0.8%pt this year. The global GDP drag associated with this shock is estimated at 0.6%pt (Table 1). Offsetting this drag is the impressive growth momentum at the start of the year. On balance, our 2026 forecast revisions have lowered GDP by only 0.2%pt so far. Fourier Transform and Frequency-Domain Connectedness Volatility spillovers do not operate uniformly across horizons: very short-term movements are dominated by market frictions, while long-term variations reflect slow structural trends that are not relevant for macro-driven risk transmission. Thus we seek to isolate the medium-term cycle that is relevant for trading purposes — typically multi-day to multi-week dynamics. To do so, we apply the Baruník–Křehlík (2018) frequency decomposition to the VAR. Mechanically, we apply a discrete Fourier transform to the VAR’s impulse-response sequences means rewrites each impulse response in terms of how strongly it loads on fast, medium, and slow frequencies, producing a frequency-domain representation for every shock–response pair. These frequency-domain responses are then combined with the VAR’s residual variance–covariance matrix to form the spectral density matrix, which shows how each currency’s forecast-error variance is distributed across cycle lengths. From this, the spectral FEVD is computed by measuring how much of the variance at each frequency is attributable to shocks in each currency. Integrating these contributions over a chosen frequency band yields a band-pass FEVD that isolates volatility spillovers operating specifically at the targeted horizon. S&P has made over 20 updates to the S&P 500 index methodology. These changes include an April 2019 reduction to the minimum required float and a March 2017 increase in the minimum seasoning requirement from 6-12 months to a full 12 months. For market participants, while index eligibility requirements are important, so are transparency and visibility regarding index rules. S&P’s recent commentary acknowledged the evolution of index methodologies but also reiterated current S&P 500 requirements for inclusion, discussed the benefits of the IPO seasoning requirement, and highlighted other S&P indices that currently fast track IPOs. In addition, S&P’s statement that investors “may rely on our public methodologies and processes to stay informed of their future index treatment” suggests the provider is unlikely to make any imminent changes without providing advance notice. The proposed index changes suggest an IPO with large total market capitalization but low float would carry a substantial weight in the Nasdaq-100 but relatively small weights in the S&P 500 and Russell 1000 Growth indices. To illustrate, a company with a total market capitalization of $1 trillion but just 5% free float would have a weight of 0.1% in the S&P 500 and 0.2% in the Russell 1000 Growth Index. However, the Nasdaq proposal to adjust the weight of low-float securities by a factor of five times its free float – capped at 100% – would point to the same company carrying a 1.4% weight in the Nasdaq-100. Interest rate spillover to credit - this is not 2022 One consequence of the war has been a rapid repricing of interest rates, with surging energy prices set to push up inflation, leading to tighter central bank policy than previously expected. Fiscal deficits are also likely to widen as the result of weaker growth and energy support packages. The front-end of rates markets have been particularly hard-hit, with c.70bp of hikes now priced by December for both the ECB and BoE. With the magnitude and duration of the disruption still highly uncertain, most central banks held policy rates unchanged this week, but after 5 years of above-target inflation, the commentary has understandably turned more hawkish. The new ECB staff forecasts (based on a cut-off of 11 March,) show headline inflation peaking at 3.1% oya in 2Q26, with core inflation now stuck at 2.2% in 2027. Correspondingly, our economists now look for hikes in both April and July, with a partial reversal (one cut) once risks of second-round effects pass in 2H2

There is the boom period when businesses aggressively build capacity on expectations for future demand, and then a bust period when the sector becomes oversupplied. This was the case during the 1970s for oil, 1990s for tech/telecom and 2010s for oil/gas (shale). Vacancy rates of data centers suggest we are a long way from oversupply in AI capacity. Jones Lang Lasalle, a firm specializing in real estate management, reports that vacancy rates for colocation data centers – third party, multi-tenant facilities – are currently below 2% and should remain depressed based on pre-leasing activity. Additionally, we find that investment in AI trails the peaks of previous investment cycles currently. And though it has been climbing sharply recently, it likely has more room to run (Exhibit 11- Exhibit 12). The improvement in terms of trade will help counteract labour market weakness in trade-exposed sectors. Overall, we have a positive outlook on the CAD and hold a long against the EUR. NOK As a large oil exporter as well enjoying a large surplus in its international investor position, we have been favourable toward the NOK for some time and we maintain a long versus the CHF. NZD New Zealand’s economy appears to have troughed and is starting to recover. Its labour market has stabilized as business manufacturing hit its highest level since Oct 2021. Meanwhile inflation remains above the RBNZ’s target range. Altogether, we concur with current rate market expectations for hikes by year end and maintain a long NZD position versus GBP. USD In contrast to this time last year the USD is now reacting more like a safe haven currency. It is also well suited to the current environment with a relatively higher starting point for rates, a big underweight still to unravel and a positive sensitivity to high oil prices. This could change if the Fed appears dovish relative to others in the face of the oil shock, but for now in the current market regime the USD looks likely to fair well. Israel’s macro policy response Fiscal policy is naturally the main avenue for responding to war shocks. Last week the cabinet approved a revised 2026 budget plan, which assumed an ILS32bn ($10.2bn) increase in defense spending to ILS143bn and an additional reserve of ILS13bn set aside in case of further war-related needs. Despite (modest) cuts to non-defense expenditures, the head- line deficit was revised higher to 5.1% from 3.9% (2025: 4.7). It is perhaps fair to presume that if the war lasts more than a few more weeks, defense spending will have to be increased further. We estimate that non-defense spending is going to rise about 12%y/y in 2026 — a large increase by historical standards and relative to sustainable nominal GDP growth — which should provide a good cushion to a war-hit economy. Our base case assumes cuts in June and September based on energy prices reversing in the next couple of months but conviction is reducing. If energy prices stay elevated for longer (which current energy future prices suggest), risks of cuts not materializing this year will rise. The BoE also opened the door to hikes. We still the BoE would need to see a larger and more persistent shock to be convinced to hike, given the economy/ labour market is weak, risks of second round effects are less than before, and rates are restrictive. Having said that modest hikes cannot be ruled out after today’s guidance with the bar somewhat lower than what we thought before this meeting, though still high. The BoE has noted that a larger or more protracted shock, which risked greater second round effects can increase risks of a hike. A scenario where BoE sees inflation move much higher or stuck above 3.5%-4% for long (rest of this year/early next year) can increase risks of second round effects and open the door to a hike. It is unclear however if we would have enough evidence by the April meeting that we are in a scenario to warrant a hike. At the time of writing, the path for energy prices implied by futures markets would suggest a scenario for monetary policy that looks closest to S3 on page 2. This would therefore suggest just under 70bp of cumulative rate hikes should be delivered. Risk management considerations also apply, and our sense is that the risk of larger-than-expected second round effects and/or a worse scenario (i.e. S4) for energy prices are sufficient to warrant the ECB delivering three cumulative hikes. The timing of hikes is more uncertain though. Providing energy prices remain stable over the coming weeks, we think the ECB will opt to wait until June to deliver its first rate hike, as it will receive more economic data, including new projections (June is when the more thorough Eurosystem-wide forecasting exercise takes place). We then loosely pencil in hikes in July and September, on the basis that swift action could reduce the need to hike more later. For the Iranian regime, the Strait of Hormuz has become their modern Thermopylae, a constrained passage near their native soil, providing disproportionate leverage with very limited military means. Almost three weeks into the war, the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively blocked by the threats of Iranian attacks on ships that try to pass. Some ships still pass, but they must have negotiated passage with Iran before. This control over the Strait gives Iran also control of about 20% of global oil supply, plus LNG, fertiliser and many other fossil fuel-related products. Hence, even though it is not a 'hemmed in ground' through which a conquering army tries to pass, the Strait of Hormuz provides Iran with the powerful to tool to choke the world of much if its energy supply. Importantly, it can do so with quite limited military capacity. Iran's Revolutionary Guards do not need to attack every ship in the Strait: once they have successfully proven that they can, the mere threat suffices to drive ship insurance premia to levels that make it de facto impossible to make the transit. Similarly, maintaining this threat on regional energy infrastructure or even civilian targets can keep the region destabilised even with limited military capacity. A missile a month, a drone a day may suffice, suggesting that Iran may be able to sustain the conflict for quite a long time. At the time of writing, a de-escalation is no in sight. records.text: Iran is now attempting to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz through mining and missile/drone attacks on vessels in addition to targeting energy infrastructure in the region with easier-to-produce drones. Heightened concerns around both production and shipping capacity have pushed energy prices higher, with Brent averaging $105/bbl in the third week of the war, up from $96/bbl in the second week and $84/bbl in the first. Markets are assigning a higher probability to a sustained risk premium, implying oil prices could remain well above the 2025 average of $66/bbl even after the conflict ends. Confirming this future for Brent price signals that oil will gradually ease towards $84/bbl by YE26 and stay close to $80/bbl throughout 2027. What are our baseline and negative scenarios? In March 2026, both Brent and European natural gas prices were roughly 45% above their 2025 averages. Current market pricing implies an average Brent price of above/around $85/bbl for 2026 (and about $84/bbl by YE26), which we adopt as our baseline scenario. As an alternative, we consider a negative scenario with Brent averaging $100/bbl in 2026 (and remaining at $100/bbl by YE26). The baseline and negative scenarios imply energy prices rises of around 30% and 50% y/y compared to last year. 20 March 2026 64 FICC Research Economics 20 March 2026 Zalina Alborova +44 (0) 20 7773 2274 zalina.alborova@barclays.com Barclays, UK Ercan Erguzel +44 (0) 20 3555 2564 ercan.erguzel@barclays.com Barclays, UK Michael Kafe

records.text: Priming potential does not exist in CLO liabilities, but does in BDCs For leveraged finance investors in the modern era, the case studies of "priming" or "uptiering" transactions are well-known (see LME: Trading through prisoner's dilemmas). For IG investors, this has not been as relevant, outside of a few more contentious LMEs of late. The concept of priming, where another party (often with a new money component) designs a transaction that dilutes existing lenders' claim on collateral, is a risk in any capital structure. If the goal is to compare the structures of CLOs to BDCs, it is a necessary difference to address. When CLO liabilities are structured and priced, the notion of a future priming is precluded. Because of the conditions that govern CLOs, there is a clearly defined payment waterfall mechanism outlining which tranche of investors bear the brunt of losses first, and which tranches of principal are most protected. In the context of BDCs' capital structures, this mechanism is much more complex because of BDCs' use of various forms of secured debt. Unsecured investors expect to be paid before equity investors, but because of unsecured investors' lack of security, as well as the fragmented nature of BDCs' secured debt capital structures, it is important to contemplate the avenues available for priming at a BDC. records.text: inflation over time. The impact plays out slowly but tends to be sticky. Second, the shock might play out as a broader supply disruption, akin to 2021-22. We see rising risks of this outcome, since shipping costs and prices of natural gas, fertilizers, helium, aluminum, etc. are also surging. Core inflation is already uncomfortably high: we and the Fed expect it to come in at 3.0% y/y in February. Another leg up to say 3.2% or higher – which would require core PCE to print at 0.24% m/m or higher over the next three months – could be a step too far for policymakers. But the details will also matter. The Fed might be willing to look through inflation that appears to be driven by tariffs, since it expects those effects to start rolling off by mid-year. As a practical matter it might be challenging to figure out if goods price increases are due to tariffs or the Iran shock. But higher core services inflation would certainly be a concern, particularly since housing and financial services are likely to weigh on core services in coming months. The Fed will also be vigilant about de-anchoring of long-term inflation expectations. They have remained remarkably stable so far, whereas they took a modest leg up after Liberation Day last year (Exhibit 4). But, as in 2022, it might also argue that hikes are needed to preempt an increase in expectations. Therefore, we wouldn’t rule out hikes even if long-term expectations remain stable, as long as spot inflation rises enough.

In their influential work on war duration, Bennet and Stam (1996) showed that when sides pursue maneuver strategies, wars tend to end quickly, as their rapid success or failure becomes clear. Attrition strate- gies rely upon tearing down the opponent; they are less risky and often last longer (think Russia-Ukraine war). Finally, punishment strategies that attempt to inflict substantial costs on the opponent and erode its resolve (think of guerrilla war- fare) tend to result in the longest wars. In the current war in Iran, the distinction between these strategies, which are well suited to describe land wars of the past, is somewhat blurred. The US and Israel approach is arguably closer to maneuver warfare; Iran’s is perhaps closer to attritional. Model predictions differ substantially depending on the strat- egy. We conclude that dealer banks including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, which have large capital market activities and greater reliance on repo and institutional funding, would capture the most benefit if the STWF coefficient used in the GSIB calculation is reduced. Last week, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman previewed a set of regulatory proposals aimed at loosening bank capital rules. These proposals will address two key pillars of regulation: the Basel II Endgame (B3E) and the GSIB surcharge. In this note, we focus on a specific revision to the GSIB surcharge highlighted in Bowman’s speech – realigning the short-term wholesale funding (STWF) component from roughly 30 percent of the surcharge today to 20 percent as originally intended. For background, the international standard for GSIB scoring uses equal 20% weighting across five different risk categories to calculate the final score. US regulators adopted an enhanced “Method 2” approach and replaced the 20% weights with fixed coefficients across different risk indicators, with the coefficients calibrated to give each risk category roughly the same weight. She added that the Council was well-positioned and well-equipped to deal with the major shock that was unfolding. Lagarde indicated that the Council would assess the duration, intensity and propagation of the conflict by looking at all commodity markets, supply bottlenecks, selling price expectations (including the ECB’s corporate telephone survey), demand indicators (such as the PMIs), and wage trackers. records.text: UK Economics and Rates 19 March 2026 Citi Research 2 The Bank of England voted today to hold the policy rate at 3.75%, as widely expected. The tone, however, took a surprisingly hawkish turn. The vote split was 9-0, with the doves all responding to the ongoing energy supply disruption. We think this meeting marks a change in attitude for the BoE from a dovish bias towards a stance that places both higher probability (and risk from) inflation overshooting through the remainder of the year. As such, we adjust our call for the bank rate path to remove all remaining cuts 2026. The MPC’s have used the policy rate decision to send a firm message to markets. T o some extent this was a surprise: The vote split was more hawkish than we expected; some members have pivoted from pushing for cuts to discussing hikes. The intent appears to be a deliberate effort to not push back against the recent shift in market pricing. The effect has been to shift away from the narrative that the bank rate is on a downwards trajectory, at least for now. We think that the communication (and specifically the absence of any dissenters) was designed to shift the ‘median’ stance of the MPC. This is a meaningful move given that even the most dovish members are now accommodating a discussion around hikes. Importantly, there was an unambiguous message that the committee was prepared to hike if it thought it necessary to do so. The value of waiting, indeed, with a twist The ECB kept rates unchanged as widely expected and verbal communication was carefully balanced to put the same emphasis on the growth and the inflation consequences of the ongoing shock – forecasts provided a slightly less neutral spin, though. Overall, for now, the ECB is in wait-and-see mode, “the implications for medium-term inflation depend crucially on the magnitude of indirect and second-round effects of a stronger and more persistent energy shock”. We have heard that many times recently. ECB President Lagarde also insisted on taking decisions meeting-by- meeting, on data dependence, and on no pre-committing. Through the end of this week, despite these headwinds, tax-exempt municipal bonds have largely been resilient. In particular, we find that municipals with maturities of seven years and shorter remain over-valued relative to taxable fixed income products, with muni/UST ratios still down 1–13 percentage points year-to-date. Deficits of the central government and municipalities were up with some decline at the regional government level. For 2026, we expect a notable fiscal expansion, in line with consensus: For 2026, we forecast a deficit expansion of 120bp, in line with the step up in consensus (realised 2025 budgets have not yet been reflected in consensus) but a smaller step up than the Bundesbank's forecast (+140bp) (Exhibit 10 ). In 2027, we expect a deficit increase of 20bp while consensus expects a stable deficit and Bundesbank sees scope for another meaningful expansion (+70bp). Potential fiscal measures to contain the energy price shock would pose further upside risk to our deficit, but, in line with our view at the euro area level, we would think this is more likely to come through if we enter a recessionary environment. Lower growth than expected before March (MSe: 1.0%Y in 2026 vs consensus 1.0%Y, Government 1.0%Y and Bundesbank 0.6%Y) is also a risk for this year's deficit.

20 March 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Bond Market Strategy Macro portfolio update: Persistent shock, bearish bias We argued last week that being long the EUR front end should be hedged with long positions in forward energy contracts given the risk of further escalation in the Middle Eastern conflict. These risks have materialised with further reciprocal attacks on gas infrastructure. We think this materially increases the potential for a more persistent impact on inflation, as reflected in higher forward energy prices and updated inflation forecasts, which now average above 2% in 2027. As we do not have the suggested oil hedge in our rates macro portfolio, we exit the long TKYZ6, which has breached its indicative stop. Generalized Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (GFEVD) While the IRFs give the structural roadmap of how shocks propagate through the system, they cannot tell us how much of an observed movement is attributable to a specific shock versus shared disturbances hitting multiple currencies simultaneously. The generalized, Pesaran–Shin FEVD (GFEVD) resolves this by operating directly on the IRF paths— derived from the estimated VAR—and weighting them using the VAR’ s residual variance–covariance matrix. In practice, the FEVD treats the residuals as the realized shocks and uses their empirical variances and covariances to determine which innovations were genuinely idiosyncratic and which were part of broader common-factor movements. However, it would likely bring Italy back under market scrutiny after several years of being largely off the radar (for more on the consequences of the referendum, see our note Italy: Assessing the Significance of the Upcoming Constitutional Referendum So far, the market has adopted a positive stance on Italy, with all rating agencies revising their credit ratings or outlooks upward. The implementation of the NextGenerationEU (NGEU) fund, the government's prudent fiscal policy, a positive current account, and positive net international investment positions (acting as a buffer against shocks) have been key factors behind this favorable assessment by the market and rating agencies. Looking ahead, however, the situation could become slightly more complicated. The boost from NGEU will diminish, and as we highlighted in our recent Europe Chart of the Week, Italy is vulnerable to energy shocks. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 20 March 2026 Citi Research 12 heavy private credit landscape is distinct from the dot-com era, the high default rates experienced by B3-rated technology companies during the 1999–2003 downturn serve as a relevant, albeit stressful, upper-bound scenario for a potential technology-led credit cycle. The Other Credit Loss Component: Recovery Rates When considering potential credit losses, default rates receive the majority of attention, but recovery rates also play a significant role. Two primary factors have historically mitigated losses in private credit. First, the majority of loans are sponsor-backed, and private equity owners have a strong incentive to provide financial support to their portfolio companies during periods of stress, as evidenced by lower default rates for sponsored deals during the 2008, 2020, and 2023 downturns (Figure 19). Second, private credit managers may intervene early through tighter covenants and steer workout processes that result in more effective capital preservation, providing a crucial structural advantage in a distressed environment. records.text: GEMs Viewpoint | 19 March 2026 17 Appendix: Backtesting Details “Cheapest” or “Richest” Z-Score Selection The selection process is cross-sectional and rules-based. For each EM currency in the IV panel, we compute a 504-trading-day rolling mean and standard deviation of its level of 3-month ATM implied vol. We then convert the latest available level history into a Z-score by de-meaning and standardizing on that 2-year window. To improve robustness and avoid chasing one-day outliers, we sum Z-scores over the past 21 trading days to create a cumulative Z. Names with the most negative cumulative Z are treated as “cheapest”, as they have spent a month trading below their own normalized mean, while names with the most positive cumulative Z are “richest.” On each selection date (monthly or weekly, as dictated by the regime), we take the three most extreme names on the appropriate side and equal-weight the active legs. When Are Signals Observed and Trades Held? The regime itself is computed from daily medium-frequency connectedness, smoothed with a 63-day exponentially-weighted moving average and then sampled at month-ends. Each month-end observation is compared to its trailing 24 end-of-month history to form quintiles; Q1 flags low connectedness, Q5 flags high. For monthly trades, the signal (both regime and Z-selection) is observed on the last trading day of the month; positions are opened on the first business day of the new month and closed on the last trading day of that month.

records.text: ating portfolio (for more detail, see slide 33 of our CLO primer). A related metric is market value OC (MVOC), which measures the asset pool at its market value rather than at par. While MVOC is not officially featured in CLO documentation, the market calculates and utilizes the metric to get a mark to market sense of how loan prices affect deal protection, particularly for junior debt tranches. If loans sell off and the manager wants to sell the portfolio and pay the debt tranches back, there will be less principal to go around. Aside from simple supply/demand dynamics, this is one mechanism through which CLO investors determine fair value for junior tranches of CLO debt. So to estimate the mark-to- market effect of a continued selloff of software loans on CLO tranches, we want to 1) determine the sensitivity of CLO debt spreads to changes in MVOCs; and then 2) determine how much a software sell-off affects MVOCs. CLO tranche spread sensitivities to CLO asset coverage (MVOC) Anecdotally speaking, CLO asset coverage (MVOC) matters the most to junior debt investors (BBs, BBBs), which face the most credit risk (besides equity) from portfolios losing value, leading to a causal relationship between MVOC drops and CLO spread widening. Coupled with an already relatively conservative stance heading into the war (the economy in good shape, demanding little policy support, even as lower inflation opens space for a slight downward adjustment in rates) we think the chances for near-term rate cuts are slim. With uncertainty elevated and the inflation out- look worsening, we expect the BoI to remain in wait-and-see mode at the next few meetings. We have pushed out 50bp of previously expected 75bp of cuts into next year, but continue to see the terminal rate at 3.25% next year. Instead of relying on traditional insurance products with strict guarantees, the government is now focusing on capital markets because of their higher long-term return potential. The system would include a monthly public grant of EUR 10 for children aged 6 to 18, turning them into shareholders in the global economy. n Model calculations demonstrate that the Frühstart-Rente could create a strong foundation for private pension provision, especially in combination with the proposed "Altersvorsorgedepot". The scheme could act as a catalyst for a necessary cultural shift as it systematically opens up stock markets to the broader population that so far invests heavily in bank deposits and insurance contracts. records.text: on March 30 (see Japan Rates Watch: JGB issuance unlikely to increase before autumn 18 March 2026). - Tomonobu Yamashita, Rates strategist FX: BoJ may hike, but depreciation pressure may return Today’s BoJ policy meeting delivered a hawkish impression, hinting at a possible rate hike in April. This triggered a yen-positive reaction, particularly following Governor Ueda’s press conference—very much in line with our expectations (see Liquid Insight: BoJ preview: A quiet pause ahead of the rate hike 17 March 2026). The fact that the BoJ did not strike a more cautious tone despite the escalating situation in Iran strongly suggests that yen weakness remains a key consideration. While the government has stepped up verbal intervention, its effectiveness is questionable amid a backdrop of a strong USD and higher oil prices. Moreover, FX reserves are also the source of funding for U.S. investments, meaning authorities will want to avoid deploying actual reserves unless absolutely necessary. If they were to intervene, they would likely prefer to do so in tandem with a BoJ rate hike to amplify the effect.

In a fluid situation, we stand ready to adjust the call as needed. But our probability-adjusted view is now a prolonged hold. What was the key takeaway today? We, and the consensus, expected a 7:2 vote split, but the MPC was unanimous on rates for the first time since September 2021. Considering the slight difference in emphasis between Governor Bailey's voting paragraph and his comments to the press pool on rate hikes following the decision, we are less certain than normal around our key takeaways. Our view is still that near-term hikes are not the preferred course of action for the median MPC member at this juncture. But the minutes did not push back against this as resolutely as we thought would be the case. On the one hand...: In the minutes, the messaging seems clear: the BoE is on hold, but also ready to hike if needed. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 19 March 2026 11 US vs China AI capex: the landscape so far A key factor in determining how long the investment cycle lasts will be what the future of AI models looks like. When it comes to generative AI, at least, the US and China are the main players. Below we contrast the two global leaders, with the caveat that our comparison is limited by several factors, including a lack of transparency into Chinese data. 1. US is the global leader in AI, but China is catching up fast. The US continues to dominate global AI capex. This investment advantage translates into superior AI capabilities (Exhibit 19). The US’s end‑to‑end strength across advanced semiconductors, frontier AI algorithms, and leading AI applications remains unmatched globally. However, China is rapidly narrowing the gap, though still far behind – e.g. the Stanford Global AI Vibrancy Tool (GVT), which assesses AI-specific sector depth and capability, puts China’s at #2 globally, though its score at 37 is a big gap vs 78.6 for the US. Chinese models have improved significantly, trailing US performance by only a few months (Exhibit 20). Moreover, China leads in AI-related publications and patents, signalling deep research momentum and long-term innovation potential. 2. US firms control more than half of the world’s AI accelerators, and US hyperscalers anchor the world’s most capable cloud infrastructure. On a broader note, even if Israel’s conflicts sometimes had limit- ed impact on growth, they nevertheless had a profound impact on the economy through other channels. For instance, decades of stand-off with Arab countries led to the accumula- tion of large debt in 60s and 70s, culminating in a fiscal crisis. Wars also have large opportunity costs due to conscription, delayed entry into the labor market, and loss of human capi- tal. That said, the IDF has been an integral part of the success of Israel’s tech story. Yet, among all the wars Israel has gone through, we think the last year’s 12-day war with Iran presents the cleanest template to the current conflict. It also makes it clear why the duration of the current war plays a significant role in Israel’s near-term outlook. Missile barrages flying from Iran (and Lebanon) present a significant disruption to the operating environment for most businesses and households. Distance learning, work from home, disrupted logistics and air links, call-up of reserv- ists and outflows of foreign labor, delays in investment proj- ects, etc. — all pile up to generate a significant contraction in activity. Back in June 2025, a twelve-day war was associated with a 4.6%m/m decline in BoI’s index of economic activity (Figure 6) and we estimate that it cut around 0.5%pt off the country’s annual GDP. 90 100 110 120 130 140 17 19 21 23 25 27 Index, 4Q16=100 Figure 6: Israeli GDP

Indeed, the literature is far from settled on the causality (see Killian and Vigfusson (2014) for a discussion), generally finding a negative effect, but one that’s hard to separate from other factors. For example, high oil prices can reflect strong economic growth and high inflation, eliciting a hawkish response from the central bank. That can expose other fragilities, ending in a downturn. For instance in 2008, oil rose above USD200/barrel when measured in 2025 dollars. Yet the shock layered on top of a housing downturn that had started two years earlier, accompanied by tighter credit conditions and the Lehman Brothers collapse in September 2008. Central banks, including the European Central Bank and the Fed, reacted hawkishly to inflation risks (see June 2008 speech from Fed Chair Bernanke), worsening the drag. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 20 March 2026 Citi Research 9 Solution: A Hybrid Approach in Default Forecast T o overcome these previously mentioned challenges in forecasting the default rate, we developed a novel quantitative model. The model synthesizes public market sentiment with private portfolio data, creating a robust framework for forecasting the S&P private credit default rate. Our model is built on two intuitive and independent predictors: 1) Public Market Expectation: S&P BDC Index’s Price-to-NAV (8-Month Lag). Public market sentiment, while volatile, serves as a crucial early warning signal. The aggregate discount or premium to Net Asset Value (NAV) of Business Development Companies (BDCs) encapsulates the market's collective expectation of future credit performance. Our analysis reveals a strong negative correlation: a steeper discount to NAV today precedes a higher default rate in the future. We identified an 8-month lag as the optimal, confirming that market perception is a medium-term leading indicator that anticipates fundamental deterioration before it appears in reported metrics. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 20 March 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS Food for Hawks Just when all eyes are on the war in Iran and its stagflationary implications for the global economy, we had all major central banks meeting this week. As largely expected, the Fed, ECB, BoE, and BoJ all remained on hold. But the focus was on communication, with an across-the-board hawkish shift acknowledging the uncertainty around the implications of the war on the outlook for inflation and growth. Markets took notice, with zero cuts priced in for the remainder of the year following Powell’s hawkish remarks. The starkest repricing, however, happened after the BoE voted unanimously for a hold and released a hawkish statement that opened the door to hikes. ECB communication, in turn, was more balanced, but markets are now pricing more than 50bp of hikes for both the ECB and BoE. The BoJ had hawkish undertones, but pricing did not move very much, likely because hikes were already priced to begin with. The question is whether all this repricing is warranted (Exhibit 1). Markets seem to be pricing mostly an inflation shock. The US dollar is stronger, and rates are up for the most part, but the S&P 500 is just 4% below its peak. In our view, more disruptive scenarios for global growth are underpriced, and growth concerns could prevail, tilting some central banks to look through the shock. For short-term wholesale funding, which has a fixed coefficient of 350, the contribution to the total GSIB score was roughly 28% as of the end of 2025 when averaged across the eight US GSIBs. However, there is also significant variability in how much STWF contributes to each bank’s GSIB score. For Wells Fargo and JPMorgan, the contribution is toward the low end of the range, around 15%. For Bank of New York Mellon and State Street, the contribution is closer to 60%. Additionally, the banks’ sizes and their business models are quite varied, as reflected in their GSIB scores. For example, at the end of 2025, JPMorgan had the highest GSIB score of 1,089, nearly five times larger than the smallest (State Street, 223). Given these dispersions, a revised coefficient to realign the contribution of STWF could have uneven effects across these banks, with some capturing more regulatory relief than others. While the Fed historically has tended to look though energy-driven inflation, investors are doubting this reaction function because most other central banks are now expected to hike rates and investors remember the experience of 2022 where the Fed ended up hiking aggressively after an oil price shock. Further, the issue of the fiscal effect of the war in Iran is still open, and estimates for funding needs have started edging up as high as $200bn, which is nearly two-thirds a percentage point of GDP . Long-end swap spreads at -81bp, nearly 20bp from their wides are already suggesting that there has been a substantial deterioration in the long-term fiscal outlook. The ongoing conflict is now likely meaningfully creating term premium uncertainty. Finally, a lot of investors came into this period structurally short vol, either explicitly or implicitly through carry trades that work best when the policy path is well anchored. But as noted, we are not entirely insensitive to the messaging from the minutes, and we will monitor the subsequent guidance from the core MPC members. For now, we do think a lot more evidence on actual second-round effects emerging is needed before the majority of the MPC entertains hikes. Hence, even in the case of more sustained disruption to oil and gas supply out of the Middle East (i.e. beyond this next month), we would not see policy tightening as plausible in 1H26. By the time summer comes, there ought to be more information on corporate pricing power, some initial assessments of next year's pay settlements, as well as concrete evidence on the resilience of consumer demand. For the avoidance of doubt, we are near-certain inflation expectations will surge next month - the relationship between spot fuel and food prices and near-term inflation expectations is the tightest one in all of UK macro. That said, we also think that - like last year - in an economy with as much slack as the UK, this will not translate to more persistent core inflation. Rates strategy: The market interpreted the meeting as hawkish, as the minutes suggest that risks of tightening have increased, likely by more than investors had been expecting. Baseline projections In the baseline scenario, Brent oil prices and TTF gas prices were assumed to average around $81/bbl in 2026 and €46/MWh, respectively, roughly 30% and 57% above the levels prevailing at the time of the December projections. Under these assumptions, near-term growth was revised lower, with GDP growth averaging 0.9% in 2026 and a cumulative downgrade of around 0.6pp to the quarterly growth path over 2026, driven by downward revisions to private consumption and investment. Over the medium term, however, growth was projected to converge back to its pre-conflict trajectory, picking up slightly above trend, with quarterly growth ranging 0.3-0.4% q/q in 2027-28. On the inflation front, headline inflation was projected to closely follow developments in energy inflation, as well as refining and distribution margins for transport fuels. Headline inflation was seen to average 2.6% in 2026, peaking at 3.1% y/y in Q2. Over the medium term, inflation was projected to return to target in 2027, averaging 2.0% over the year, before edging slightly higher in 2028, reflecting the effect of the ETS2 mechanism. Under the baseline, core inflation was projected to average 2.3% in 2026, 2.2% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, with indirect effects from higher energy prices expected to remain limited. 20 March 2026 3 Barclays | ECB forecast change

Hungary appears much better cushioned in this crisis thanks to high positive real rates to start with (4-5%), macro upside prospects from the 12 April elections, longer-term hedging of energy prices and more secure energy supply, and relatively less risks of local FX outflows vs 2022-23. However, with price caps on fuel (temporary) and gas/electricity (permanent) in place, investors will have the balance these supportive factors with CPI risks after fuel caps expire, and the negative impact of fiscal needs for gas subsidies. The recently-turned-dovish CNB may be able to resist rate hikes altogether, as real rates will likely remain positive even with much higher energy from here. In terms of easing room when energy stabilises, we see Czechia, followed by Hungary (subject to post-elections developments), as the best positioned. The outlook is highly uncertain, but assuming some normalisation in energy prices towards year end, rate cuts considerations could resume from 4Q’25/1Q’26. records.text: After a bullish start to the year, with our Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) shifting n above 1, a combination of concerns about AI disruption, private credit and more recently sharply higher oil prices and the Middle East war has weighed on risk appetite. Expectations of a continued ‘Goldilocks’ backdrop have faded quickly due to the resulting energy price shock and a sharp hawkish repricing of central bank policy paths. This has weighed on multi-asset portfolios with a limited opportunity set for diversification - the risk of a larger 60/40 portfolio drawdown (a ‘Balanced Bear’) has increased. We shifted tactically (3m) more defensive in our asset allocation shortly after the n conflict escalated (OW cash, N equities/bonds/commodities, UW credit). We see continued risks of an equity correction and think the buffer from bonds will remain limited near term. We remain modestly pro-risk in our asset allocation for 12m (OW equities, N bonds/commodities/cash, UW credit) - in case of a larger ‘risk off’ move, e.g. if our Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) drops closer to -2, we would look to add risk, especially for longer investment horizons. Since the start of the Middle East war our World portfolio proxy, tracking roughly n US$300 tn of global assets, has lost c.US$11 tn (c.4%). Very bullish risk appetite is not automatically a bearish signal as positive macro conditions can linger and often take time to moderate - this explains some of the resilience in the past few weeks. This is important because we view June as the earliest meeting at which the Fed can start to hike rates. The “sweet spot” for hikes We still think cuts are more likely than hikes. If the oil shock subsides quickly, the Fed is likely to look through it and reinstate the dovish bias that Powell adamantly disavowed at the March press conference. And if the shock is large enough, the Fed will probably be too concerned about the labor market to hike rates. Moreover, a very large supply shock would likely cause enough demand destruction that upside risks to inflation would start to diminish. Particularly if the shock is accompanied by a sustained selloff in stocks. The resulting negative wealth effects could weigh on higher-income spending growth, which has been an important GDP driver given K-shaped consumer dynamics. In other words, risks to the u-rate are likely to increase non-linearly with the size of the Iran shock. Risks to inflation should rise initially but then fall if the disruption is large enough. Hikes are only feasible when the shock is sustained but moderate, such that concerns about inflation meaningfully outweigh worries about the labor market. records.text: 04 15% Source: J.P. Morgan, S&P Capital IQ Pro And in other policy news… A week ago the White House put out an executive order on mortgage lending. Most of the provisions seem to be focused on removing some of the red tape that built up in the wake of the GFC, particularly through rules promulgated by the CFPB. Originators will certainly welcome the administration revisiting the frictions imposed by regulations like TRID, and there’s potential to remove some cost and inflexibility from the system. But it will take time for new regulations to be written up, vetted, and implemented, and so we don’t expect a significant short-term impact on mortgage valuations from the EO. What might be more notable was what wasn’t in the order—any mention of MIP cuts, g-fee changes, or other significant tweaks to the government-controlled mortgage programs. Some investors we spoke with think that this could be implicit confirmation that a MIP cut isn’t in the works. We’ll admit that, the further we get into the spring selling season without a cut, the less likely it becomes. And, as far as we know, there haven’t been any public men- tions of a MIP cut by the administration (unlike things like the 529 proposal that the presi- dent later shot down). That being said, it’s a demand side subsidy lever that they can pull without Congress and without delay—so it’s hard to entirely cross off the bingo card.

Risk to our call of further easing, door opened to hikes Overall today’s message implies risks to our call of further easing this year, which will depend on persistence and size of the energy shock. Our base case assumes cuts in June and September based on energy prices reversing in next couple of months, but conviction is reducing. If energy prices stay elevated for longer (which current energy future prices suggest), risks of cuts not materializing this year will rise. The BoE also opened the door to hikes. We still think BoE would need to see a larger and more persistent shock to be convinced to hike, given the economy/ labour market is weak, risks of second round effects are less than before, and rates are restrictive. Having said that modest hikes cannot be ruled out after today’s guidance, with the bar somewhat lower than what we thought before this meeting (though still high). It is unclear however if we would have enough evidence by the April meeting that we are in a scenario to warrant a hike. An extended hold/hike may be followed by deeper cuts in 2027. records.text: ative growth drag than Australia, reflecting its heavier reliance on imported fuel and the absence of an energy-export offset, in our view. RBA & RBNZ: Global forces, domestic constraints While markets have priced a similar degree of additional tightening since the oil shock, Australia’s starting point argues for a more inflation-focused RBA response. A tight labour market, sticky underlying inflation, and a positive output gap increase the risk of second-round effects, particularly if inflation expectations lift. The growth cushion from energy exports also limits the downside to activity, leaving the RBA more exposed to upside inflation risks. We expect the RBA will hike 25bps in May to 4.35% with a front-loaded hiking cycle, and while we expect this is likely the peak, persistently sticky inflation could see another hike in August. We expect the RBNZ will remain firmly on hold through 2026 as the energy shock introduces two-sided risks. The RBNZ is likely to look through near-term, oil-driven inflation given its supply-side nature, with a larger negative growth impulse expected to weigh on medium-term inflation. Inflation expectations remain the key risk which could prompt a hike, but spare capacity should help contain pass-through. With financial conditions already tightened, we expect more dovish RBNZ communications than markets price, with added clarity when Governor Breman speaks on 24 March. 0% 20% 40% 60% South Korea Singapore Malaysia Other Australia NZ 0 2 4 6 2010

When shocks propagate swiftly from one currency to the rest of the basket, it tells you market micro-diversification is falling: a given disturbance has a higher chance of being amplified rather than absorbed. In practice, we see that rises and falls in connectedness tend to lead moves in aggregate EMFX vol, so monitoring connectedness gives an earlier warning than watching vol levels alone. As the ‘connectedness’ of the asset class rests on fundamental economic connections (i.e..: shared exposure to global financial and economic conditions), it tends to be more mean-reverting than vol levels alone. As such, lows in connectedness are more likely to reflect levels where positioning and thematic convictions have outstripped economic realities, creating an early-warning trigger for mean-reversion in the asset class.
